meanings.def: a circular net with weights and a draw rope around its edge; used in fishing
meanings.note: An ἀμφίβληστρον had small weights attached to the outer border, and it was normally thrown in such a manner as to encircle fish. In trying to obtain a satisfactory equivalent expression in another language, it is not necessary to try to duplicate all the details of form. What is important is that such a net was thrown rather than being dragged.

meanings.def: to put on clothes, implying the clothing being completely around; see also

meanings.def: pertaining to not being subject to blame and hence morally irreproachable

meanings.def: pertaining to having no defect or blemish
meanings.note: In the overall context is figurative, but the immediate meaning must be regarded as literal.

meanings.def: pertaining to being without fault and hence morally blameless

the father of Josiah
the father of Ματταθίας[a]

For example, to pull something by means of a rope may be entirely different from a term indicating that the object itself has been seized and is being drawn or dragged.

to become able to see, whether for the first time or again
meanings.note: There is nothing in the statement of to indicate whether this is a matter of being able to see for the first time or being able to regain one’s lost sight. It is, however, better to assume that it is a matter of regaining sight unless the context specifies ‘being blind from birth’ or ‘always blind.’

meanings.def: to become able to see, whether for the first time or again

g: to cause to have completely wrong views

meanings.def: to no longer believe what is true, but to start believing what is false
meanings.note: Though in some languages one can preserve the figurative meaning of ‘to wander’ or ‘to go astray’ in connection with truth, it is not possible to do so in many languages, and therefore it may be necessary to spell out in some detail precisely what is involved, for example, ‘to stop believing what is true and to start believing what is false.’

meanings.def: to sail away from a point
to conform to some standard as a means of demonstrating its purpose
meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only, instead of ἀναπληρώσετε, in, ms. P46 (apparatus).

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning employing the base [a] ‘to choke,’ ) to cause the death of plants by other plants crowding them out and/or overshadowing them
to die as the result of drowning
to be in perplexity, with the implication of serious anxiety
to be in perplexity, with the implication of serious anxiety
to throw oneself off from some object (as from a ship)

(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀπορφανίζω ‘to cause to be an orphan,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause someone to be spacially separated, with the implication of additional emotional deprivation
the shape or shade cast by an object which blocks rays of light
meanings.note: In a number of languages a term for ‘shadow’ has a number of very important meanings. In some instances it is regarded as a part of personality which goes on to the next world, since a dead person no longer ‘casts a shadow.’ The shadow may also be regarded as a kind of counterpart of the personality, a type of alter ego. In cases of severe illness one may say ‘his shadow has walked away,’ and in many parts of the world the shadow of a person is an important element in the practice of black magic, for to damage a shadow may be regarded as a means of causing harm to a person.|In one may translate ‘shifting shadow’ as ‘a shadow which constantly changes.’

meanings.def: to pull or draw away from or out of
(figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to pull out, to drag,’ ) to cause a change of belief so as to correspond more with the beliefs of the person or factor causing the change
to draw oneself away from, suggesting that the movement was not sudden
to rise up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands
meanings.note: It is also possible that ἀποστασία differs slightly in meaning from ἐπίστασις[b] by virtue of the differences in prefixal formation, but there is insufficient contextual evidence to support such a view.

meanings.def: a written statement prepared by a husband and given to a wife as evidence of a legal divorce
to take the roof off of a house
meanings.note: In ἀποστεγάζω refers to only a part of the roof, and therefore in a number of languages it may be necessary to translate as ‘they made a hole in the roof.’ In view of the type of houses built in Palestine in NT times, the roof no doubt would have been flat, held up by heavy beams over which were laid planks or sticks and then covered with sun-baked clay.

meanings.def: to cause someone to depart for a particular purpose
to send a message, presumably by someone
(an idiom, literally: to send a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
to take something from someone by means of deception or trickery
to cause someone not to possess something
meanings.note: Though the resulting state of ἀποστερέω[b] may be the mere absence of something, nevertheless the implication is that some activity has taken place to cause a person no longer to possess something. This meaning may then be expressed in some languages as to have something taken away from someone.

meanings.def: to not pay someone for what is owed
the role of one who has been commissioned and sent as a special messenger
meanings.note: See also [a] ().

meanings.def: one who fulfills the role of being a special messenger (generally restricted to the immediate followers of Jesus Christ, but also extended, as in the case of Paul, to other early Christians active in proclaiming the message of the gospel)
meanings.note: The relationship of an apostle to Jesus Christ is sometimes expressed as ‘being Christ’s messenger’ or ‘being a special messenger of Jesus Christ.’ In such a phrase, the term ‘special’ refers to having been commissioned by Jesus Christ for a particular task or role.

meanings.def: (derivative of [b] ‘to send a message,’ ) one who is sent with a message
to question someone with hostile intent
to cause someone to turn away from a previous belief
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in, see. For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in, see.
g: to cause to turn away from
to cause to change one’s belief

meanings.def: to cause someone to depart from correct behavior and thus engage in serious wrongdoing
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in, see.

meanings.def: to cause something to be in a place where it was formerly
to cause something to turn into or to become something else or to become removed from something or someone
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀποστρέφω ‘to cause to turn back from,’ not occurring in the NT) to cease doing something, with the implication of rejection
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in, see.

meanings.def: to no longer continue to believe as one has and hence to turn away from or to reject a previous set of beliefs
to abandon a former relationship or association, or to dissociate (a type of reversal of beginning to associate)
to refuse to provide help to someone
to have a strong dislike for someone or something, implying repulsion and desire for avoidance
a state of having been excommunicated from membership in a synagogue
meanings.note: In rendering it is important to indicate clearly that this is not a matter of an individual merely being forced outside of a synagogue building, but excluded from membership and thus from worship in the synagogue. In some languages this is made explicit by saying ‘his name will be erased from the list of those belonging to the synagogue’ or ‘he will no longer be able to enter a synagogue’ or ‘he will be rejected as a member of the synagogue.’

meanings.def: to employ formalized expressions appropriate to leaving or saying farewell to someone, possibly involving the communication of final arrangements for leaving
to say goodbye and to leave
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to take leave of’ or ‘saying goodbye’ is highly idiomatic, for example, ‘to snap fingers as one leaves,’ ‘to raise one’s hands together,’ ‘to clasp one’s hands before leaving,’ or ‘to bow to one another as one leaves.’

meanings.def: to willingly give up or set aside what one possesses
to bring an activity to a successful finish
meanings.note: It is also possible to translate ἀποτελέω in as ‘am performing,’ but the focus evidently is upon the completion of a series of such healings. The final phrase of, καὶ τῇ τρίτω τελειοῦμαι ‘and on the third day I will be finished,’ points to a possible distinction between ἀποτελέω and τελειόω, in which the first apparently serves to mark the end of a particular series, while the second points to the completion of anything and everything involved.

meanings.def: to put or take something away from its normal location
meanings.note: In the semantic element of ‘out of the way’ is implied in the activity of ‘putting in prison.’
g: to put out of the way

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to put away,’ ) to cease doing what one is accustomed to doing
to shake something out or off, in order to get rid of an object or a substance
meanings.note: In a number of languages quite different terms for shaking will be required for the contexts of and, since in the first instance it is an animate being which clings, and in the second instance it is simply a substance that adheres.|In a number of languages, however, the symbolic meaning of ‘shaking dust off one’s feet’ is not at all clear, so that it may be necessary to add a type of classifier to indicate that such an action symbolizes the breaking off of association. It is for this reason that the expression ἐκτιναξάμενος τὰ ἱμάτια in is often translated as ‘he protested by shaking the dust from his clothes.’

meanings.def: (a technical, legal term) to pay compensation for damages or costs
meanings.note: It is also possible to translate this expression in as ‘I will pay you for any loss which you have had.’

meanings.def: to be particularly bold or daring in what one does
to act harshly toward someone
(derivative of ‘to show harshness,’ ) pertaining to acting or dealing harshly with someone
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of () or ἀποτόμως is a negative expression combined with showing kindness, and therefore one may translate ‘to refuse to show kindness.’ In a number of circumstances, however, the equivalent of or ἀποτόμως is a highly idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to refuse to look at,’ ‘to frown upon,’ or ‘to push aside.’

meanings.def: purposely to avoid association with someone
g: to have nothing to do with

meanings.def: the state of being absent
to carry something away from a point
to lead or take away from a particular point
to become safe from danger by avoiding or escaping
to speak, with focus upon verbal sound rather than upon content
to cause a load to be carried off
the activity of using up something
to move away from, with emphasis upon separation and possible lack of concern for what has been left
to move away from a normal location, with the implication of disappearing
meanings.note: It would be difficult to translate ἀποχωρίζομαι in as meaning literally ‘to go away,’ for this would seem strange in a reference to the sky. If, however, one employs an expression meaning to disappear, it may be necessary to say literally ‘could no longer be seen.’ For another interpretation of ἀποχωρίζομαι in, see.

meanings.def: to separate more or less definitively one from another (evidently somewhat more emphatic in meaning than [a] ‘to separate,’ )
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀποχωρίζομαι in, see ἀποχωρίζομαι[a].

meanings.def: to lose one’s consciousness temporarily
meanings.note: It is possible that ἀποψύχω in refers primarily to a psychological experience rather than a physiological one. Some scholars, however, have interpreted ἀποψύχω in this context as meaning ‘to die.’ For another interpretation of ἀποψύχω in, see ἀποψύχω[b].

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to faint,’ ) to become totally disheartened and thus ready to give up
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀποψύχω in, see [a].

meanings.def: a market town south of Rome
pertaining to not being capable of being approached
meanings.note: It may be necessary to indicate, either in the text or in a marginal note, the reason why the light cannot be approached, for one could interpret this passage to mean that the light was either so small as not to be generally visible or so far away that it could not be reached. If, however, one uses a term for ‘light’ which implies extreme intensity of light, then the context should indicate the basis for its being unapproachable.

meanings.def: pertaining to being blameless in view of not having given offense
meanings.note: In a number of languages the concept of ‘being blameless’ as in and can only be expressed by a verbal expression involving some measure of complaint. For example, the expression in may be rendered as ‘I do my best to live in such a way that neither God nor people can blame me’ or ‘… can complain against me.’

meanings.def: pertaining to not causing offense
pertaining to behaving in an unprejudiced manner
pertaining to not having failed to keep the law (of God)
to cause the process of burning to begin
meanings.note: As already noted in the series of terms listed in, languages differ appreciably in terms employed for different phases and results of burning. For example, to set something on fire for the sake of providing warmth may be expressed by quite a different term from that which is used in speaking of the process of setting something on fire in order to destroy it.

meanings.def: to hold on to an object
to touch, with the implication of relatively firm contact
to cause some relatively light physical, moral, and/or spiritual harm to
a Christian woman, probably the wife of Philemon
to use force in pushing or thrusting someone or something away or aside
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to push away,’ ) to no longer pay attention to previous beliefs
act of destroying or causing the destruction of persons, objects, or institutions
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is difficult to find a general term for ‘destruction.’ What has often happened is the extension of meaning from a more specific type of reference, for example, ‘to smash,’ to a more generic meaning of ‘to destroy,’ and whether one understands the specific or more generic meaning depends largely upon the context. Accordingly, in one may find a figurative usage of a term meaning ‘to smash’ (though understood in a more generic sense), for example, ‘Saul then worked in order to smash the church.’

meanings.def: an action demonstrating complete disregard for the value of something
meanings.note: In the context of the understanding of ἀπώλεια in the literal sense of ‘destruction’ (see ) does not seem to be adequate. The following verse concerning the three hundred denarii would seem to indicate that it was disregard for the value of something rather than destroying the perfume. In fact, the use of the perfume would not have been a matter of destroying. Accordingly, an equivalent of ‘waste’ seems to be far more satisfactory. In some languages the equivalent of this question in is ‘why did she not think about the value of the perfume?’

meanings.def: the content of what is expressed in a curse
meanings.note: It may be difficult or even meaningless to speak of a person’s mouth as being ‘full of bitter curses,’ but one can often say ‘they are constantly cursing harshly’ or ‘… speaking heavy curses’ or ‘… constantly uttering harmful curses.’

meanings.def: a marker of result as an inference from what has preceded (frequently used in questions and in the result clause of conditional sentences)
a marker of the possibility of something being true
a degree of uncertainty
a marker of a negative response to questions, usually implying anxiety or impatience
meanings.note: In order to attempt to do some justice to the occurrence of the particle ἆρα, one may introduce a variety of terms which make a question somewhat more emphatically negative. In the case of one might translate ‘will he indeed find faith?’ In the case of one might translate ‘how, then, could Christ ever be a servant of sin?’

meanings.def: probably a reference to the Sinai Peninsula
a person in the genealogy of Jesus (;, apparatus)
(derivative of ῥάπτω ‘to sew together,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to being without a seam, that is, without being sewn together
meanings.note: In some languages it may be necessary to describe such a seamless robe as ‘his robe was woven as just one piece of cloth.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘Arabia,’ ) a person who is a native of Arabia
(derivative of [a] ‘idle, not working,’ ) to not be functioning
pertaining to not working
pertaining to habitually refusing to work (probably with a more unfavorable connotation than in the case of, )
pertaining to not giving careful consideration to something
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀργός in, see ἀργός[e]. It is also possible that ἀργός in means useless (see ἀργός[d] ).

meanings.def: pertaining to being useless, in the sense of accomplishing nothing
pertaining to showing indifference as to whether something is as it should be
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret ἀργός in as meaning ‘without thought’ (ἀργός[c] ), ‘worthless,’ or even ‘useless’ (ἀργός[d] ).

meanings.def: the metal silver; after gold the next most highly valued metal in the ancient world
meanings.note: As in the case of ‘gold’ (), there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘silver’ in most languages. In, however, there is a problem in speaking of silver and gold that ‘perish,’ or even as something that can be ‘destroyed,’ since in reality one does not destroy such elements, and silver and gold do not really ‘perish.’ On the other hand, silver and gold can become oxidized and lose their value, especially if they are impure (see ). Therefore, it seems far better to emphasize the lack of value in translating. A suitable rendering may then be ‘not with things that can lose their value as silver and gold.’

meanings.def: silver in the form of stamped coins used as money
(an idiom, literally: silver and gold) a generic expression for currency
one who makes objects out of silver (especially jewelry and fine utensils)
the metal silver; after gold the next most highly valued metal in the ancient world
meanings.note: As in the case of ‘gold’ (), there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘silver’ in most languages. In, however, there is a problem in speaking of silver and gold that ‘perish,’ or even as something that can be ‘destroyed,’ since in reality one does not destroy such elements, and silver and gold do not really ‘perish.’ On the other hand, silver and gold can become oxidized and lose their value, especially if they are impure (see ). Therefore, it seems far better to emphasize the lack of value in translating. A suitable rendering may then be ‘not with things that can lose their value as silver and gold.’

meanings.def: silver in the form of stamped coins used as money
(derivative of [a] ‘silver,’ ) pertaining to being made or consisting of silver
(literally: hill of Mars) the location of an Athenian court, traditionally associated with a rocky hill close to the Acropolis, though probably located in the marketplace at the foot of the hill
meanings.note: For another interpretation of Ἄρειος Πάγος in, see [b].

meanings.def: an advisory council of Athens dealing with ethical, cultural, and religious matters
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand τοῦ Αρείου Πάγου as referring to the location rather than to the council (see [a]).|It is probably wise in translating Αρειος Πάγος[b] to simply transliterate the expression, since it has the status of a proper name. On the other hand, it is extremely important that some footnote be employed so as to indicate something of the significance of this advisory council of Athens.

meanings.def: a member of the council of the Areopagus
that which causes someone to be pleased with something
to cause someone to be pleased with someone or something
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to cause someone to be pleased with something’ is expressed as ‘to cause someone to be happy about’ or ‘to cause someone to feel good about.’

meanings.def: pertaining to that which pleases someone
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of ‘this pleased the Jews’ is ‘this caused the Jews to be happy’ or even ‘this caused the Jews to say, That’s fine.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being proper or right, with the implication of desirable
a king of Nabatean Arabia
the quality of moral excellence
meanings.note: It is possible, however, that ἀρετή in denotes the manifestation of (divine) power (see ).

meanings.def: a manifestation of power characterized by excellence
an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
young of sheep (); often used for ritual sacrifice
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between male and female lambs. It is therefore essential in any figurative reference to male persons to employ an appropriate term for lamb. In a number of languages, of course, a lamb is simply referred to as a ‘young sheep’ or ‘child sheep.’|Perhaps the most widespread story about cultural differences in Bible translation is the one which refers to the translation of ‘lamb’ as ‘little seal of God’ in an Eskimo language. However, there is no evidence that this type of rendering was ever used, since in matters of appearance, habitat, and behavior, lambs and little seals have practically nothing in common. Furthermore, Eskimo languages have terms for ‘lamb’ and in some instances, at least, use the expression ‘young, woolly goat,’ since wild goats are well known and wool is well known as an imported product.

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘number,’ ) to employ numbers in determining a quantity
any cardinal number
meanings.note: It may be important to add a marginal note to to indicate that the number 666 was actually derived from adding up the numerical values of the letters of a name.

meanings.def: the sum or total of a numbered quantity
a city in Judea
a companion of Paul
to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
meanings.note: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.

meanings.def: to eat the earlier meal of the day
meanings.note: Some scholars, however, interpret ἀριστάω in as meaning any kind of meal (see [a], ), and therefore one would translate as ‘Jesus said to them, Come have something to eat’ or ‘… have a meal.’|In a number of languages the earlier meal of the day may be spoken of as ‘the morning meal’ or ‘the first meal.’ In some languages it is actually called ‘the leftovers meal,’ but see the discussion on meals at different times of the day at.

meanings.def: pertaining to being to the left of some point of reference
meanings.note: In the phrase ὅπλον ἀριστερόν, literally ‘left-hand weapon,’ refers to a weapon used by the left hand and therefore a defensive weapon, while ὅπλον δεξιόν, literally ‘weapon for the right hand,’ refers to an offensive weapon.|For an interpretation of ἀριστερός as part of an idiom in, see.

The left hand is designated in a number of languages by an idiomatic phrase which normally contrasts with expressions for the right hand. For example, one may often speak of the left hand as ‘the bad hand’ or ‘the weak hand,’ and in some instances as ‘the anus hand,’ since this is the hand used in cleansing the body after defecation. See also.

meanings.def: a person whose family is greeted in the Epistle to the Romans
a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of ἄριστον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of [b], )
meanings.note: Though ἄριστον[a], [a], and [b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

meanings.def: a less important meal, normally in the earlier or middle part of the day
pertaining to what is sufficient for some purpose and accordingly resulting in satisfaction
to be sufficient or adequate for a particular purpose, with the implication of leading to satisfaction
to be happy or content as the result of having what one desires or needs to be
meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘to be content’ is expressed negatively, for example, ‘to not complain.’ In other instances, one may be forced to employ a type of direct or indirect discourse, for example, ‘to acknowledge that it is enough’ or ‘to say, It is all that is needed.’

meanings.def: large wild four-footed mammal with thick fur and doglike face; walks on all fours but may stand up on its back legs to get a better view; may be 2 m. tall when standing up and weigh over 200 kilos; feeds on roots, berries, wild fruit, mice, and lizards, and, occasionally, small livestock; Ursus arctos syriacus; dangerous when provoked or robbed of cubs; associated with violence and danger
meanings.note: The term ἄρκος ‘bear’ occurs in the NT only in as a description of the apocalyptic beast. In languages where a term for bear is not known, it is probably best to borrow a word and describe the referent in a footnote or glossary. In a somewhat descriptive phrase is sometimes employed, for example, ‘with large feet having claws like those of an animal called bear.’ By this means the information about the bear’s feet has been incorporated into the text, but usually it is better to leave such information to a marginal note.

meanings.def: open vehicle with two or four wheels; harnessed to and pulled by horses; used in war or for travelling
meanings.note: In the reference is to war chariots drawn by horses, while in the reference is to a travelling chariot in which the Ethiopian official was riding. In languages which have no technical term for chariot, it is possible to speak of a war chariot as ‘a war carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn cart for fighting.’ A travelling chariot may be described as ‘a travelling carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn vehicle.’ A further description of such chariots may be given in a glossary.

meanings.def: a cryptic place name designating the territory which will be the scene of the final battle of the forces of good and evil
an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
to promise a person for marriage
meanings.note: It may be important to note in the margin of a text that in biblical times the act of betrothal was regarded as binding, so that the breaking of a betrothal was legally equivalent to divorce.

meanings.def: a part of the body which joins two parts together
meanings.note: In the use of ἁρμός the emphasis is not upon the joints as a moving part of the body but as a means by which different parts of the body are effectively joined together. Accordingly, ἁρμός overlaps in meaning with [a] (). For problems in translating, see.

meanings.def: to say that one does not know about or is in any way related to a person or event
meanings.note: In translating ἀρνέομαι[a] and ἀπαρνέομαι[a], one can often use an equivalent phrase such as ‘to say that one does not know’ or ‘to say that one has nothing to do with.’|In denying an event, as in, it may be possible to translate ‘but they all said they knew nothing about it.’ It is also possible to deny having done something, and therefore one may translate the response in as ‘but they all said that they did not do it’ or ‘… that they did not touch him.’

meanings.def: to deny any relationship of association with someone
meanings.note: In a number of languages one may best translate ‘deny’ as ‘to make manifest not to know.’ Accordingly, one may translate the first part of as ‘whoever shows people that he does not know me’ or ‘whoever refuses to admit that he does know me.’ Denial need not involve some verbal formulation, though in some languages this is the most common practice. See also.

meanings.def: to refuse to agree or consent to something
to refuse to give thought to or express concern for
meanings.note: There are a number of problems involved in rendering appropriately ἀρνέομαι[d] and ἀπαρνέομαι[b] as in and.|In a number of languages it simply makes no sense to translate ‘to say No to oneself,’ nor is it possible in many instances to use an expression such as ‘to deny oneself,’ since it almost always implies to deny oneself something. Sometimes the meaning may be expressed in a figurative or idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to refuse to pay attention to what one’s own desires are saying’ or ‘to refuse to think about what one just wants for oneself.’ In certain instances other kinds of idioms may be employed, for example, ‘to put oneself at the end of the line’ or even ‘to say to one’s heart, Keep quiet.’

meanings.def: to refuse to follow someone as a leader
to behave in a way which is untrue to one’s real self, in a sense of denying certain valid aspects of one’s personality
meanings.note: It is possible in some languages to translate ‘he cannot be false to himself’ in as ‘he cannot be different from what he really is’ or ‘he cannot be otherwise than good.’

meanings.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
(derivative of ‘lamb,’ ) young of sheep (); often used for ritual sacrifice; or a sheep of any age
meanings.note: In the one context in the NT, namely,, in which ἀρνίον refers literally to a sheep, it is used in a phrase referring to the horns of an ἀρνίον. In such a context the reference is undoubtedly to a ‘ram,’ that is to say, the adult male of sheep.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘lamb,’ ) a follower of Christ, with the implication of helplessness and dependence
meanings.note: Compare and.
g: a person who is like a lamb

meanings.def: a title for Christ
meanings.note: ἀρνίον[c] as a title of Jesus Christ occurs only in the book of Revelation, but it is used there more than twenty times. In contrast with [b] in βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου ‘feed my lambs’ (; see ), designating people who need care and help, the supplementary components of meaning in ἀρνίον[c] involve the atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross. Some persons have wanted to eliminate the notion of ‘lamb’ in this title, especially in the case of languages in which sheep are looked down on as relatively worthless scavengers (as is the case in certain tropical areas of the world), but in view of the significance of the symbolism of ‘lamb’ in terms of OT sacrificial practices, it is wrong to avoid a term meaning ‘lamb.’ A marginal note, however, may be necessary to explain the significance of this title.

meanings.def: to plow, as a means of preparing land for sowing
meanings.note: In biblical times plows did not turn over the soil but were used simply to break the surface, seldom to a depth of more than about ten inches (or twenty five centimeters).

meanings.def: a flat triangular blade (the “plowshare”) made of hard wood or metal, connected to a handle; used to cut the soil in preparation for the sowing of seed or the planting of seedlings
meanings.note: In most parts of the world at least some type of plow is known, and in ancient Palestine the plow was not a turning plow, but one which simply dug a relatively shallow furrow, but in doing so, loosened the soil. Where plows are not known or used, it is possible to employ a descriptive phrase such as ‘a tool for preparing the ground for sowing.’ For ἄροτρον as part of a Semitic idiom in, see.

meanings.def: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
(derivative of [a] ‘act of plunder,’ ) that which is taken by force or plundered
a state of strong desire to gain things and, if necessary, by violent means
to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
meanings.note: This interpretation of reflects the position of Jesus after the incarnation and the fact that he had no thought of trying to become equal with God because he already possessed all of the qualities of deity. Some traditional translations have rendered the latter part of as ‘did not think it robbery to be equal with God,’ but see.

meanings.def: that which is to be held on to forcibly
meanings.note: Compare the rendering of [a] in. Since ἁρπαγμός may mean not only ‘to grasp something forcefully which one does not have’ () but also ‘to retain by force what one possesses,’ it is possible to translate in two quite different ways. This second interpretation of ἁρπαγμός presumes the position of Jesus prior to the incarnation and hence his willingness to experience the kenosis or ‘emptying’ of his divine prerogatives. In any translation of it is important that both possible renderings be clearly indicated, one in the text and the other in the margin.

meanings.def: to grab or seize by force, with the purpose of removing and/or controlling
meanings.note: In the context as a whole is figurative, but a more or less literal rendering of ‘snatches’ or ‘seizes’ is probably satisfactory.

meanings.def: to attack, with the implication of seizing
meanings.note: It is also possible that in ἁρπάζω is to be understood in the sense of ‘attack’: βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν ‘violent men attack it.’

meanings.def: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
to gain control over by force
meanings.note: Though in ἁρπάζω would appear to be in a literal context in view of the expression ἐκ τῆς χειρός μου ‘out of my hand,’ nevertheless ἁρπάζω is certainly figurative in meaning and so is χείρ ‘hand.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ἁρπάζω[a] ‘to carry off by force,’ ) one who carries off the possessions of another by force
meanings.note: For an interpretation of ἅρπαξ as an adjective in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to being destructively vicious
pertaining to being violently greedy
meanings.note: In ἅρπαξ may also be interpreted as a noun (see ).

meanings.def: the first or initial payment of money or assets, as a guarantee for the completion of a transaction or pledge (in the NT ἀρραβών is used only figuratively in referring to the Holy Spirit as the pledge or guarantee of the blessings promised by God)
pertaining to what cannot or must not be spoken
to be sick or ill, as a state of powerlessness
a male partner in homosexual intercourse
meanings.note: It is possible that ἀρσενοκοίτης in certain contexts refers to the active male partner in homosexual intercourse in contrast with [b], the passive male partner ().

meanings.def: the male of any living creature
(an idiom, literally: male that opens the womb, and closely related in meaning to [a], ‘firstborn,’ ) the first male offspring of a female
meanings.note: A literal translation of the idiom ‘male that opens the womb’ may be extremely misleading in some languages, since it may refer to the first act of sexual intercourse and not to the birth of the first, male child.

meanings.def: a friend of Paul
a Greek goddess worshiped especially in Asia Minor
a cloth attached above a boat in such a way as to catch the wind and thus propel the boat through the water
meanings.note: In (the only occurrence of ἀρτέμων in the NT) the reference may be to the foresail, that is, a relatively small sail toward the prow of the ship. A sail may be described in some languages as ‘a piece of cloth to make the ship move’ or ‘cloth on the ship to catch the wind.’

meanings.def: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself
a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event (in a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items)
(an idiom, literally: the present hour) an emphatic reference to a point of time which is simultaneous with another point of time
pertaining to having been born recently
meanings.note: ‘Newly born babies’ may be rendered as ‘babies who have just been born’ or ‘babies who have just begun to live.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being qualified to perform some function
a relatively small and generally round loaf of bread (considerably smaller than present-day typical loaves of bread and thus more like rolls or buns)
any kind of food or nourishment
meanings.note: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: bread of the placing forth) bread which was set out as an offering in the presence of God in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple
meanings.note: In some languages ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως is rendered as ‘bread placed before God’ or ‘bread placed in the presence of God.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
meanings.note: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’. No doubt the reference in is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to eat one’s own bread) to earn a living by one’s own efforts
to add condiments to food
meanings.note: In rendering it may be necessary to translate ἀρτυθήσεται as ‘to cause it to taste like salt again’ or ‘to cause it to taste right again.’

meanings.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a chief or highly important angel
meanings.note: An archangel may be described as ‘one who commands other angels’ or ‘a leading angel’ or ‘a chief angel.’

meanings.def: pertaining to having existed for a long time in the past, with the possible implication of such existence from the beginning of an event or state
the son of Herod I
initiation of an action, process, or state of being
meanings.note: It would also be possible to treat ἀρχή in as indicating sequence (Domain 61), so that the contents of verse 1 could be regarded as a type of title for the following section. It seems far better, however, to regard ἀρχή in as being closely related to what immediately follows in verse 2, so that one may translate ‘the good news about Jesus Christ the Son of God began as the prophet Isaiah had written …’

meanings.def: a point of time at the beginning of a duration
one who or that which constitutes an initial cause
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand ἀρχή in as meaning ‘ruler’ (see ).

meanings.def: the sphere of one’s authority or rule

(title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
meanings.note: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.|In some instances a measure of meaning may be obtained by somewhat paraphrastic expressions. meanings.def: elementary and preliminary aspects defining the nature of something
meanings.note: Compare also the occurrence of ἀρχή[g] in in which it serves to reinforce the meaning of στοιχεῖα (see ).

meanings.def: the corner of a two-dimensional object, such as a sheet of cloth
one who causes something to begin
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀρχηγός in, see ἀρχηγός[b].

meanings.def: a person who as originator or founder of a movement continues as the leader
meanings.note: In order to indicate clearly the significance of ἀρχηγός in, it may be important to employ a translation such as ‘who established a way of salvation and leads people to it.’ But it is also possible to understand ἀρχηγός in as meaning only the ‘initiator’ or ‘founder’ (see [a] ).

meanings.def: (derivative of [b] ‘high priest,’ ) pertaining to the high priest
a principal priest, in view of belonging to one of the high-priestly families
meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘chief priests’ are referred to simply as ‘big priests’ or ‘important priests.’

meanings.def: the principal member among the chief priests
the head shepherd who directs the activities of other shepherds (in its only NT occurrence; a figurative reference to Christ)
a Christian in Colossae
one who is the head of and who directs the affairs of a synagogue
one who is a master or expert builder
chief tax collector, in the sense of one who controlled activities of certain other tax collectors
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand ἀρχιτελώνης as meaning a principal or important tax collector rather than one who controlled the activities of other tax collectors.

meanings.def: the head servant in charge of all those who served at meals or feasts

meanings.def: a point of time at the beginning of a duration

meanings.note: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. meanings.def: (a title, literally: ruler of the Jews) a member of the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews
an aromatic resin of a lily-like plant, often used for embalming a corpse
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of ἄρωμα is ‘sweet-smelling herbs’ or ‘good-smelling leaves’ or ‘perfumed oil.’

meanings.def: an alternative form of, (, apparatus)

meanings.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to a fire that cannot be put out
meanings.note: It may be necessary in some languages to render ‘unquenchable’ by an active equivalent, for example, ‘a fire that no one can put out.’

meanings.def: to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice

meanings.def: to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice

behavior completely lacking in moral restraint, usually with the implication of sexual licentiousness

meanings.def: pertaining to being obscure or insignificant, with the possible implication of lacking in noble descent
meanings.note: In a number of languages, however, it would be important to avoid the double negative in (despite the effectiveness of the litotes in Greek) by translating ‘a citizen of an important city.’

meanings.def: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
a state of incapacity to do or experience something
meanings.note: A literal rendering of this expression in may not be meaningful, and in fact can be quite misleading. δύναμις is best interpreted as ‘God’s power’ and ἀσθένεια as the weakness which Paul experienced. Therefore, one may be able to translate as ‘my power is greatest when you are weak’ (see Today’s English Version).

meanings.def: the state of being ill and thus incapacitated in some manner
meanings.note: It may be extremely difficult in some languages to speak of ‘taking illness’ or ‘carrying away diseases.’ A strictly literal rendering of such an expression might suggest immediately that Jesus was a type of medicine man who healed others by taking upon himself precisely the same kinds of diseases (a widespread shamanistic practice). It may therefore be necessary in some languages to translate as ‘he caused us to no longer have illness and disease.’ In this way, one may avoid a specific type of shamanistic practice which would be inappropriate in this context.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘weakness,’ ) a state of timidity resulting from a lack of confidence
to be in a state of incapacity or weakness
meanings.note: In some languages it may be better to translate this expression in as ‘welcome those who have only a little faith.’

meanings.def: to be sick and, as a result, in a state of weakness and incapacity
(derivative of [a] ‘to be weak,’ ) an instance of weakness or limited capacity
meanings.note: In some languages it may be appropriate to translate τὰ ἀσθενήματα as ‘times when they are weak.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘weakness,’ ) pertaining to a state of limited capacity to do or be something
pertaining to being morally weak and hence incapable of doing good
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand ἀσθενής in as a helpless condition rather than moral weakness (see ἀσθενής[d] ).

meanings.def: pertaining to being ill and, as a result, weak and incapacitated
pertaining to a state of helplessness in view of circumstances
meanings.note: The meaning of ‘helpless’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘when we could not do anything about it.’ For another interpretation of ἀσθενής in, see ἀσθενής[b].

meanings.def: pertaining to being physically weak
meanings.note: Such a literal translation of this expression in, however, may be misleading, for in general τῷ γυναικείῳ is interpreted as a reference to one’s wife. Therefore, one may translate as ‘treating with respect one’s wife as the physically weaker partner’ or ‘… as of the weaker sex.’

meanings.def: the Roman province of Asia, primarily the western part of present-day Turkey
(derivative of ‘Asia,’ ) a person who is a native of Asia
a high-ranking official in Asia Minor (in an area which is now Turkey)
a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite
a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite
to engage in some activity, with both continuity and effort
a bag made of skin or leather; used for temporarily storing and carrying wine
meanings.note: A number of translators have attempted to substitute ‘bottles’ for ‘wineskins,’ but this has not been satisfactory, since fermenting wine does not normally break glass bottles, while it would break old wineskins. In circumstances in which the use of wineskins is not known, it may be necessary to employ some type of descriptive phrase (for example, ‘a container made of skin’ or ‘a closed bag of skin’ or ‘a goat skin like a bottle’) and a fuller explanation in the margin.

meanings.def: pertaining to experiencing happiness, implying ready and willing acceptance
pertaining to not being wise
to employ certain set phrases as a part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
meanings.note: It is possible that in some contexts ἀσπάζομαι[a] could be interpreted as ‘to visit,’ so that in one may render ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν as ‘visiting the church’ rather than as ‘greeting the church.’

meanings.def: to be happy about something, on the basis that it would prove particularly welcome (thus implying a type of future orientation)
meanings.note: In order to render the future implications of ἀσπάζομαι in, one may be able to translate ‘and looked forward with happiness to what was going to happen.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in, see ἀσπάζομαι[c].

meanings.def: to welcome something or someone, with focus upon the initial greeting
meanings.note: In some languages, however, it may be difficult to speak of ‘welcoming promises,’ but one can often render this relationship as ‘they were happy to know about what had been promised.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in, see ἀσπάζομαι[b].

certain set phrases that are part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
pertaining to having no spot or stain
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘spotless, without stain,’ ) pertaining to being without that which might mar one’s moral character
kind of poisonous snake; associated with lurking danger
meanings.note: The terms ἀσπίς and ἔχιδνα[a] may be used to refer to almost any kind of poisonous snake, and since at least some type of poisonous snake occurs in practically all parts of the world, there is usually little difficulty involved in finding an appropriate term. One can, however, always employ a descriptive expression, for example, ‘a snake whose bite causes death.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being unwilling to be reconciled to others
g: unwilling to be at peace with others

meanings.def: an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
a Roman copper coin worth 1/16 of a denarius
meanings.note: See.

a city of Mysia
to be without a permanent residence and thus engaged in travelling from one place to another

g: to wander from place to place
to be constantly going from place to place

meanings.note: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in, see [a].

a star or a planet
meanings.note: Since in godless people are likened to ‘wandering stars’ or ‘planets,’ it may be best to introduce this expression by a simile, for example, ‘they are like wandering stars.’ In some languages there is a serious difficulty involved in translating ἀστὴρ πλανήτης as ‘planet,’ since the planets or their courses through the heavens are regarded as beneficial. In the focal meaning is upon the heretical nature of these godless persons who do not keep on the right course. It may therefore be necessary to translate ἀστέρες πλανῆται in as ‘stars that do not stay where they should stay’ or ‘… do not remain in their right places.’ See also.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: morning star) a planet which is conspicuous in the morning sky (usually either Venus or Mars)
meanings.note: In the singular pronoun αὐτῷ refers to any and all of the persons in Thyatira, and therefore it is usually best rendered as plural. A literal rendering of may be confusing, since it would suggest that God would be handing over the morning star to persons in Thyatira. A more satisfactory rendering may be ‘I will cause the morning star to shine upon them’ or possibly ‘I will bring light into their hearts.’
g: bright star in the morning sky

to go astray as the result of departing from the truth
the flash of lightning
meanings.note: Terms referring to thunder and lightning often have important taboo connotations. The specific terms for thunder and lightning may be avoided and figurative expressions employed in their place in order to avoid danger which might occur from being struck by lightning or frightened by a thunderstorm. One can, therefore, expect in some languages a number of different terms, and it is important to avoid expressions which might have wrong connotations.

meanings.def: shafts or beams of light radiating from a source
meanings.note: It is often better to render ἀστραπή[b] as a type of qualifying adverb, for example, brightly.

meanings.def: to give off or to reflect a very bright light
a star or a planet
meanings.note: In selecting a term for ‘star,’ it is important to avoid an expression which may relate to only one set of stars, that is to say, a particular constellation, since there may be connotations associated with such a constellation which can radically alter the intent of a particular passage. Some constellations, for example, may be regarded as kindly disposed toward mankind, while others may be regarded as hostile.

meanings.def: a group of stars
meanings.note: Normally a constellation may be described as ‘a group of stars’ or ‘a family of stars’ or ‘stars that travel together’ or even ‘stars that live together.’ It is possible, however, to interpret the occurrence of ἄστρον in as being a reference to a particular planet (namely, Saturn) rather than a constellation.

It is, of course, this latter meaning which is involved in the use of ἀσύνετος in these contexts.

meanings.def: pertaining to not being bound or not regarding oneself as bound by any covenant or agreement
meanings.note: It is also possible to translate ἀσύνθετος in as ‘they feel no obligation to keep their agreements’ or ‘they do not feel bound to do what they have promised to do.’

meanings.def: a state of safety and security, implying a complete lack of danger
meanings.note: In some languages safety or security is expressed in a negative way, for example, ‘without any danger’ or ‘without anything that might possibly harm.’

meanings.def: a state of certainty with regard to a belief

meanings.def: to act in defiance of social and moral standards, with resulting disgrace, embarrassment, and shame
meanings.note: Behavior involving disgrace, embarrassment, and shame is often expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bury one’s face,’ ‘to hide one’s eyes,’ or ‘to feel stabbed by people’s eyes.’ Since shame is seemingly a universal type of feeling, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory equivalent.

meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘to live recklessly’ is ‘to live without thinking’ or ‘to live without being concerned.’

meanings.note: In rendering ‘his commandments are not burdensome,’ it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘it is not difficult to do what he has commanded.’

the action of ruling as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
meanings.note: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

meanings.def: an area or district ruled by a king
meanings.note: Since in many areas of the world kingship is not known (that is to say, the succession of rulers within a family and by inheritance), it may not be possible to find a technical term meaning ‘kingdom.’ Usually, however, one may employ an expression which is roughly equivalent in meaning to ‘domain,’ so that, for example, the last part of may be rendered as ‘up to a half of the region which I rule.’

meanings.def: pertaining to a king

to rule as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin

An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

meanings.note: In a number of languages, however, it may be impossible to personify death as being capable of ‘reigning’ or ‘ruling.’ Sometimes the equivalent meaning may be expressed as ‘from the time of Adam to that of Moses there was no way for people to escape death’ or ‘… to die was certain’ ().

meanings.def: pertaining to a king
meanings.note: The expression ‘his royal robes’ may be rendered as ‘his clothing which he had as king,’ and the phrase ‘the royal priesthood’ may be rendered as ‘priests who are like kings.’

Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.
g: to be prepared to suffer even unto death

meanings.def: a Hebrew liquid measure of between eight and nine gallons or approximately thirty-five liters
meanings.note: Because of the possible symbolic numerical values used in the Parable of the Dishonest Steward, it is important to retain the numerals, while making some adjustment in the case of the term βάτος. Accordingly, one may speak of ‘one hundred barrels of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred containers of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred large jars of olive oil.’

meanings.def: tailless amphibian with a squat body, moist smooth skin, and long hind legs for jumping; about 70 mm long; brown or olive-green; develops from tadpole; Rana esculenta (Edible frog) or Rana punctata (Spotted frog)
meanings.note: In this only reference to frogs in the NT, the connotation is of something unclean and abhorrent. In a number of societies, however, frogs are regarded as very valuable and worthwhile animals, since they are often an important source of food. On the other hand, in such areas there are usually certain types of frogs or toads which are particularly poisonous and whose names, therefore, do carry bad connotations.

However, it seems more likely that βόσκω in should be understood as an instance of figurative usage, and as such it may also be interpreted as βόσκω[b] ‘to take care of,’.

meanings.def: eating by animals

In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

meanings.def: to cause rain to fall
meanings.note: In a number of languages one cannot say literally ‘to send rain,’ for this would seem to imply that someone was carrying the rain to some destination. It may be more appropriate, therefore, to speak of ‘causing rain to fall’ or ‘causing rain to come down.’ It may be necessary, however, in some languages to indicate whether the occurrence of rain is for the detriment or the benefit of persons involved, and therefore it may be necessary to say in some instances ‘to cause rain to come down upon for the benefit of’; otherwise the reader might infer that the rain was some kind of punishment.

meanings.def: to make something wet or moist

It may be important, however, to suggest the significance of this symbolic action, namely, ‘gnashing their teeth in suffering’ or ‘to of suffer so much as to gnash the teeth.’ As in the case of, it is important to avoid an expression for ‘gnashing the teeth’ which will suggest ‘gritting the teeth’ in the sense of determination or courageous resistance.

meanings.def: the grinding or the gnashing of the teeth, whether involuntary as in the case of certain illnesses, or as an expression of an emotion such as anger or of pain and suffering

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to grind one’s teeth) to express and manifest intense anger
meanings.note: As noted in, it is possible to understand the expression βρύχω τοὺς ὀδόντας in both a literal as well as a figurative sense. The persons may very well have ‘ground their teeth’ as a sign of their anger and fury, so that a statement about what such persons did could be true in a literal as well as in a figurative sense.

meanings.def: to cause a forceful and abundant supply of a liquid
meanings.note: This flow from a spring may be referred to in some languages as ‘to cause to come out’ or ‘to cause to flow out.’

meanings.def: any kind of food or nourishment
meanings.note: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

Note, for example, in English the use of China Sea, North Sea, Bering Sea, in contrast with Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.|γεννάω also occurs together with ἐξ αἱμάτων () and ἐκ τῆς σαρκός () in reference to physical birth.
