meanings.def: the one supreme supernatural being as creator and sustainer of the universe
meanings.note: The componential features of θεός involve a basic, underlying ambivalence. On the one hand, θεός is regarded as unique to the exclusion of all other gods: οὐδεὶς θεὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ‘there is no God but one’. This is strictly a monotheistic view of θεός. On the other hand, there occur such expressions as εἴπερ εἰσὶν λεγόμενοι θεοί ‘even if there are so-called gods’ (), and in the OT the Lord is described as being ‘far above all gods’ (), ‘the God of gods’ (), and the ‘great King above all gods’ (), which is essentially a henotheistic view of θεός. Fundamentally, however, the NT view may be most succinctly reflected in, τοῖς φύσει μὴ οὖσιν θεοῖς ‘those who by nature are not really gods.’ In other words, the gods of the pagans (see ) are not to be viewed in the same category as θεός[a].|A further semantic problem is involved in the use of θεός[a] in reference to Christ. In, the ‘the Word was God,’ the meaning of θεός may be described on the basis that all the componential features of θεός[a] are applied to the referent λόγος, which is in turn identified with ‘Christ.’ This is not to be interpreted as indicating that the two referents are identical (which was, of course, the position of those who maintained the so-called patropassian heresy), but that the distinctive features of θεός[a] are also fully applicable to another referent, namely, the λόγος or Christ; that is to say, it is legitimate to interpret as ‘the Word was God’ but not as ‘God was the Word.’|Translational equivalents of ‘God’ are of three major types: (1) proper names, (2) descriptive titles, and (3) borrowed terms. There are a number of problems involved in each of these types of translational equivalents.|If translators wish to employ in the biblical text a proper name in the receptor language, it is essential that the characteristics of the referent of such a name be sufficiently close to those which characterize the biblical God, so that the message may not be unduly distorted. In fact, the equivalent should be sufficiently close that ready identification can be made. The essential features of such a receptor language term should include (1) benevolent disposition and behavior, (2) creative and sustaining activity in the world, and (3) supreme power. In most instances it has not been found necessary for such a term to refer to a strictly monotheistic view (that is to say, having an existence which precludes the existence of any other gods), but it is essential that the name apply to a referent who is regarded as supreme over all others.|There may, however, be a number of difficulties involved in the use of an indigenous expression for θεός[a], since the views concerning such a god may involve such factors as (1) psychological distance (the idea that such a god, though all powerful, is still very remote from mankind) and (2) the necessity for constant propitiation (as though such a god needs to be constantly entreated or sustained by means of gifts in order to make him favorably disposed toward mankind).|In some instances problems have arisen in the use of an indigenous term for God because such a name may be perfectly appropriate in one area in which a language is spoken, but have quite a different meaning or value in another part of the language area. For example, in one area of East Africa the name for ‘God’ in one tribe is the name for the devil in a nearby, closely related tribe.|Descriptive titles for God (which often become essentially names) may focus upon a number of different features or characteristics. In some instances such descriptive titles are traditional for certain receptor languages. In other instances they have been constructed by translators on the basis of indigenous models. The following are illustrative examples of various types of descriptive titles: ‘he who made us,’ ‘the supreme powerful one,’ ‘the one who performs miracles,’ ‘the owner of all,’ ‘he who is sufficient,’ ‘our great father,’ ‘the highest one,’ ‘the great spirit,’ ‘the unending spirit,’ ‘the commanding spirit,’ ‘the great chief,’ ‘the self-existing one,’ and ‘the truly sacred one.’|Some Bible translators have attempted to avoid semantic complications by borrowing a term from a dominant language. In Latin America, for example, many early missionaries borrowed the Spanish term Dios, but in explaining the meaning of Dios as the great and all-powerful creator, they simply provided another name for what people already understood to be the sun. The difficulty with borrowed proper names is that they are essentially zero in meaning, that is to say, they are words with a significant absence of meaning which must be filled in one way or another, and this is usually done merely by equating the meaning of such a zero term with already existing concepts. Hence, rather than avoiding wrong views of God, borrowed terms often perpetuate wrong views indirectly.|There may also be additional complications in the use of a borrowed term, since it may not provide a basis for certain syntactic or morphological modifications. For example, some missionaries have borrowed the term Allah for ‘God,’ but in speaking of ‘gods’ they have attempted to add a plural to the underlying form Allah. In most instances this procedure has resulted in something which is not only conceptually and grammatically impossible, but also highly offensive to receptors.|One special problem involving θεός[a] results from the occurrence of ‘God’ in expressions of possession, for example, ‘my God’ or ‘our God.’ In a number of languages one simply cannot say ‘my God,’ for one cannot ‘possess God.’ Rather, one must say ‘the God whom I worship’ or ‘the God in whom I trust.’ Similarly, it may be impossible to speak of ‘the God of Abraham’ without implying that such a God would only be an idol, that is to say, ‘the God that Abraham personally possessed.’ Under such circumstances it may be necessary to translate ‘the God of Abraham’ as ‘the God in whom Abraham trusted.’|Ideally, one should employ a well known receptor-language term for ‘God’ which would be applicable not only to the one supreme being, but could also refer to the ‘gods of the heathen,’ that is to say, a rendering of θεός[a] should be a generic expression which could be made particular and even exclusive by some such qualifier as ‘the’ or ‘the one’ or ‘the unique.’ Sometimes this can only be done by a qualifier such as ‘the great’ or even ‘the supreme.’

meanings.def: any one of many different supernatural beings regarded as having authority or control over some aspect of the universe or human activity
meanings.note: Some translators have made a practice of trying to render the meaning of θεός[b] by terms which mean essentially demons or evil spirits, but this is a mistake, for though the gods of the ancient pagans may be regarded as having had no existence at all, nevertheless, the NT does not speak of them as being evil.|In those languages in which there is no contrast between ‘gods’ and ‘spirits,’ that is to say, in instances in which people believe only in indwelling spirits rather than in supernatural beings who have control over natural phenomena, it may be possible to distinguish ‘gods’ by speaking of them as ‘powerful spirits.’ In certain instances, therefore, the equivalent of ‘God’ () is ‘the all-powerful Spirit.’

meanings.def: a female deity
meanings.note: In some languages it may seem quite strange to attribute female sex to a divine being. However, one can almost always say ‘a woman god’ or ‘a spirit like a woman’ or ‘a spirit thought of as being like a woman.’

meanings.def: (a title applied to Jesus, literally: son of God, parallel in semantic structure to phrases consisting of υἱός followed by the genitive of class or kind; compare ) one who has the essential characteristics and nature of God
meanings.note: Before adopting a translation of υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ such as ‘Son of God,’ one must always investigate the extent to which such an expression might already be used in a particular language. For example, in the Tarahumara language of Mexico mankind is divided into two classes: (1) ‘sons of God,’ who are Tarahumaras and (2) ‘sons of the devil,’ all other people. In these circumstances it is necessary in translating υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ to use an expression which will identify ‘the unique Son of God’ or ‘the one who is truly the Son of God.’

meanings.def: appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs
meanings.note: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

meanings.def: pertaining to hatred for God
meanings.note: It is possible, though unlikely, that θεοστυγής in could be interpreted as ‘those whom God hates.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘God,’ ) the nature or state of being God
meanings.note: The expression ‘divine nature’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘just what God is like’ or ‘how God is’ or ‘what God is.’ In ‘deity’ may sometimes be expressed as ‘the fact that he is God’ or ‘… is truly God.’|In ‘to share in the very being of God,’ one may speak of ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to become in a measure like God.’ It is important, of course, to avoid the implication that people can become completely God.

meanings.def: an important Christian to whom the books of Luke and Acts were dedicated
causing someone to recover health, often with the implication of having taken care of such a person
the group of servants working in a particular household
to cause someone to recover health, often with the implication of having taken care of such a person
to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
meanings.note: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [b] ‘to serve,’ ) a person who renders service
meanings.note: In rendering θεράπων, ὑπηρέτης, and διάκονος[a] in the sense of ‘servant,’ it is important to avoid a term which would be too specific, for example, ‘one who serves meals’ or ‘one who works around the house.’ It may, in fact, be necessary to use an expression which means essentially ‘helper.’

meanings.def: to cut ripe grain and to gather bundles of such grain together
act of cutting ripe grain and gathering bundles of such grain together
that which is harvested
(derivative of ‘to harvest,’ ) a person who gathers in a crop
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no specific term for ‘reapers,’ and therefore it may be necessary in to say ‘… I will say to those who are working in the fields’ or ‘… who are cutting down the grain.’

meanings.def: to cause oneself to become warm
meanings.note: In some languages a literal meaning of ‘to warm oneself’ would mean ‘to increase in anger,’ and therefore it may be necessary in a case such as to say simply ‘when she saw Peter there near the fire.’

meanings.def: a state of a relatively high degree of heat
the warmest period of the year and primarily the season for the growth of vegetation
meanings.note: In some areas of the Tropics, there are difficulties involved in arriving at a satisfactory term for θέρος. It may not be possible, for example, to use ‘the warm season,’ since that may refer to the end of a dry season just before the rains begin. Normally, therefore, one can equate θέρος with ‘the rainy season,’ but a context such as may be difficult, for one would not normally say ‘when you see that the trees are putting out leaves, you know that the rainy season is near,’ for trees normally do not put out the leaves until after the rainy season has begun. It may, therefore, be necessary to render as ‘when you see the trees putting out leaves, you know that the time for growth is near’ or ‘… the time for trees to produce fruit.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘Thessalonica,’ ) a person who lives in or is a native of Thessalonica
a city of Macedonia
a Jewish insurrectionist
to observe something with continuity and attention, often with the implication that what is observed is something unusual
to come to understand as the result of perception
to experience an event or state, normally in negative expressions indicating what one will not experience
(derivative of [a] ‘to observe,’ ) an unusual object or event which is observed

a case or bag about the size and shape of a sword, used to cover and to carry the sword; made of leather, cloth, metal, or even wood; attached to a strap or belt that could be hung over the shoulder or tied around the waist
meanings.note: In this one occurrence of θήκη in the NT, the reference is to a ‘sheath’ for a sword, which may be rendered in some languages as ‘a leather bag for a sword’ or ‘a covering for a sword’ or ‘something in which a sword is carried.’

meanings.def: the activity of a baby feeding at the breast
meanings.note: In a number of languages there are highly specific terms for the manner in which babies nurse, including ‘to suck upon’ or ‘to pull at the breasts.’ There may also be distinctions in terminology depending upon whether the child in question is a helpless infant held in the arms or a small child capable of moving about. See also discussion at.

meanings.def: to cause a baby to feed at the breast
meanings.note: In many languages entirely distinct terms are employed for the causative and noncausative meanings of ‘to nurse.’ Still additional distinctions may be employed depending upon the age of the child. One term may be used in speaking of helpless infants, while another may be used of small children who are able to walk around, but who still are nursed from time to time.

meanings.def: the female of any living creature
a device used for trapping, especially of animals other than birds
(figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘trap,’ ) an instrument or means for gaining control, implying an element of surprise
meanings.note: In a number of languages, it is possible to reflect something of the figurative meaning of θήρα by translating this term as a verb, for example, ‘may they be caught and trapped at their feasts’ or ‘may their feasts snare and trap them’ (see ).

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of term meaning literally ‘to hunt,’ ‘to trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to acquire information about an error or fault, with the purpose of causing harm or trouble
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is possible to retain the figurative meaning of ‘trap’ or ‘catch,’ but in a number of instances other figures are used, for example, ‘to cause to trip,’ ‘to cause to fall,’ ‘to hear wrong words from his mouth,’ or ‘to use his words against him.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θηριομαχέω ‘to be forced to fight with wild animals,’ not occurring in the NT) to be in conflict with forceful opposition
meanings.note: Some persons have assumed that θηριομαχέω in is to be understood in a literal sense, but this is very unlikely. One can, however, preserve something of the figurative force of this expression by rendering this question in as “if I have, as it were, fought ‘wild beasts’ here in Ephesus simply from human motives, what have I gained?” (TEV). By making a metaphor into a simile one can preserve something of the figurative value of the phrase, while at the same time not introducing possible misunderstanding.
g: to be in a serious struggle with

meanings.def: any living creature, not including man
any four-footed animal, either wild or domesticated
meanings.note: A high percentage of languages appear to have no generic term to identify all kinds of quadrupeds whether wild or domesticated. Rather, they tend to make quite clear distinctions between wild and domesticated animals, and therefore it may be necessary to indicate both types in those contexts where the reference is to both wild as well as domesticated animals. For example, one may sometimes speak of ‘animals of the grass and animals of the forest’ or ‘animals of the barn and animals of the mountains.’|In the reference is primarily to wild animals, since for the most part wild animals would be those designated as unclean. However, swine were also regarded as unclean, and they were domesticated.|In ff two visionary creatures are referred to by the term θηρίον ‘beast.’ Despite their strange symbolic appearance, they would no doubt be included within the potential range of reference of θηρίον[b].

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [b] ‘(wild) animal,’ ) a bad person, in the sense of being both harmful and dangerous
meanings.note: The translation of θηρίον[c] as merely ‘wild animal’ may be seriously misunderstood in some languages, since speaking of a person as ‘a wild animal’ might be a compliment based upon the idea of strength and courage. It may, therefore, be necessary to use some such expression as ‘dangerous animal’ or ‘harmful wild animal.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [c] ‘treasure,’ ) to keep safe that which is of great value
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to treasure up,’ ) to cause something of a more extensive nature to happen in the future
g: to cause to happen more intensely or more extensively

meanings.def: a room for the storage of valuables
meanings.note: ταμεῖον[b] and θησαυρός[a] may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In θησαυρός[a] is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

meanings.def: a box in which money was kept
meanings.note: A ‘treasure box’ may be referred to as ‘a box with valuable objects’ or ‘a box with objects costing a great deal of money.’

meanings.def: that which is of exceptional value and kept safe
to come in contact with
meanings.note: It is also possible in that θιγγάνω is to be understood in the sense of ‘to kill’ (see ).

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to touch,’ ) to cause the death of someone, perhaps suggesting some supernatural or mysterious means
to crowd in hard against
to cause someone to suffer trouble or hardship
to suffer hardship
trouble involving direct suffering
meanings.note: For a number of languages ‘trouble and suffering’ may be expressed as ‘that which causes pain.’

meanings.def: the process of dying
meanings.note: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.

meanings.def: pertaining to being liable to death (that which will eventually die)
meanings.note: The phrase ‘mortal bodies’ () may be rendered as ‘bodies which will die.’

meanings.def: to be emotionally upset by a concern or anxiety
meanings.note: In the meanings of () and θορυβάζομαι reinforce each other.

meanings.def: to cause people to riot against
to be emotionally upset by a concern or anxiety
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret θορυβέομαι in as referring to the evident commotion caused by the fall of Eutychus from a window. Accordingly, one may translate as ‘stop this commotion; he is still alive.’

meanings.def: noise or clamor marked by confusion
meanings.note: In some languages it may be legitimate to translate θόρυβος in as ‘so much noise from so many people shouting’ or ‘because so many people were shouting different things.’

meanings.def: disorderly behavior of people in violent opposition to authority
to cause serious trouble to, with the implication of dire consequences and probably a weakened state
domesticated four-footed animals, primarily livestock
meanings.note: τὰ θρέμματα in would include cattle (bulls, cows, oxen), sheep, goats, donkeys, and possibly camels. It is difficult, however, to obtain in certain languages an expression which is sufficiently generic as to include all such domesticated animals. Sometimes, however, one can use a phrase such as ‘animals that people take care of’ or ‘animals that are herded’ or even ‘animals that are owned.’

meanings.def: to weep or cry, especially in mourning for the dead
meanings.note: For another interpretation of θρηνέω in, see.|Mourning and wailing for the dead are frequently expressed by a term very different from expressions employed in referring to events not involving death.

meanings.def: to sing or chant expressions of mourning
to wail and lament for the dead, implying a ritualized form of mourning at funerals
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: a song expressing grief and mourning
meanings.note: This meaning is only found as a variant reading: θρῆνος καὶ κλαυθμός ‘a song of grief and wailing’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs
meanings.note: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θριαμβεύω ‘to lead prisoners of war in a victory procession,’ not occurring in the NT) to demonstrate one’s successful conquest of opposition
meanings.note: Since the leading of prisoners of war in a victory procession is at the present time a relatively rare cultural phenomenon, it may be impossible to employ such a literal rendering of θριαμβεύω. One may, however, wish to employ a marginal note to indicate the background meaning of θριαμβεύω in this context.

meanings.def: to cause someone to completely triumph over
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of triumphing without indicating the goal of such an event, but in there is no specified object over which triumph occurs. It is possible to introduce Satan as the one over whom the believer is victorious (see ). However, it is also possible to understand θριαμβεύω in as being essentially similar in meaning to [a] () and thus to translate as ‘for in union with Christ we are always led by God as prisoners in Christ’s victorious procession.’

meanings.def: hair, either of a person or of an animal
meanings.note: In a number of languages important distinctions are made between the hair of animals and the hair of humans. Further distinctions may also be made between the hair of the head, the hair of the beard, and general body hair. In certain instances special terms are also used for pubic hair.

meanings.def: to be in a state of fear associated with surprise
meanings.note: For the reference of διὰ πνεύματος in, see commentaries.

meanings.def: a small amount of blood in coagulated form
a relatively large and elaborate seat upon which a ruler sits on official occasions
meanings.note: In some languages ‘throne’ is rendered as ‘the seat of judging’ or ‘the seat of decision-making for a ruler.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘throne,’ ) a ruling power, with the implication of royal status
meanings.note: Most scholars understand θρόνος in as meaning a supernatural power, whether angelic or demonic (see ), but it is possible that θρόνοι in means human rulers.

meanings.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
meanings.note: See also,, and.

meanings.def: position of power and authority to rule
meanings.note: There are serious complications in attempting to translate θρόνος in literally as ‘throne,’ since this might refer specifically to the seat on which David earlier sat. It may in fact be necessary to translate this expression in as ‘the Lord God will cause him to rule in the way in which his ancestor David ruled.’

meanings.def: the place from which authority or rule is exercised
meanings.note: In the phrase τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος is clearly a reference to God, and therefore in a number of languages it may be necessary to translate ‘let us therefore with boldness approach God, who shows grace.’

meanings.def: to break into a number of relatively small pieces
meanings.note: This word is only found as a variant reading: τοῦτό μού ἐστιν τὸ σῶμα τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν θρυπτόμενον ‘this is my body which is broken into pieces for you’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: a city in Lydia
immediate female offspring
meanings.note: A literal rendering of, namely, ‘whoever loves his son or daughter more than me,’ may be misleading, since in some languages it could refer to only one particular son or daughter. A more indefinite expression may therefore be preferable, namely, ‘any one of his sons or daughters.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘daughter,’ ) a woman for whom there is some affectionate concern
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate θυγάτηρ[b] literally as ‘daughter,’ since this would imply that Jesus was acknowledging that the woman was in fact his own daughter. An obvious adjustment must be made in such instances, and therefore one may use such expressions as lady or my dear woman.

meanings.def: (an extended meaning of [a] ‘daughter,’ ) a nonimmediate female descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations)
meanings.note: See discussion at [c] and its footnote.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘daughter,’ ) a female inhabitant of a place
(an idiom, literally: daughter of Zion) the inhabitants of Jerusalem
(a diminutive derivative of [a] daughter,, with possible emphasis upon young age and probable implication of affection)
meanings.note: In the text indicates specifically that the daughter was twelve years of age, and it may very well be that in (the only other passage in which θυγάτριον occurs in the NT) the daughter may have been of approximately the same age. In languages in which some indication of relative age is obligatory, one could employ a term identifying a girl about the age of puberty.

meanings.def: sudden and violent gusts of winds, often from varied directions
meanings.note: In a number of languages a strong wind which causes the waves or a storm on water must be referred to by a special term. Compare, for example, the English term squall; this would mean a wind of relatively short duration but sufficiently intense so as to create relatively high waves.

meanings.def: pertaining to being made or consisting of citron wood (that is, from a citron tree, a coniferous tree related to cypresses, pines, and cedars; up to 9 m high; scaly leaves, reddish brown bark, sweet-smelling wood)
meanings.note: The citron tree belongs to the citrus family of plants, and it produces a pale yellow fruit somewhat larger than a lemon, the rind of which is often candied. In, however, the focus is upon the fine quality of the wood, and since citron trees are not known in many parts of the world, it may be useful to translate πᾶν ξύλον θύϊνον simply as ‘all kinds of valuable wood.’

meanings.def: any aromatic substance (usually a resin) burned for its pleasing aroma
meanings.note: Since some form of incense is almost universal, there is normally no difficulty involved in finding some term to designate ‘incense.’ However, it is always possible to employ a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘a substance which gives off a sweet-smelling smoke’ or ‘… a good-smelling smoke.’

meanings.def: to burn aromatic substances as an offering to God
a relatively small altar used for burning incense; made of wood
meanings.note: θυμιατήριον may be rendered in some languages as ‘place where incense is burned in worship of God.’ One must avoid a rendering which would imply that the altar was made of incense.

meanings.def: to burn aromatic substances as an offering to God
to be extremely angry, with the implication of violence
meanings.note: For another interpretation of θυμομαχέω in, see.

meanings.def: to engage in an angry quarrel with someone
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: a state of intense anger, with the implication of passionate outbursts
meanings.note: In a number of contexts θυμός[a] is combined with [a] () in such a manner that the meaning of one simply heightens the intensity or significance of the other, as in, τοῖς δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πειθομένοις δὲ τῇ ἀδικίᾳὀργὴ καὶ θυμός ‘and to those who out of jealousy reject the truth and adhere to evil, there will be fury and anger.’ But in a number of languages it is necessary to specify who experiences such anger or fury, and therefore it may be necessary to translate ‘God will be furious and angry against them.’ The fury and anger of God is generally interpreted in terms of ‘divine retribution and punishment.’

meanings.def: an intense, passionate desire of an overwhelming and possibly destructive character
(derivative of [a] ‘anger,’ ) to be extremely angry, even to the point of being in a rage
meanings.note: In some instances it may be possible to speak of ‘being extremely angry’ as ‘to be so angry as not to be able to think.’

meanings.def: the door to a house or building (often occurring in plural form and designating double doors or gates)
the entranceway into a building or structure
meanings.note: In θύρα[b] is used figuratively to refer to Jesus as the means of access to salvation: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα δἰ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθω σωθήσεται ‘I am the door; whoever comes in by me will be saved.’ In the emphasis is upon the door as a passageway and not as an object closing off an entrance. Literal translations of ‘I am the door’ may often lead to misinterpretation, since the term used for ‘door’ is likely to refer to a literal door rather than to the entranceway, thus suggesting that Jesus Christ functions primarily to prevent passage rather than making entrance possible.

meanings.def: a point of time subsequent to another point of time and indicating imminence, that is to say, the subsequent event is regarded as almost begun
a long, oblong shield; used to protect the entire body in battle; made of wood, metal, leather stretched over wood, or plaited strips of wood or reeds
meanings.note: In some languages ‘shield’ is described as ‘protection one carries when one fights’ or ‘protection carried to prevent blows from the enemy.’ The phrase ἀναλαβόντες τὸν θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως may thus be rendered as ‘take hold of faith as a protection against the enemy’ or ‘regard your faith as a protection to prevent the attacks of the enemy.’

meanings.def: an opening in a wall for the entrance of light and air and for the purpose of seeing in or out
one who guards the door giving access to a house or building
that which is offered as a sacrifice

any type of altar or object where gifts may be placed and ritual observances carried out in honor of supernatural beings (in the NT θυσιαστήριον is employed to refer to a number of different types of altars; including the altar for burnt offerings in the Temple; the altar of incense; the altar which Abraham built; and the heavenly altar mentioned in the book of Revelation)
meanings.note: A descriptive equivalent of ‘altar’ occurs in some languages as ‘a place where offerings are made to God’ or ‘a place where gifts are given to God.’ In some contexts it may be necessary to add phrases such as ‘where sacrifices are burned to God’ or ‘where incense is burned to honor God.’

meanings.def: to slaughter an animal in a ritual manner as a sacrifice to deity
to slaughter, either animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
one of the twelve apostles; see also
a piece of armor covering the chest to protect it against blows and arrows
the portion of the upper trunk covered by the breastplate
meanings.note: Note, however, that in it is possible to understand the first occurrence of in the sense of ‘breastplate,’ the meaning which it normally has in other biblical contexts (for example, and ). The passage could then be translated as ‘their breastplates were iron breastplates’ (see ).

meanings.def: a synagogue official
the patriarch Jacob, a son of Isaac
the father of [b] in the genealogy of Jesus
one of the twelve apostles and the son of Zebedee and brother of John
a brother of Jesus
the son of Alphaeus and one of the twelve apostles
meanings.note: Some scholars consider Ἰάκωβος[c] and [d] to be the same person.

meanings.def: the son of [d] and called ‘the younger’ in
meanings.note: Some scholars consider [c] and Ἰάκωβος[d] to be the same person.

meanings.def: the father of Judas, one of the twelve apostles
a tax collector called ‘James’ rather than ‘Levi’ (, apparatus)
(derivative of [a] ‘to cause to be well again, to heal,’ ) the capacity to cause someone to become healed or cured
meanings.note: In some languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘giving the power to heal.’ A more natural form of expression is ‘cause to be able to heal.’

meanings.def: an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jannes opposed Moses before Pharaoh
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jambres opposed Moses before Pharaoh
to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
meanings.note: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to heal,’ ) to cause something to change to an earlier, correct, or appropriate state
the father of Enoch in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
meanings.note: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

meanings.def: jasper; probably green in color (see )
the host of Paul and Silas in Thessalonica
a person who sends greetings in
one who causes someone to be healed
pertaining to being the exclusive property of someone
pertaining to that which is peculiar or distinctive to some entity
a reference to each one individually
persons who in some sense belong to a so-called reference person
(an idiom, literally: according to that which is private) pertaining to what occurs in a private context or setting, in the sense of not being made known publicly
a person who has not acquired systemic information or expertise in some field of knowledge or activity
meanings.note: In ἰδιώτης is used to refer to a class of persons who were neither unbelievers nor fully instructed Christians, but who were inquirers or catechumens. In such a context, ἰδιώτης may be rendered as ‘ordinary, uninitiated’ (ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς ἐν πνεύματι, ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμήν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ ‘when you give thanks to God in spirit only, how can an ordinary, uninitiated person taking part in the meeting say “Amen” to your prayer of thanksgiving’).

meanings.def: a mountainous region south of Judea (Edom of the OT)
the watery fluid excreted through the pores of the skin
King Ahabs notorious queen
a city in Phrygia
the role of being a priest
the role of being a priest
to serve as a priest in the performance of religious rites and duties
meanings.note: In contrast with the prophet who speaks to people on behalf of God, the priest is often defined as one who represents the people before God. In reality, however, the priest is one who is primarily engaged in religious ritual and ceremony in contrast with the prophet, whose primary activity is involved in proclaiming a message. In societies in which there is no organized priesthood and where there are only medicine men or shamans, it has often been possible to translate ἱερουργέω and ἱερατεύω as simply ‘to be God’s shaman.’ Whether such an expression can be used depends very largely upon the connotations associated with shamanism.

Since leprosy was regarded as a defilement and hence made a person ritually unacceptable, it also meant excommunication from normal social life. The removal of leprosy was regarded as an important religious matter, and the healing had to be verified by the priests before an individual was regarded as ritually cleansed. In a number of languages, however, it is quite impossible to speak of ‘cleansing a leper,’ for this would mean only ‘giving a bath to a leper.’ Accordingly, it may be essential to say ‘to heal a leper’ or ‘to cure a leper’ or even ‘to make a person’s leprosy disappear.’ In such instances it is usually essential to have some kind of marginal note or glossary explanation so as to indicate the religious implications of leprosy and the resulting ritual defilement.

meanings.note: Because of the variety and complexity of the components involved in reconciliation, it is often necessary to use an entire phrase in order to communicate satisfactorily the meanings of the terms in this subdomain. In some languages, however, reconciliation is often spoken of in idiomatic terms, for example, ‘to cause to become friends again,’ ‘to cause to snap fingers again’ (a symbol of friendly interpersonal relations in many parts of Africa), ‘to cause to be one again,’ or ‘to take away the separation.’ A particularly crucial element in terms for reconciliation is the assigning of responsibility for original guilt in causing the estrangement. Some terms, for example, imply that the individual who initiates reconciliation is by doing so admitting his guilt in causing the estrangement. This, of course, provides a completely untenable meaning for reconciliation in speaking of God reconciling people to himself through Christ.|In a number of languages the contextual basis for an expression for reconciliation is often found in terms relating to the reconciliation of husbands and wives. If pertains merely to Theophilus ‘being told’ something, then one might assume that Theophilus was not a Christian, in which case he may have been a government official to whom the joint publications (the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles) would have been directed as a defense of Christianity. On the other hand, if one understands κατηχέω in the sense of ‘to be taught’ or ‘to be instructed,’ then one would assume that Theophilus was a Christian who had been instructed in the faith. The relationship of Theophilus to the message would then determine in a number of contexts the difference between ‘we’ inclusive and ‘we’ exclusive.

Perhaps this should be understood in the sense of ‘many are invited to apply, but few are selected.’ In this context, of course, both the invitation and the selection would be by God.

meanings.def: a dome-like structure made of clay, in which wood and dried grass were burned, and then after being heated, was used for baking bread
meanings.note: The function of κλίβανος may be described as ‘a place heated for baking bread,’ and it may be useful in some instances to employ a more extensive description of a κλίβανος in a glossary, but this is rarely necessary since function is far more important than form.

meanings.def: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration
meanings.note: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.
g: district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)

meanings.def: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
meanings.note: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

meanings.def: any piece of furniture employed for reclining or lying on
meanings.note: In a rendering such as ‘stretcher’ or ‘cot’ is certainly more advisable than the traditional rendering ‘bed,’ which might imply a large piece of furniture. In each passage one must employ a term which is most likely to identify the type of object which fits the context.

meanings.def: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
meanings.note: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

meanings.def: to cause something to incline
meanings.note: See also.

meanings.def: to cause to flee or run away from
to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
meanings.note: For another interpretation of κλίνω in, see.

meanings.def: to begin to come to an end, with particular reference to the period of a day (a figurative meaning dependent upon the position of the sun)
meanings.note: For another interpretation of κλίνω in, see.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to incline the face to the ground) to prostrate oneself before someone as an act of reverence, fear, or supplication
(an idiom, literally: to lay down the head) to experience the rest which comes from sleep
meanings.note: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνω ‘the Son of Man has no place to lie down to rest’, implies that Jesus possessed no permanent home. In this same expression must be understood not as an idiom but as a case of literally bowing the head (see ).

meanings.def: a group of persons engaged in eating together
meanings.note: Note that Luke employs κλισίας in essentially the same type of context in which Mark uses συμπόσια.

meanings.def: to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else
a moving ridge or succession of swells on the surface of a body of water
to be tossed back and forth by the motion of waves
meanings.note: The imagery in is based upon a person in a boat being tossed about by the waves. It may, therefore, be necessary to introduce a boat or ship in the context.
g: to be tossed about by waves

meanings.def: the husband of Μαρία 5, one of the women at the crucifixion
(an idiom, literally: to itch with respect to hearing) to have one’s ears tickled by what is heard
g: to desire to hear what one wants to hear

meanings.def: a peninsula on the southwest coast of Asia Minor
a Roman copper coin worth 1/4 of an assarion () or 1/64 of a denarius ()
meanings.note: See.

meanings.def: the entire digestive apparatus, including stomach and intestines
the uterus
(figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘belly,’ ) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling
meanings.note: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between [b], κοιλία[c], and, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

meanings.def: desire for gratification of the body
meanings.note: It is also possible that κοιλία in refers to Jewish dietary laws and regulations.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
meanings.note: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

meanings.def: the state of being asleep
meanings.note: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to sleep,’ ) to sleep, as a euphemistic expression for the state of being dead
meanings.note: Some translators have attempted to preserve the figure of speech in [b] and κοιμάομαι[b] by translating ‘to sleep’ rather than ‘to have died’ or ‘to be dead.’ Such a practice, however, has resulted in misunderstanding in a number of instances and has sometimes led to the doctrine of so-called ‘soul-sleep.’

meanings.def: the state of being asleep
meanings.note: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’|In κοίμησις is combined with apparently to stress the fact that the sleep was an ordinary or natural sleep.

meanings.def: pertaining to sharing with someone else in a possession or a relationship implying mutual interest
meanings.note: Since the emphasis in is upon the fact that Paul and Titus have the same faith, one may also translate as ‘… the faith that you and I have’ or ‘… the faith we both believe in.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being ritually unacceptable, either as the result of defilement or because of the very nature of the object itself (for example, ritually unacceptable animals)
meanings.note: It is possible that there is some subtle distinction in meaning, particularly on a connotative level, between κοινός[b] and ἀκάθαρτος in, but it is difficult to determine the precise differences of meaning on the basis of existing contexts. The two terms are probably used in primarily for the sake of emphasis.

meanings.def: pertaining to being of little value, in view of being ordinary and common
pertaining to being in common between two or more persons
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand κοινός in as [a] ‘shared, mutual’ (see ).

meanings.def: to cause something to become unclean, profane, or ritually unacceptable
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to translate literally the concept of unclean, for physical cleanliness and ritual acceptability are completely unrelated. In some languages it is necessary to translate κοινόω[a] or βεβηλόω as to take away its holiness or to make something unacceptable to God. In many cultures one must express this concept as involving so-called negative taboo.

meanings.def: to call or to regard something as common or defiled
to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
to join with others in some activity
(an idiom, literally: to share blood and flesh) to have the characteristics and nature of a human being
an association involving close mutual relations and involvement
to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
(derivative of [a] ‘to share,’ ) that which is readily shared
(derivative of [a] ‘to share,’ ) pertaining to willing and ready sharing
one who participates with another in some enterprise or matter of joint concern
a piece of furniture used for sleeping
meanings.note: It is not necessary to understand to mean that the children were in the same bed with the man, but it is, of course, possible that the reference here is to a relatively humble house in which all the members of the family would sleep on a single raised platform. See also.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘bed,’ ) to have sexual relations
meanings.note: In some languages one may speak of ‘sexual life’ as ‘the way one lives with one’s wife’ or ‘how one treats one’s wife.’

meanings.def: to engage in immoral sexual excess
(an idiom, literally: to have bed, though in combination with ἔχω, κοίτη early acquired the metonymic meaning of sexual relations) to be in a state of pregnancy
meanings.note: This expression contrasts with the meaning of [b],, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.

meanings.def: a room in a house for sleeping
meanings.note: It would be wrong to render the expression ‘who was in charge of the king’s bedroom’ in as meaning simply one who kept the bedroom clean. A person such as Blastus would have been a highly respected person with considerable responsibility for the king’s living quarters and personal affairs. The expression may be adequately rendered in by speaking of Blastus as ‘a high official.’

meanings.def: a dye obtained from egg-clusters of a cochineal, collected from the leaves of Quercus coccifera
meanings.note: In ‘scarlet robe’ may have implied high military rank.

meanings.def: a reddish-purple cloth dyed with a substance obtained from the murex shellfish; expensive to produce; associated with wealth and royalty
the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
meanings.note: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, [a], ), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

meanings.def: to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
meanings.note: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

meanings.def: praise as a means of gratifying someone’s vanity
to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
meanings.note: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

meanings.def: to strike or beat with the fist, either once or repeatedly
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to beat with the fist,’ ) to cause injury or weakness or possibly a circumstantial difficulty
meanings.note: Though differences of interpretation exist concerning the meaning of ‘a thorn in my flesh’ (), especially since some scholars have felt that this must refer to some kind of physical disability, it seems more likely to assume that it refers to some special personal circumstance such as the opposition Paul encountered in preaching the gospel, a reference suggested by (see also ).|Without some clear understanding of the reference of ‘a thorn in my flesh,’ it is difficult to determine precisely how κολαφίζω is to be interpreted in.

meanings.def: to begin an association with someone, whether temporary or permanent
meanings.note: Though the Greek text of says literally ‘join this carriage,’ in reality, of course, the association is not directly with the carriage, but with the man riding in the carriage. It is therefore necessary in a number of languages to translate κολλήθητι τῷ ἅρματι τούτῳ as ‘join the man riding in this carriage.’

meanings.def: to stick or cling to something
(an idiom, literally: to cling to heaven) to increase enormously the number of something, with the implication of reaching the attention of God
an ointment for the eyes
meanings.note: κολλούριον may often be rendered simply as ‘a medicine for the eyes.’

meanings.def: one who exchanges currency, either in terms of different types of currency or different values of the same currency
to cause something to be reduced in number or extent
meanings.note: There may be difficulties involved in a strictly literal rendering of ‘those days will be shortened,’ for it might appear that each day would become shorter rather than that the number of days would be decreased. Therefore, one must render this expression in in a number of languages as ‘those days will be fewer.’

meanings.def: a city in Phrygia in Asia Minor
the region of the body extending from the breast to the legs, especially when a person is in a seated position
meanings.note: The term κόλπος occurs in several idiomatic phrases in the NT. For example, the expression ‘who was in the bosom of the Father’ in denotes an association of intimacy and affection (see ). In a context referring to the position of a person at a meal (as in ), κόλπος indicates an honored place (see ). In κόλπος Ἀβραάμ signifies the heavenly abode (see ).

meanings.def: the fold of a garment forming a type of pocket or container
a part of the sea which is partially enclosed by land
meanings.note: A ‘bay’ may be described as ‘a protected area of the sea’ or ‘a part of the sea protected by land.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: Abraham’s bosom) the heavenly abode, with the implication of close interpersonal relations
meanings.note: A literal rendering of κόλπος Ἀβραάμ as ‘the bosom of Abraham’ or ‘the lap of Abraham’ is often misleading. In some languages it may even suggest homosexuality, and in other cases it implies that Lazarus was either a baby or was changed into a baby in heaven. Since κόλπος Ἀβραάμ is generally interpreted as a reference to the eschatological heavenly feast, one may be justified in rendering as in TEV ‘the poor man died and was carried by the angels to sit beside Abraham at the feast in heaven.’ In some languages κόλπος Ἀβραάμ in this context is translated as ‘he was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side’ or ‘… to be with Abraham.’

meanings.def: movement through water by the use of limbs
meanings.note: A number of languages have several different terms for ‘swim’ depending on whether it is a person, an animal, a fish, or an eel (or a snake). Care must be exercised in choosing the appropriate term for this context.

meanings.def: a relatively large construction for collecting water
meanings.note: The term κολυμβήθρα occurs in the NT only in, and refers to a pool having five porches, one on each of four sides and another porch which went across the middle of the pool

meanings.def: a city or town with special privileges in that the inhabitants of such a town were regarded as Roman citizens (such towns were originally colonized by citizens of Rome)
meanings.note: A translational equivalent of ‘colony’ is frequently a phrase, for example, ‘a city where people were Romans’ or ‘a city of people who regarded Rome as their hometown.’

meanings.def: to wear long hair as part of one’s attire
meanings.note: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate κομάω as ‘to let one’s hair grow long’ or ‘not to cut one’s hair.’

meanings.def: hair of the head of human beings
to carry or bring something to someone, usually implying a transfer
to cause someone to experience something on the basis of what that person has already done
g: to cause to experience in return
to cause to experience in proportion to

meanings.def: to receive as a type of compensation
to receive back something which one has previously possessed or its equivalent
the state of being in better health after a previous state of relative lack of health
to apply whitewash to a surface
meanings.note: For many languages the closest equivalent of the phrase ‘whitewashed tombs’ is simply ‘tombs that have been painted white.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: whitewashed wall) one who pretends to be one thing, while in reality he is something quite different
dust, soil (see also )
meanings.note: ‘Shake the dust from your feet’ may be expressed as ‘kick the dust from your feet.’ In some instances, however, the more appropriate equivalent would be ‘get rid of the dust from your feet’ or even ‘remove the dust from your feet and leave it there.’

meanings.def: to cease, in reference to some type of movement
meanings.note: Languages may differ considerably in expressions relating to the ceasing of wind, for example, ‘the wind died,’ ‘the wind stood still,’ ‘the wind refused to move,’ or ‘the wind could not be felt.’

meanings.def: beating the breast and lamenting as an expression of sorrow
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

meanings.def: a violent and extensive slaughter, especially associated with armed conflicts
to engage in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble
to be tired or weary, as the result of hard or difficult endeavor
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret κοπιάω in as [a] ‘to work hard’ (see ).

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [b] ‘to be tired,’ ) to become emotionally fatigued and discouraged
act of engaging in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble
a state characterized by troubling circumstances
(derivative of ‘manure,’ ) a pile or heap of manure
fecal matter used as agricultural fertilizer
to cut, by means of a sharp-edged instrument (for example, knife, sword, or ax)
meanings.note: In a number of languages important distinctions are made for various types of cutting. For example, terms referring to the cutting of flesh may be different from those involving wood or stone. Similarly, important distinctions may be made as to whether there is simply an incision by cutting or whether a particular object is cut in two or cut off.

meanings.def: to beat the breast and lament as an expression of sorrow
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

meanings.def: large black bird with thick strong beak, and fairly short legs; highly intelligent; Corvus family; crows and ravens belong to the same family of birds but differ in size, ravens being somewhat larger and being more inclined to feed on dead bodies
meanings.note: In some languages one must be especially sensitive to connotations relating to terms for ‘crow’ or ‘raven,’ since these birds may be either particularly disliked or may be regarded as symbols of death and sickness. If such is the case, it may be preferable to simply use a more generic term for birds.

meanings.def: (a diminutive derivative of κόρη ‘girl,’ not occurring in the NT, but seemingly having lost the diminutive feature of meaning) a girl about the age of puberty
meanings.note: In κοράσιον is equated in meaning with the Aramaic term ταλιθα (see ), and in this girl is identified as being twelve years of age. Compare also ἠνέχθη ἡ κεφαλὴ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πίνακι καὶ ἐδόθη τῷ κορασίῳ ‘his head was brought in on a plate and given to the girl’ (). It is impossible to determine the age of Herodias’ daughter, but in view of her role as an attractive dancer, she was probably of the age of puberty.

meanings.def: (a borrowing from Hebrew) that which has been set aside as a gift to be given later to God, but which is still at the disposal of the owner
meanings.note: In some languages it is important to translate ‘corban’ as ‘what I have promised to later give to God.’

meanings.def: a room in the Temple used as a treasury
the leader of a rebellion against Moses
to be happy or content with what one has, with the implication of its being abundant
meanings.note: Note that in this statement in there is evidently a significant element of irony, and it is for that reason that some translations employ a question, for example, ‘do you already have everything you need?’ For another interpretation of κορέννυμι in, see.

meanings.def: to have enough, often with the implication of even more than enough
meanings.note: This first statement in is probably to be understood ironically, and therefore it may be readily translated as a question, for example, ‘do you already have everything you need?’ or as a statement referring to what the people of Corinth evidently presumed, for example, ‘you think you already have all you need.’ For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘Corinth,’ ) a person who lives in or is a native of Corinth
a city in Greece
a Roman centurion to whom Peter ministered
a Hebrew dry measure for grain, flour, etc., of between ten and twelve bushels or about 390 liters
to cause something to be beautiful by decorating
pertaining to the earth
(derivative of [c] ‘world system,’ ) pertaining to the system or standards of the world
meanings.note: In τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας may also be rendered as ‘the desires which people in this world have,’ but in this context the term ἐπιθυμίας should imply wrong desires.

meanings.def: pertaining to being modest in the sense of moderate and wellordered
meanings.note: For another interpretation of κόσμιος in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to being proper or suitable in terms of being attractive
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: one who rules over the whole world
meanings.note: The expression ‘world ruler’ should not be understood in terms of merely ruling over the earth as a physical object but of ‘ruling over those who are on the earth.’ Most scholars, however, interpret κοσμοκράτωρ in as meaning a supernatural power (see ), though it is possible to understand κοσμοκράτωρ in this context as meaning a human ruler.

meanings.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
meanings.note: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

meanings.def: the universe as an ordered structure
meanings.note: In many languages there is no specific term for the universe. The closest equivalent may simply be ‘all that exists.’ In other instances one may use a phrase such as ‘the world and all that is above it’ or ‘the sky and the earth.’ The concept of the totality of the universe may be expressed in some languages only as ‘everything that is on the earth and in the sky.’

meanings.def: the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below
the way humans typically conduct themselves in the world; the way things typically happen in human society
meanings.note: It may be particularly difficult to speak of the world being crucified (), and therefore in a number of languages one must employ a somewhat fuller restructuring, for example, ‘because of Christ, the way in which people in this world live is as though it were dead as far as I am concerned, and I am dead, so to speak, as far as the way in which people in this world live.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘cosmos, universe,’ ) people associated with a world system and estranged from God
to cause something to be beautiful by decorating
meanings.note: For another interpretation of κόσμος in, see.

meanings.def: an object which serves to adorn or beautify
meanings.note: Adornments may be described as ‘things to make one look beautiful’ or ‘things with which one tries to appear attractive.’ For another interpretation of κόσμος in, see.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘world, universe,’ ) a great sum of something, implying an almost incredible totality
meanings.note: In some languages the phrase ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας may be rendered as ‘the very symbol of evil,’ ‘a sign of what is truly evil,’ or ‘what is completely evil.’

meanings.def: title for supernatural forces and powers: a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
meanings.note: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.|In some instances a measure of meaning may be obtained by somewhat paraphrastic expressions. For example, is rendered in some languages as ‘at that time you lived in the way in which the spirit that governs this world dictated you should live. This is the way the one who rules over the power in space commanded you to live. This is the very spirit that now commands the people who disobey God.’

meanings.def: a Christian who sent greetings in
(an Aramaic expression) to stand up from a reclining position
meanings.note: Note that κουμ is translated in by [b] (see ).

meanings.def: a group of soldiers serving as a guard
to cause something to weigh less
a relatively large basket used primarily for food or produce
meanings.note: Translators often find it difficult to obtain satisfactory equivalents of () and κόφινος, since in various receptor languages there are highly specific terms for particular kinds of baskets depending upon type of construction and size. Unfortunately, there is no way of determining from the Greek text precisely the size or type of baskets involved in references to and κόφινος.

meanings.def: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
meanings.note: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

meanings.def: to shout or cry out, with the possible implication of the unpleasant nature of the sound
drunken behavior which is completely without moral restraint
meanings.note: In a number of languages it may be possible to translate κραιπάλη as ‘bad things people do when they are very drunk.’

meanings.def: the bony framework of the head, especially the upper portion
meanings.note: In rendering κρανίου τόπος ‘place of the skull’ it may be necessary to indicate clearly the relationship between place and skull. A literal rendering of such a phrase might simply mean ‘a place where there was a skull.’ However the meaning of Golgotha has been interpreted generally as ‘a hill resembling a skull’ and therefore κρανίου τόπος may be more satisfactorily rendered as ‘a place resembling a skull’ or ‘a hill looking like a skull.’ See.
g: skull (in the NT κρανίον is used only as a name for the hill of Golgotha)

meanings.def: decorative tassel attached to the bottom edge of a long outer garment
meanings.note: The edge of the garment designated by κράσπεδον[a] could have been plain or decorated. In κράσπεδον denotes the tassels worn at the four corners of the outer garment (see ). It is also possible that in all instances in which κράσπεδον is used in reference to Jesus’ clothing, the reference may be specifically to the tassels and not merely to the fringe or edge of the garment. The interpretation of such passages depends upon how strictly Jesus may have followed the Mosaic law and the manner in which the authors may have understood the meaning of κράσπεδον.

meanings.def: the tassels which Jews were obliged to wear on the four corners of the outer garment (see )
meanings.note: In some languages tassels may be described as ‘decorated corners’ or ‘ribbons at the corners.’ See the discussion at.

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘power,’ ) pertaining to being powerful or mighty
meanings.note: In χεῖρ is, of course, to be interpreted as power (see ).

meanings.def: to become strong and healthy, with the implication of physical vigor
meanings.note: In employing an expression to translate ‘to become strong,’ it is important to avoid the impression of ‘to become muscular.’ The emphasis is upon total physical vigor, not mere muscular strength.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘powerful,’ ) to become strong psychologically

a deed manifesting great power, with the implication of some supernatural force

the flesh of animals used as food

meanings.def: to hang down from some point

meanings.def: (derivative of [c] ‘to judge,’ ) the content of the process of judging
any one of several types of flowers, usually uncultivated

meanings.def: to come to a conclusion in the process of thinking and thus to be in a position to make a decision

meanings.def: to judge something to be better than something else, and hence, to prefer
to make a judgment based upon the correctness or value of something
to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
to decide a question of legal right or wrong, and thus determine the innocence or guilt of the accused and assign appropriate punishment or retribution
meanings.note: The process of legal judging is often expressed idiomatically. In Africa, one of the standard phrases for judging is ‘to cut a palaver,’ but other expressions in other languages may be ‘to find guilt,’ ‘to point the finger at wrong,’ or ‘to untangle strife.’
g: to try a case (in the passive to stand trial)

meanings.def: to judge a person to be guilty and liable to punishment
to rule over people

Furthermore, there seems to be a significant Semitic influence in the meaning of κρίνω, since the corresponding Hebrew term likewise involved far more than merely making judicial decisions.

meanings.def: act of deciding a question of legal right or wrong, and thus determining the innocence or guilt of the accused and assigning appropriate punishment or retribution
meanings.note: The process of legal judging is often expressed idiomatically. In Africa, one of the standard phrases for judging is ‘to cut a palaver,’ but other expressions in other languages may be ‘to find guilt,’ ‘to point the finger at wrong,’ or ‘to untangle strife.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [e] ‘to judge legal cases,’ ) the authority or right to judge guilt or innocence
a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence
meanings.note: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

meanings.def: the legal decision rendered by a judge, whether for or against the accused
act of judging a person to be guilty and liable to punishment
the administration of justice
meanings.note: It may be difficult to speak of ‘justice triumphing,’ and so in some languages it may be necessary to translate ‘so that all accusations are judged justly’ or ‘so that everyone receives what he should’ or ‘until all judgments are just.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [c] ‘to judge,’ ) the content of the process of judging
meanings.note: It may also be possible to translate ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνετε () as ‘judge in a righteous manner’ or ‘judge according to true standards.’

meanings.def: the basis for rendering a judgment
meanings.note: It is also possible to render κρίσις in as ‘how judgment works’ or ‘the reason for God judging.’

meanings.def: punishment, with the implication of having been judged guilty
meanings.note: It is also possible, of course, to interpret κρίσις in as meaning ‘condemnation’ (see ), but as such, punishment is certainly implied.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to fall under judgment) to be condemned for acting contrary to laws and regulations
