meanings.def: a leader of the synagogue in Corinth
a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence
meanings.note: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

meanings.def: legal action taken in a court of law against someone
meanings.note: In most languages there are technical terms for lawsuits or cases in court, but where these do not exist, one may always use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘to accuse someone before a judge’ or ‘to argue against someone in court’ or ‘to say in court that someone has done a person harm.’

meanings.def: one who presides over a court session and pronounces judgment
(derivative of [e] ‘to judge legal cases,’ ) pertaining to the ability or capacity to judge legal cases
g: to have the capacity to judge

meanings.def: to knock on a door, as a means of signaling one’s presence to those inside
meanings.note: A literal rendering of κρούω in may be misleading in a number of languages, since in some areas only thieves knock on doors. This is done in order to determine whether anyone is at home, in which case, of course, the thief runs off. The more general practice for signaling one’s presence may be to cough, to clap the hands, or to call out one’s name.

meanings.def: (locative derivative of ‘secret, hidden,’ ) a place which is secret or hidden and thus not generally known, possibly referring to a structure built underground for hiding or storing objects
pertaining to not being able to be known, in view of the fact that it has been kept secret
meanings.note: In a number of languages there may be complications involved in what could be regarded as a triple negation in the sense that ‘nothing,’ ‘secret’ (in the sense of ‘not known’), and ‘not be made known’ are all semantic negations. It may therefore be better to render as ‘everything that is now not known will be made known.’|In a number of languages ‘secret’ is regularly expressed as ‘not known’ or ‘what is kept from being known.’
g: not able to be made known

meanings.def: (idiom, literally: the hidden (person)) the psychological faculty, including intellectual, emotional, and spiritual aspects, in contrast with the purely physical aspects of human existence
meanings.note: A strictly literal rendering of ἀλλ ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ Ἰουδαῖος might be misunderstood in to refer only to the fact of circumcision, which would be something which would normally not be evident.|In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of the psychological faculty of a person as being merely ‘that which is within.’ It is frequently necessary to refer to a particular organ of the body, for example, ‘the heart’ or ‘the liver’ or ‘the spleen.’ In some languages, however, one may refer to this faculty as being ‘the person who stands inside’ or ‘the real person’ or even ‘the other person.’|In the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in the statement ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν ‘look, God’s reign is within you’ may constitute a reference to the same inner being designated by the phrases ὁ ἔσω and ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. On this basis some scholars have suggested that the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can be interpreted as a potentiality for participation and hence be translated ‘within your grasp,’ but it is more likely that one should understand the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in as a spacial relationship, for example, ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’ (see ).

meanings.def: the content of what is not able to be known
pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
to cause to be safe or protected by hiding, in some contexts with the intent of not being found
meanings.note: Since κρύπτω also means ‘to make invisible,’ some scholars believe that this statement in means that ‘your life is concealed in Christ’ or ‘… hidden from view …’ (see ). For another interpretation of κρύπτω in, see.

meanings.def: to cause something to be invisible, with the intent of its being not found
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: to cause something to be invisible (in the sense of being hidden), but for the purpose of safekeeping and protection
meanings.note: The evident implication of this statement in is to emphasize the fact that the true life of the believer is not some material, visible object or happening, but something spiritual and thus only visible to those spiritually enlightened or concerned. For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: to cause something not to be known
meanings.note: In a number of languages, the causative relationships involved in must be made somewhat more explicit, for example, ‘because you have kept the wise and learned people from knowing and have caused the unlearned to know.’ In νήπιος is used figuratively in reference to unlearned people.

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘crystal,’ ) to shine in the same way that crystal shines
a very hard, translucent, and usually transparent type of quartz
meanings.note: The equivalent of ‘crystal’ is often a descriptive phrase such as ‘a brilliant stone’ or ‘a shining stone’ or ‘a glass-like stone.’ In developing a satisfactory term for crystal, it is important to avoid possible confusion with diamond.|Some scholars, however, interpret κρύσταλλος in as being a reference to ice (see ).

meanings.def: frozen water
meanings.note: In both and (the only two passages in which κρύσταλλος occurs in the NT) the meaning may, however, be ‘rock crystal’ rather than ‘ice’ (see ).|Though in the Arctic regions people may have a number of different terms for various kinds and forms of ice, there are many areas in the world in which there is no existing local term for ‘ice.’ Sometimes a descriptive phrase such as ‘hardened water’ is employed, and in a number of languages a term is simply borrowed from a dominant language of the region. However, in and it is possible to focus upon the brilliance of color rather than the particular substance and thus to speak of λαμπρὸς ὡς κρύσταλλος as ‘that which is sparkling white’ or ‘… bright white.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being secret as a result of people not knowing
pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
to acquire possession of something

meanings.note: It is also possible to understand σκεῦος in as one’s wife (see ). σκεῦος in may also be understood as one’s body, and therefore the phrase τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι may be rendered as ‘to control his own body’ (see ).

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to acquire,’ ) that which is owned or possessed (usually land)
a larger type of domesticated animal, primarily one used for riding or carrying loads
meanings.note: In (ἄλλη δὲ σὰρξ κτηνῶν, ἄλλη δὲ σὰρξ πτηνῶν, ἄλλη δὲ ἰχθύων ‘another is the flesh of animals, another the flesh of birds, and another the flesh of fish’) one might argue that κτηνῶν is simply a highly generic expression for all kinds of animals, but in view of its meaning in so many other contexts, it probably applies even in to large domesticated animals.|As in so many instances, the translator must render passages in terms of expressions which are appropriate to particular contexts. For example, in a translation such as ‘horses’ would be appropriate, while in the term ‘donkey’ would be fitting, and in κτήνη (in which κτῆνος contrasts with πρόβατα ‘sheep’) would perhaps best be translated as ‘cattle.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to acquire,’ ) one who owns or possesses property
to make or create something which has not existed before
g: creation (in the NT, used exclusively of God’s activity in creation)

meanings.def: act of making or creating something which has not existed before
g: creation (in the NT, used exclusively of God’s activity in creation)

meanings.def: that which has been created
the universe as the product of God’s activity in creation

However, in a number of contexts, the process of creation is no longer focal, and what is in focus is the total physical universe. In some languages the meaning may be best expressed as ‘the world and all that is in it’ or even ‘everything that exists.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to create,’ ) a human institution or social structure as something which has been created
meanings.note: It is possible that κτίσις in may have the implication of authorized institution. It might even be possible to render κτίσις in such a context as ‘authority’ (compare [e] in ).

meanings.def: an instituted authority, with the implication that such an authority has been created or formed
meanings.note: The expression ‘human authority’ may be rendered as ‘every person who has the right to rule.’ For another interpretation of κτίσις in, see.

meanings.def: that which has been created
(derivative of ‘to create,’ ) one who creates
trickery that results from craftiness (κυβεία literally refers to dice playing)
(derivative of κυβερνάω ‘to steer a ship, to guide,’ not occurring in the NT) the ability to lead
meanings.note: ‘The gift of leadership’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘being able to lead others’ or ‘being able to get others to follow.’

meanings.def: one who commands a ship
meanings.note: In some languages a captain is simply ‘the chief of a ship’ or ‘one who commands the sailors.’

meanings.def: to move in such a way as to encircle an object
a position completely encircling an area or object
a position on the total outside surface of a three-dimensional object
to move around an object

meanings.def: to move in such a way as to encircle an object

meanings.def: the motion of an object rolling back and forth or rolling about
meanings.note: It is rare that one can use in a language the same or related terms for the rolling of a person in an epileptic fit and the wallowing of a pig in the mud. The first is chaotic and uncontrolled, while the second is both purposeful and slower.

a moving ridge or succession of swells on the surface of a body of water

meanings.def: probably the plant Cuminum cyminum; same family as carrot; branches from the base and has similar leaves and flowers, though seeds have a sharper smell; planted and harvested each year, reaching a height of about 50-60 cm; seeds are used in cooking and as medicine
meanings.note: In designating ‘cumin’ as well as ‘dill,’ ‘rue,’ and ‘mint,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called cumin.’

meanings.def: relatively small light brown domestic animal, feeding on anything from household refuse to animal carcasses and excreta; Canis familiaris putiatini; associated with all sorts of uncleanness, aggression, greediness, low status (diminutive of [a] dog,, but in the NT the diminutive force may have become lost, though a component of emotive attachment or affection is no doubt retained and thus the reference is presumably to a house dog)
(derivative of ‘Cyprus,’ ) a person who is a native of Cyprus
an island off the south coast of Asia Minor
to bend over into a stooping position

a city on the coast of north Africa
the imperial governor of Syria
a title of respect used in addressing or speaking of a woman
meanings.note: It is likely, however, that κυρία in refers to the church as a lady.

Therefore, it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘the meal at which the Lord presided’ or ‘the meal which the Lord had for his disciples’ or ‘the meal which the Lord ate with his followers.’

meanings.def: to rule or reign over, with the implication in some contexts of lording it over
(a title for God and for Christ) one who exercises supernatural authority over mankind (see also )
meanings.note: The most common equivalent of ‘Lord’ is a term meaning ‘chief’ or ‘leader,’ but frequently this cannot be employed as a title for ‘God.’ One may, however, combine such an expression with a term for ‘God’ and employ a phrase meaning ‘God our leader’ or ‘God our chief.’ In some instances, however, a term for ‘Lord’ is related to a verb meaning ‘to command’ or ‘to order,’ and therefore ‘Lord’ is rendered as ‘the one who commands us’ and combined with ‘God’ may form a phrase such as ‘God, the one who commands us.’

meanings.def: one who owns and controls property, including especially servants and slaves, with important supplementary semantic components of high status and respect
one who rules or exercises authority over others
meanings.note: For the meaning of κύριος as a title for God or for Christ, see.

meanings.def: a title of respect used in addressing or speaking of a man
(an idiom, literally: to his own master he stands or falls, probably a familiar adage) whether one maintains one’s status or relationship to a master depends on the master's judgment or evaluation
g: honor or disgrace depends on the person whom one serves

meanings.def: (derivative of [c] ‘one who rules,’ ) a supernatural ruling power
meanings.note: In general, the series of terms θρόνοι, κυριότητες, ἀρχαί, and ἐξουσίαι in (as well as in ) are understood as being supernatural cosmic powers, whether angelic or demonic (see ), but it is possible that these should be understood in terms of human rulers.

meanings.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
meanings.note: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

meanings.def: to invest something with power or force
meanings.note: In order to express the meaning of this phrase in, it may be necessary in some languages to make more specific the arrangements involved, for example, ‘if people have signed an agreement, no one can disregard it’ or ‘if an agreement has been confirmed, no one can say it does not exist’ or, as in some languages, ‘if an agreement has been tied, no one can untie it.’

meanings.def: to cause someone to recognize the reality of something
g: to show something to be real

meanings.def: relatively small light brown domestic animal, feeding on anything from household refuse to animal carcasses and excreta; Canis familiaris putiatini; associated with all sorts of uncleanness, aggression, greediness, low status

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘dog,’ ) a particularly bad person, perhaps specifically one who ridicules what is holy
meanings.note: It is also possible that κύων in may be interpreted as meaning ‘pervert’ (see ).|A term for ‘dog’ may have quite a different connotation than it does in English. For example, to call a person ‘a dog’ in some languages is to compliment him for his faithfulness, but in other languages it may be merely a way of attributing promiscuous sexual behavior.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘dog,’ ) one who is a sexual pervert or possibly one who is sexually promiscuous
meanings.note: It is also possible, however, that in κύων means ‘a wicked person’ who might have complete contempt for what is holy, a meaning which parallels the significance of the adage in (see ).

meanings.def: the dead body of a person, especially one which is still unburied
meanings.note: Though in the Greek text reads literally ‘whose dead bodies fell in the wilderness,’ it would normally be a mistake to translate this clause literally, since it might suggest that the people died while they were still standing, and that only the corpses fell. A more natural equivalent is ‘they died in the wilderness’ or ‘they died and their bodies lay in the wilderness.’

meanings.def: to cause something not to happen
a relatively unimportant population center (in contrast with [b] ‘city,’ )
the inhabitants of a village
meanings.note: Though in English it may seem perfectly appropriate to speak of ‘announcing the good news to a town’ or ‘… a village,’ in a number of languages this is simply not possible, for any announcement of good news must be directed to people and not to a place or area.

meanings.def: a city that had the status of a () as far as its legal standing or constitution was concerned
drinking parties involving unrestrained indulgence in alcoholic beverages and accompanying immoral behavior
small flying insect; feeds on human or animal blood; regarded as pest
meanings.note: The straining of liquids referred to in is based on the regulations in Leviticus 11, in which the gnat is the smallest of the unclean creatures and the camel the largest.|For the only occurrence of κώνωψ in the NT, one may use a term which refers to any small flying insect which might fall into a beverage and thus have to be strained out.

meanings.def: an island in the Aegean Sea
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to not being able to speak or talk
pertaining to being unable to hear

meanings.def: to receive, with the implication that the process is related somehow to divine will or favor

meanings.def: to choose by lot, probably by the use of marked pebbles or pieces of pottery

meanings.def: to be selected by a decision based on the casting of lots, with the possible implication of reflecting divine choice
the brother of [b] and
a beggar in a parable
pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
sudden and violent gusts of winds, often from varied directions
meanings.note: In a number of languages a strong wind which causes the waves or a storm on water must be referred to by a special term. Compare, for example, the English term squall; this would mean a wind of relatively short duration but sufficiently intense so as to create relatively high waves.

meanings.def: to burst open, probably from internal pressure
(an idiom, literally: to kick against the goad) to react against authority in such a way as to cause harm or suffering to oneself

an (Aramaic) interrogative expression of reason

meanings.note: A number of languages differ radically in terms for ‘taking hold of,’ depending upon whether force is employed, whether the object is a thing or an animate being, and whether the language incorporates into a verb of ‘taking hold of’ a classification as to the objects involved, for example, long and thin, round and flat, ball-like, angular, or lumpy.

meanings.def: to come to believe something and to act in accordance with such a belief
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to take hold,’ ) to take advantage of someone by trickery or deception

to cause to experience, normally implying something grievous
meanings.note: It is, of course, possible to understand in in a more or less literal sense (see ) and thus to translate this expression as ‘the guards took him and slapped him.’

meanings.def: to put on an article of clothing
a marker of an agent relation with numerable events, with the implication of having assumed some initiative
(an idiom, literally: to take a rule, to receive a rule) to receive from someone else the power or authority to reign as a king
(an idiom, literally: to take courage) to become confident or courageous in the face of real or possible danger
(an idiom, literally: to take face) to make unjust distinctions between people by treating one person better than another
meanings.note: ‘To show favoritism’ or ‘to be partial’ is expressed in an idiomatic manner in some languages, for example, ‘to look only upon a person’s face,’ ‘to call a sparrow a chicken,’ or ‘to give one’s clansman the best piece of meat.’

meanings.def: (a productive idiomatic expression, literally: to take one’s cross) to be prepared to endure severe suffering, even to the point of death
meanings.note: The idiom ‘to carry one’s cross’ or ‘to take up one’s cross’ involves a number of important features of meaning. Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.
g: to be prepared to suffer even unto death

meanings.def: to attempt to do something, with the implication of not succeeding
meanings.note: In a number of languages expressions such as πειράζω[d], πειράομαι, and πεῖραν λαμβάνω may be expressed as to start to do something, but not be able to or to think that one can do something, but discover it is impossible.

meanings.def: the father of Noah in the genealogy of Jesus
a stick or bundle of sticks carried about as a light
a light made by burning a wick saturated with oil contained in a relatively small vessel
meanings.note: In some languages the closest equivalent of λαμπάς[b] and λύχνος is a kerosene lamp. What is to be avoided is a word which suggests a flashlight, which would of course be highly anachronistic.

meanings.def: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source
pertaining to being clear and also bright
pertaining to being brilliant or splendid, though with the possible implication of ostentatious or superficial
meanings.note: See note at.

meanings.def: the state of brightness or shining
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between some object which is bright in and of itself (that is to say, the source of brightness or radiance) and objects which are bright because they reflect light from some source. In the case of (which is generally regarded as a reference to the Shekinah presence of God), the cloud would not be merely reflecting light but would be a source of light (see ).

meanings.def: pertaining to living in ostentatious luxury
meanings.note: The equivalent of λαμπρῶς in the sense of ‘luxuriously’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘richly’ or ‘with things which cost a great deal’ or ‘with more possessions than one can count.’

meanings.def: to shine or to produce light, as in the case of heavenly bodies, lightning, candles, torches, etc.
meanings.note: Terms for ‘shining, giving light’ often differ depending upon the type of source. There may be, for example, a contrast between the shining of a heavenly body in contrast with some source on earth. There may also be a difference between a continuous shining such as of the sun and the moon and a brief flash, as in the case of lightning or sparks from a fire.

meanings.def: to cause oneself to not be known, with the implication of concealment and secrecy
meanings.note: In some languages this expression in may be rendered as ‘he was not able to keep people from knowing where he was’ or ‘he was not able to keep secret where he was.’

meanings.def: to not recall information and thus to lose sight of its significance
meanings.note: In a number of languages the fact of ‘forgetting’ or ‘not remembering’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to lose out of one’s heart,’ ‘to have one’s thoughts walk away,’ or ‘to have words disappear from one’s liver.’

meanings.def: to not have knowledge about or to be unaware of something, with the implication that something can readily escape notice or be hidden
pertaining to having been hewn out of rock
meanings.note: In ‘rock’ must be understood as a basic outcropping of rock, so that the grave would have been a cave-like structure cut into a rock outcropping.

meanings.def: a city in Phrygia in Asia Minor
(derivative of ‘Laodicea,’ ) a person who lives in or is a native of Laodicea
the largest unit into which the people of the world are divided on the basis of their constituting a socio-political community
meanings.note: In a number of languages a term meaning basically ‘tribe’ has been extended in meaning to identify ‘nations.’ In other instances different nations are spoken of simply as ‘different peoples.’ In certain cases distinct nations are classified primarily in terms of their diverse languages, for example, ‘those people who speak different languages.’ Such an expression should not, however, be used if it only refers to multilingual persons.

meanings.def: a collective for people who belong to God (whether Jews or Christians)
meanings.note: The phrase ‘people of God’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘the people who belong to God’ or ‘the people whom God possesses,’ but in a number of languages the relationship between the people and God must be expressed in terms of reverence or worship, for example, ‘the people who worship God’ or ‘the people who reverence God.’ See also.

meanings.def: a casual non-membership group of people, fairly large in size and assembled for whatever purpose
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no term corresponding to ‘crowd.’ One may, however, usually speak of such a group of people as ‘many people’ or ‘many men and women.’ Depending on the context, it may be necessary to indicate some relative difference in size, for example, ‘very large crowd’ or ‘many, many people.’ If the crowd is relatively small, one may sometimes speak of ‘just some people.’

meanings.def: the common people, in contrast with those who are rich, leaders, and/or authorities in the society, often with the implication of disdain and low esteem
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘the common people’ is ‘the poor people,’ but in some languages an equivalent depends upon geographical location, for example, ‘those who live on the edge of town’ (the opposite situation from what exists in most present-day metropolitan centers). In still other languages ‘the common people’ may be designated in terms of lack of status, for example, ‘those who have no position’ or ‘those whom the rich do not greet’ or ‘those before whom no one ever bows.’

The context of is highly figurative, and in a number of languages it may be necessary either to change the metaphor into a simile, for example, ‘their throat is like an open tomb,’ or to employ a somewhat altered equivalent, for example, ‘their speech is full of deadly deceit.’

meanings.def: a city on the south coast of the island of Crete
to shape rock by cutting, either internally or externally
meanings.note: In some languages important distinctions are made in terms for cutting rock depending upon the type of activity, for example, shaping of rock by cutting, the quarrying of rock from an outcrop, or the hewing of an area inside of an outcropping of rock (a cave-like structure hewn into rock).

meanings.def: to perform religious rites as a part of worship
to perform religious rites as a part of worship
any one of the smaller plants cultivated in a garden, for example, herbs and vegetables
one of the twelve apostles, generally regarded as being the same as Thaddaeus () (, apparatus)
an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
a Roman army unit of about six thousand soldiers
meanings.note: The expression ‘twelve legions of angels’ indicates a very large group of angels; accordingly, the meaning may be rendered as ‘many, many angels’ or ‘thousands of angels.’

meanings.def: the name of a host of demons
to speak or talk, with apparent focus upon the content of what is said
to speak of a person or object by means of a proper name
to use an attribution in speaking of a person
meanings.note: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

meanings.def: to mark the correspondence in the meaning of foreign expressions
meanings.note: The meaning of λέγω[d] must often be expressed in rather specific ways, for example, ‘which says in our language’ or ‘what is the same as what we say in our language.’

meanings.def: to say something in order to explain more fully the implications or intent of what has been said

g: to say to oneself (often used to introduce a direct quotation of one’s thoughts)

meanings.def: a relatively small part which continues to exist
pertaining to being level or smooth (that is, without rough or uneven contours)
to not possess something which is necessary
to be lacking in the sense of not being in someone’s possession

meanings.def: to perform religious rites as part of one’s religious duties or as the result of one’s role

a piece of cloth (probably made of linen) used primarily for drying
a thin layer or peel, especially of skin
meanings.note: In rendering it is possible to say ‘there fell from his eyes something which looked like a fish scale’ or ‘… a small flake of skin.’

meanings.def: a dreaded condition of the skin, including what is now regarded as leprosy, as well as certain other types of infectious skin diseases, resulting in a person’s being regarded as ceremonially unclean and thus excluded from normal relations with other people
(derivative of ‘dread skin disease,’ ) a person suffering from a dread skin disease
g: one having a dread skin disease

meanings.def: a copper (or bronze) coin worth 1/2 of a quadrans or 1/128 of a denarius
meanings.note: In practically all instances, references to (), (), or λεπτόν may be made in terms of ‘a very small coin’ or ‘a coin with very little value’ or ‘money that was not worth very much.’

meanings.def: alternative form of [a], (, apparatus)
alternative form of Λευί[a], (, apparatus)
a tax collector and one of the twelve apostles, generally regarded as being the same as Matthew,
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
the son of Μελχί[a] in the genealogy of Jesus
the son of Συμεών[e] in the genealogy of Jesus

meanings.note: In most languages Λευίτης has simply been transliterated, but in other languages it is rendered as ‘assistant priest,’ especially in those contexts in which religious activity is involved.

meanings.def: (derivative of Λευί ‘Levi,’ son of Jacob, ) pertaining to being a descendant of Levi
meanings.note: The phrase ‘through the Levitical priesthood’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘by those priests who were descended from Levi.’

meanings.def: to cause something to become white
meanings.note: This statement in may raise numerous difficulties for receptors, since blood would not be regarded as an instrument for making anything white. It may be necessary, therefore, to introduce a marginal note explaining the figurative language and suggesting the rendering ‘to make them pure.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being white or very light in color; applies to (parts of) the human body, animals, plants, inanimate objects
meanings.note: The term λευκός also occurs in in speaking of fields being ‘white for the harvest,’ but in a number of languages it would be quite impossible to use the same term for the ripe condition of a harvest as in the case of the color of wool or snow. Furthermore, there may be a serious difficulty in speaking of wool as being ‘white,’ since in many parts of the world, wool is not regarded as being particularly white.

meanings.def: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source

largest of the great cats, often about 2.8 m from nose to tip of tail, standing as high as 1 m at the shoulder; pale yellowish brown in color; adult males have a mane around the neck and shoulders that is darker than the rest of their fur; Panthera leo; unclean animal; associated with aggression and strength
meanings.note: In some languages it may be important to use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a very large cat-like animal,’ though it will be important to try to make some distinction between ‘lion’ and ‘leopard’ (). If necessary, some more extensive identification by description may be employed in a glossary.

meanings.def: to not recall information and thus to lose sight of its significance
meanings.note: In a number of languages the fact of ‘forgetting’ or ‘not remembering’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to lose out of one’s heart,’ ‘to have one’s thoughts walk away,’ or ‘to have words disappear from one’s liver.’

meanings.def: to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver, but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver
an instrument for pressing out the juice of grapes for the making of wine
meanings.note: Ancient wine presses consisted of large vats into which grapes were placed and then trampled on in order to extract the juice. Accordingly, a descriptive equivalent of wine press may be ‘a place where the juice of grapes was squeezed out’ or ‘… pressed out.’

meanings.def: speech which is complete and utter nonsense

a person who engages in insurrection
generalized, positive degree
the aromatic resin of certain trees, burned for its pleasing aroma
meanings.note: Translators may either borrow a term such as ‘frankincense’ or use a descriptive equivalent, for example, ‘a sweet-smelling incense’ or ‘a valuable, sweet incense.’

meanings.def: a bowl in which incense is burned
(a Latin name) a group of people, presumably Jews, who had been slaves but later obtained their freedom; their synagogue was also known by the same name
a district in north Africa
to kill or attempt to kill by means of hurling stones, normally carried out by angry mobs
(derivative of [a] ‘stone,’ ) pertaining to being made of or consisting of stone
meanings.note: In speaking of objects ‘made of stone’ it may be necessary in some languages to indicate more precisely the manner in which such objects have been formed, for example, ‘hewn out of stone’ or ‘made from stone by chipping.’

meanings.def: to kill or attempt to kill by means of hurling stones, normally carried out by angry mobs
stone as a substance
a piece of rock, whether shaped or natural
meanings.note: Some languages make an important distinction between ‘stone’ as a substance (as in ) and ‘stones’ as individual pieces of rock (as in ). The term λίθος in the NT may be employed in speaking of rather large stones, for example, the stone placed in front of the tomb of Jesus () and the stones of the foundation of the Temple buildings (). In all such contexts, however, the reference is to stones which have been moved into position or which are capable of being moved, even though with some difficulty.|In some languages an important distinction is made between stones which are shaped for use in building and stones which occur in a natural form, for example, ‘field stones.’ In each instance the biblical context must be studied to determine what type of expression should be used.

meanings.def: valuable stones and hard substances, especially gems and jewels
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.|Precious stones are often distinguished on the basis of cost, appearance, or function, for example, ‘stones that cost much’ or ‘stones that are beautiful’ or ‘stones that are worn for decoration.’|A number of precious and semiprecious stones (see -) are mentioned in one NT passage, namely,, and though there are certain differences of opinion among scholars as to the precise reference of certain of these terms, there is more or less general agreement as to the color of the stones in question.|In languages in which terms such as ‘jasper,’ ‘sapphire,’ ‘agate,’ etc. exist, one may simply borrow such terms and explain their color in a glossary or word list. For languages in which such terms are not known, translators normally borrow the names from a dominant language of the area and likewise provide an explanation of the color in a glossary. Some translators have attempted to introduce the corresponding color terms in the text of, but this often results in a rather extended and somewhat awkward set of descriptive expressions.

meanings.def: A large, heavy stone used to close the entrance to a cave or tomb cut out of the rock
block of stone, either fully square or not; found in nature or hewn from a quarry; used for building houses, walls, and other constructions
an area in Jerusalem, paved with flat blocks of stone and forming a kind of courtyard (not a thoroughfare)
meanings.note: In some languages one may describe ‘The Stone Pavement’ as ‘a court covered with large blocks of flat stone’ or ‘a stone-paved courtyard.’ See.

meanings.def: to crush by a destructive amount of vertical pressure
a relatively small area of the sea which is well protected by land but deep enough for ships to enter and moor
meanings.note: λιμήν may be rendered in some languages by a descriptive phrase, ‘a place where ships are safe from the storm’ or ‘a place where ships are never damaged’ or ‘a place where ships may stay.’ In it is difficult to know whether the reference of λιμήν is to the harbor as a convenient place for the ships to stay during the winter, or to the port (that is to say, the town at the harbor) as a convenient place for people to stay during the winter. Some languages make a clear distinction between the area where ships stay and where people may stay waiting to continue their voyage.

meanings.def: a relatively small body of water either natural or artificial, surrounded by land
meanings.note: The use of λίμνη to refer to the Lake of Galilee (also called the Lake of Gennesaret) normally poses no special difficulty, but in the expression ‘lake of fire’ () there are complications, as already noted in.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: lake of fire (and sulfur), occurring in some slightly different forms six times in Revelation, three times with the addition of θεῖον ‘sulfur’) a place of eternal punishment and destruction
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate literally ‘lake of fire,’ since water and fire seem to be so contradictory that a lake of fire is not even imaginable. It may be possible in some instances to speak of ‘a place that looks like a lake that is on fire,’ but in other languages the closest equivalent may simply be ‘a great expanse of fire.’ In some parts of the world people are fully familiar with the type of boiling magma in the cone of volcanoes, and terms for such a place may be readily adapted in speaking of ‘a lake of fire,’ since volcanic activity would seem to be the basis for this particular biblical expression.

meanings.def: a widespread lack of food over a considerable period of time and resulting in hunger for many people
meanings.note: In a number of languages the only way of talking about a famine is to say ‘many people were very hungry for a long time’ or ‘many people had to go for days without anything to eat.’ It is important to distinguish clearly between a famine and voluntary abstinence from food for the sake of fasting. (See Domain 53H.)

meanings.def: the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare [a] ‘fasting,’ )
meanings.note: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

meanings.def: linen cloth, normally in the form of a garment
meanings.note: Linen garments may be described as ‘clothing made out of linen cloth.’ What is important in is the quality of the garments, not so much the fact that they were made of linen

meanings.def: a linen cord in a lamp that draws up the oil
meanings.note: A wick may often be referred to as ‘a small strip of cloth.’

meanings.def: a Christian who sent greetings in
pertaining to being splendid, with the implication of luxurious
meanings.note: In λαμπρός () and λιπαρός serve primarily to reinforce one another.

meanings.def: a Roman pound, weighing about twelve ounces or about 325 grams
meanings.note: In speaking of perfume in it may be far better to indicate quantity rather than weight, and therefore one may translate ‘then Mary took a pint of perfume.’ In translating λίτρα in the NT, one need not identify the pound as being ‘a Roman pound.’ It is better to employ a common term for pound (normally weighing sixteen ounces) or to provide a rounded-off equivalent of the amount in metric units, for example, three hundred grams or one-half liter.

As in the case of the intermediate direction ‘northwest’ (), one may also express ‘southwest’ in some languages as ‘a little south of west’ or ‘toward the south, but actually somewhat west’ or ‘veering to the right of south.’

meanings.def: the act of collecting contributions, especially those involving voluntary response
meanings.note: In some instances it may be important to translate λογεία as ‘to receive gifts of money,’ but the focus is upon the activity of the person or persons engaged in obtaining the contributions. This may be expressed in some instances as ‘to go from one person to another to receive their contributions.’

meanings.def: to think about something in a detailed and logical manner
to keep a mental record of events for the sake of some future action
meanings.note: ‘To keep a mental record of something’ may be rendered as ‘to add up in one’s mind’ or ‘to make a list in one’s heart.’

meanings.def: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
to keep records of commercial accounts, involving both debits and credits
pertaining to being genuine, in the sense of being true to the real and essential nature of something
meanings.note: Since in the context is figurative, some translators have preferred to render λογικός as ‘spiritual,’ so as to make the reference not literal but figurative.

meanings.def: the content of various utterances
pertaining to attractive and convincing speech
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand λόγιος in as meaning ‘learned’ (see ).

meanings.def: pertaining to one who has learned a great deal of the intellectual heritage of a culture
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand in as meaning ‘eloquent’ (see ).

meanings.def: to think about something in a detailed and logical manner
fallacious and deceptive reasoning and, by implication, based on evil intentions
meanings.note: It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘false arguments,’ especially if the equivalent of ‘arguments’ is a verb meaning ‘to argue’ or ‘to discuss against someone.‘ One can, however, express the semantic content of ‘false arguments’ (as reflected in λογισμός[b]) by translating as ‘what people say when they argue, but their words are not true’ or ‘they argue with words that are not true.’

meanings.def: to argue or quarrel about the meaning or use of words
arguing or quarreling about the meaning or use of words
that which has been stated or said, with primary focus upon the content of the communication
meanings.note: Any difference of meaning between λόγος[a] and [b] would be only a matter of stylistic usage.|In λόγος may be rendered as ‘question’ in view of the preceding [a] ‘to ask’ ().

the content of what is preached about Christ or about the good news
a relatively formal and systematic treatment of a subject

a title for Jesus in the Gospel of John as a reference to the content of God’s revelation and as a verbal echo of the use of the verbs meaning ‘to speak’ in Genesis 1 and in many utterances of the prophets
a record of assets and liabilities
meanings.note: The phrase εἰς λόγον in is a technical expression referring to the settlement of an account and indicates that this is a credit to the account. Accordingly, one may properly translate λόγον as ‘the amount of an account.’

a happening to which one may refer
that which is thought to be true but is not necessarily so

speaking in a highly insulting manner

an extent of time beginning with the time of a discourse

Similarly, in, λουτρόν has generally been regarded as referring to baptism.

wild, four-footed, predatory canine; light-brown fur, similar to jackal, but much bigger; Canis lupus; regarded as ravenous and fierce; commonly prey on flocks; symbol of roaming, opportunistic, dangerous, fierce, and clever banditry
meanings.note: In areas of the world in which wolves are not known, some translators have rendered λύκος[a] by the local equivalent of ‘leopard’ or ‘jaguar.’ This may be satisfactory for initial translations of the Scriptures, but such shifts in reference are normally rejected at a later stage by those readers who become more acquainted with the types animals which exist in other parts of the world. In most instances in which local terms for ‘wolf’ do not exist, translators have used descriptive phrases such as ‘wild dog’ or ‘fierce, wild dog,’ or they may have borrowed a term from a dominant language in the area and have added a qualifying phrase, for example, ‘a wild animal called wolf.’ One may, of course, simply use a more generic expression with some kind of qualifier. For example, in it is possible to use ‘fierce, wild animals,’ for the meaning of the passage is primarily figurative, and a specific designation of wolf is not required.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘wolf,’ ) a person who is particularly vicious and dangerous
meanings.note: In situations where wolves are not known, it may be possible to translate as ‘men like fierce animals will come among you.’ In some instances λύκος in has been rendered as ‘fierce, wild dogs.’

meanings.def: to cause injury or harm by maltreatment
meanings.note: It is also possible that λυμαίνομαι in may mean ‘to destroy’ (see ).

meanings.def: to destroy or to cause the destruction of persons, objects, or institutions
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is difficult to find a general term for ‘destruction.’ What has often happened is the extension of meaning from a more specific type of reference, for example, ‘to smash,’ to a more generic meaning of ‘to destroy,’ and whether one understands the specific or more generic meaning depends largely upon the context. Accordingly, in one may find a figurative usage of a term meaning ‘to smash’ (though understood in a more generic sense), for example, ‘Saul then worked in order to smash the church.’|It is also possible that λυμαίνομαι in may mean ‘to injure severely’ (see ).

Claudius Lysias, a Roman officer in Jerusalem; see
to dissolve the marriage bond

Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

meanings.def: to be of an advantage to someone

For example, in the case of one may translate ‘don’t you realize that if one man dies for the people, then you are much better off.’

meanings.note: ‘To liberate’ many may be expressed in many languages as ‘to cause people to go free’ or, in a more idiomatic manner, ‘to untie many’ or ‘to unchain many.’

meanings.note: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘being set free’ without specifying the particular manner or circumstances involved. In the case of, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘to liberate Israel’ as ‘to cause Israel to be free from foreign control’ or ‘… from the power of Rome.’ A similar type of translation may be required in, but in the case of it may be necessary to specify ‘we are set free from sin’ or ‘we are set free from our bad desires.’

meanings.def: to release or set free, with the implied analogy to the process of freeing a slave
meanings.note: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘being set free’ without specifying the particular manner or circumstances involved. In the case of, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘to liberate Israel’ as ‘to cause Israel to be free from foreign control’ or ‘… from the power of Rome.’ A similar type of translation may be required in, but in the case of it may be necessary to specify ‘we are set free from sin’ or ‘we are set free from our bad desires.’

meanings.def: a construction of two flat stones between which grain was ground into flour by rotating the top stone
meanings.note: Some mills were relatively small and operated by hand and could well be considered as artifacts. Others, however, were quite large, and animals were used to rotate the upper stone.|In almost all parts of the world grain is ground in one way or another. Quite frequently mills are of the same general structure as those used in ancient times, in which two relatively large, round, flat stones were placed one on top of the other, and the grain was ground between the two stones. Grain entered the mill through a round hole in the upper stone, and the flour gradually emerged from around the edges of the two stones. In other parts of the world, however, grain is prepared by means of grinding stones called metates. In still other parts of the world, a mortar and pestle are used for the grinding or preparation of grain. In most contexts, what is important is either the large size of the stones or the function of grinding grain, not necessarily the particular form. However, in contexts which speak about tying a millstone to a man’s neck (see ) and his being thrown into the depths of the sea, it is important to refer to relatively large stones which would cause a person to sink immediately. In such a context the use of a term for ‘mortar,’ especially one of wood, would hardly be appropriate since it would normally float. Frequently μύλος may be rendered as ‘stones for grinding grain.’ In other instances, even a more generic expression may be used, for example, ‘a large stone.’

meanings.def: one who is an expert in interpreting religious law (with a probable exception of (see ), always in reference to the Jewish Law)
a specialist in civil law
meanings.note: It is possible that νομικός in may have designated an expert in interpreting religious law (see ) rather than a general legal practitioner.

meanings.def: pertaining to being correct according to rules and regulations
common and official currency
a person who is skilled in the teaching and interpretation of the law (in the NT referring to the law of the OT)
to give or to establish a law
meanings.note: Though in English it is normal to speak of ‘giving a law,’ such an expression can be entirely misleading, since in some languages ‘to give a law’ can mean ‘to annul a law’ in the sense of giving back to people a rule or regulation. A more frequent expression for ‘giving a law’ may be ‘commanding a law’ or ‘ordering a law.’|In νομοθεσία refers specifically to the giving of the Jewish Law.

meanings.def: to give or to establish a law
meanings.note: Though in English it is normal to speak of ‘giving a law,’ such an expression can be entirely misleading, since in some languages ‘to give a law’ can mean ‘to annul a law’ in the sense of giving back to people a rule or regulation. A more frequent expression for ‘giving a law’ may be ‘commanding a law’ or ‘ordering a law.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to give a law,’ ) one who gives or enacts laws
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is not possible to speak literally of a ‘lawgiver’ as ‘one who gives laws,’ for laws seem to be quite distinct from gifts. However, the same meaning is often communicated by somewhat different expressions, for example, ‘one who decides what people must do’ or ‘one who makes a law stand’ or ‘one who gives strength to a law.’

meanings.def: a formalized rule (or set of rules) prescribing what people must do
meanings.note: The difference between ‘a law’ and ‘a command’ is that a law is enforced by sanctions from a society, while a command carries only the sanctions of the individual who commands. When, however, the people of Israel accepted the commands of God as the rules which they would follow and enforce, these became their laws.|The occurrence of νόμος two times in poses certain problems of both translation and interpretation: ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἠλευθέρωσέν σε ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας καὶ τοῦ θανάτου ‘for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus freed you from the law which leads to sin and death.’ In the second occurrence of νόμος, the meaning is clearly the rules and regulations of the OT law, but in the case of the first occurrence of νόμος, there is no such formulation of decrees. The reference in this instance must therefore be to certain basic principles. If, however, one understands νόμος in the sense of a type of abstract ‘governing power,’ it is possible that the reference in the phrase νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς is to this governing power of the Spirit of life which frees one from the law which stipulates sin and death.

meanings.def: the first five books of the OT called the Torah (often better rendered as ‘instruction’)
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is not possible to use a singular expression such as ‘the Law,’ for since the Torah consisted of five books and included a number of regulations and instructions, it is necessary in many languages to use ‘the laws.’ Furthermore, to distinguish this body of laws from common, ordinary customs or legal regulations, it may be necessary to employ a phrase such as ‘the laws given to Moses’ or simply ‘the laws of Moses.’

meanings.def: the sacred writings of the OT
meanings.note: It is clear from the content of the quotation in that the reference of νόμος is not restricted to the first five books of the OT, for the passage comes from the Psalms.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: law of the man, or: law of the husband) the law which binds a woman to a man in marriage
meanings.note: It may be especially difficult in some languages to speak of ‘being free from the marriage law.’ An appropriate equivalent in some languages may be ‘she is no longer obliged to remain the wife of the dead man,’ but in other languages it is more meaningful to say ‘she is then permitted to marry another man.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: the Law and the Prophets) all of the sacred writings of the OT, including the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings
to have an unhealthy or morbid desire for something
meanings.note: In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘an unhealthy desire’ would be ‘to desire something that one should not desire.’
g: to desire in an unhealthy manner

meanings.def: the state of being diseased
meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only: ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο οἵῳ δήποτ οὖν κατείχετο νοσήματι ‘was healed from whatever disease he had’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: the state of being diseased
a collective for the young of birds hatched in a nest
the young of any bird
the young of any bird

meanings.note: In most languages east and west are related to the rising or setting sun, although in some languages there may be some local geographical feature which serves as a marker of direction, for example, the location of a particular mountain, the ocean, or a river. For north, some languages employ ‘to the left of the rising sun,’ that is to say, the direction is oriented in terms of the left hand of a person facing toward the rising sun. Similarly, south would be ‘to the right of the rising sun.’

meanings.def: a wind which blows from the south
meanings.note: A number of languages have terms for winds coming from or going toward different directions. In a number of cases, however, directional expressions are not included in the terms for such winds. For example, a north wind may be simply called ‘a cold wind,’ and a south wind might be called ‘a wind from the sea.’ Such expressions depend upon local geographical features. Even in the instance in which a south wind is described in terms of direction, it may be necessary to use a somewhat expanded phrase, for example, ‘a wind from the right of the rising sun.’ Such an expression is based upon the experience of a person facing the rising sun and determining the south in terms of the right side of the person.

meanings.def: to provide instruction as to correct behavior and belief
to advise someone concerning the dangerous consequences of some happening or action
to provide instruction as to correct behavior and belief
to admonish someone for having done something wrong

meanings.def: to advise someone concerning the dangerous consequences of some happening or action
meanings.note: νουθετέω in may also be understood in the sense of ‘to admonish’ (see ).

meanings.def: pertaining to ability to reason and hence understand
the psychological faculty of understanding, reasoning, thinking, and deciding
meanings.note: In some languages there is no noun such as English mind, and therefore one must use a verb expression meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to reason,’ or ‘to understand,’ depending upon the particular context. In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘mind’ may be a figurative extension of a term meaning ‘head,’ but more often than not, thinking is regarded as being in some other part of the body, for example, ‘heart’ or ‘liver.’

meanings.def: a particular manner or way of thinking
meanings.note: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘way of thinking’ by a clause, for example, ‘how people think.’ In the case of, it may be necessary to translate ‘you too must strengthen yourselves by thinking just like Christ thought.’

meanings.def: a Christian woman or man mentioned in (text and apparatus)
a woman who is about to be married or who has just been married

meanings.def: the wife of one’s son
meanings.note: For languages which do not have specific terms for ‘mother- in-law’ and ‘daughter-in-law’ it may be possible to render by translating ‘women will be against the wives of their sons, and young women will be against the mothers of their husbands.’

meanings.def: a man who is about to be married or has just been married
meanings.note: In a number of languages a term for bridegroom must indicate explicitly whether the marriage is about to take place or has just taken place. Therefore, one may have to employ some such phrase as ‘a man who is going to be married soon’ or ‘a man who has just been married.’ A corresponding type of expression may be required for ‘bride’ (see ).

meanings.def: a relatively large room, often serving as a place for a wedding
meanings.note: Υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος, literally ‘sons of the wedding hall,’ is an idiom denoting the bridegroom’s friends or the wedding guests (see ).

meanings.def: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself
a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

darkness of the night in contrast with daylight (see )

meanings.def: (ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα - literally, forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
meanings.note: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

meanings.def: (expressions, literally: night and day, day and night, respectively) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits

meanings.def: a period consisting of a night and a day (essentially similar in meaning to [a] ‘day,’, but somewhat more explicit and emphatic)
a preacher of repentance who built an ark
pertaining to being sluggish or slow to become involved in some activity

the back part of the body from the neck to the pelvis
meanings.note: The phrase τὸν νῶτον … συγκάμπτειν may be regarded as an idiom, since its meaning may be to suffer oppression and trouble. An equivalent expression for ‘and bend their backs forever’ () may be ‘to make them slaves forever’ or ‘to make them toil hard forever’ (see ).

meanings.def: to comb wool as an initial step in the making of wool thread

meanings.def: to receive and show hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend

g: to receive a stranger as a guest

meanings.def: (compare ‘unknown, surprising,’ ) to experience a sudden feeling of unexpected wonder
meanings.note: The experience of ‘surprise’ may be expressed idiomatically in some languages, for example, ‘to be left with one’s mouth open’ or ‘to have one’s eyes made wide open.’

meanings.def: to receive and show hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend
meanings.note: To receive a stranger as a guest is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to let a stranger sit at one’s table,’ ‘to offer a bed to a stranger,’ or ‘to let a stranger enter one’s house.’
g: to receive a stranger as a guest

meanings.def: pertaining to not being previously known and hence unheard of and unfamiliar
a person belonging to a socio-political group other than the reference group

meanings.def: a person who shows hospitality to guests
meanings.note: In rendering ‘host’ it may be necessary to employ a phrase, for example, ‘who welcomed and took care of us in his home.’

meanings.def: (a borrowing based on Latin sextarius, a Roman measure equal to about a half liter, one pint) a kind of small pitcher or jar
to cause something to become dry
(derivative of [a] ‘dry,’ ) to become dry
meanings.note: It may be more appropriate in a number of languages to translate this clause in as ‘and immediately her menstrual bleeding stopped.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘dry,’ ) to become ripe, with reference to grain which dries in the process of ripening

meanings.def: pertaining to being dry

dry land, in contrast with the sea
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘wood,’ ) pertaining to being made or consisting of wood
wood as a substance
meanings.note: A number of languages make a clear distinction between wood as a substance used in artifacts and constructions and wood used for heating or cooking. A further distinction may be made between durable wood (not readily subject to rot or to the effects of termites and borers) and less durable and therefore relatively unsatisfactory wood.

meanings.def: wood as a substance used to burn for heat
meanings.note: ξύλον in may also be interpreted as a live green tree (see ). If one assumes that the meaning here is ‘firewood,’ then it may be necessary to translate ‘wood which has not had an opportunity to dry out’ or ‘wood which is still green’ or ‘… which is still wet with sap.’

meanings.def: large perennial plant, usually having a woody central stem, called a trunk, with secondary branches growing from it
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand ξύλον in as ‘firewood.’ One may therefore translate the first part of this conditional sentence as ‘if they do these things to firewood which has recently been cut’ or ‘if they do these things to firewood which hasn’t dried out’ (see ).|In and ξύλον τῆς ζωῆς ‘tree of life’ may cause certain complications if the passage is translated more or less literally ‘I will give him to eat of the tree of life.’ In some languages a literal rendering would mean ‘to gnaw on the tree of life,’ that is to say, to eat the wood or the bark. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘to eat the fruit of the tree of life’ or ‘… the fruit from the tree that causes life’ or ‘… causes people to live.’

meanings.def: a heavy stick used in fighting
an instrument consisting of heavy blocks of wood through which the legs were placed and then securely fastened
meanings.note: Stocks were employed primarily as an instrument for imprisonment, but also as a means of punishment.

meanings.def: to shave the head or beard

a reference to indefinite alternatives

to guide or to direct, with the implication of making certain that people reach an appropriate destination

one who guides or leads

meanings.def: to be on a journey, presumably with the focus upon being en route
to be on a journey, presumably with the focus upon being en route
a general term for a thoroughfare, either within a population center or between two such centers
to be in the process of travelling, presumably for some distance

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘road,’ ) a customary manner of life or behavior, with probably some implication of goal or purpose

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: a straight road) the right or correct pattern of behavior

Even in the case of it may be necessary to use two different terms for teeth, since human teeth may be referred to by expressions quite different from those used in referring to the teeth of animals. In the idiom ‘to grind one’s teeth’ denotes anger (), but a literal rendering of ‘to grind the teeth’ may mean in some languages merely ‘to be nervous.’ The expression βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων ‘gnashing of the teeth’ is used in connection with the tortures of hell (), but a literal rendering of such a phrase can be quite misleading, since it may refer merely to the eating of some hard substance. See.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘great distress,’ ) to experience great distress or anxiety

Accordingly, in rendering οἰκία[a] or [a] it is necessary to use a number of different terms roughly equivalent to the English series ‘cottage,’ ‘house,’ ‘official residence,’ ‘palace,’ ‘temple,’ etc.|In a number of languages one must distinguish carefully between a house and a home. In, for example, it is significant to indicate that Jesus was dwelling in the house through the roof of which the paralyzed man was let down.

meanings.def: the family consisting of those related by blood and marriage, as well as slaves and servants, living in the same house or homestead
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of οἶκος[b] or [b] would be ‘those who live together’ or ‘those who have the same fence’ (this being a reference to a group of huts surrounded by a fence and thus constituting a single so-called ‘family unit’).|In οἶκος can mean the household over which Joseph was placed, or it can mean the property of Pharaoh (see ).

Some scholars, however, interpret [c] history, ).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).|In there appears to be no significant difference in meaning between οἶκος and, and in some receptor languages it would be sufficient to use a single term essentially equivalent to ‘lineage.’ The two terms appear to simply reinforce their shared meaning.

meanings.note: Though some persons have argued that whenever mention is made of Jesus either making or drinking wine, one must assume that this was only unfermented grape juice, there is no real basis for such a conclusion. Only where οἶνος νέος ‘new wine’ () is mentioned can one assume that this is unfermented grape juice or grape juice in the initial stages of fermentation.|In a number of languages there is no indigenous term for wine, and some expression may simply be borrowed from a dominant language. On the other hand, it is sometimes possible to employ a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘fermented fruit juice.’ In some languages the equivalent for ‘wine’ is more specifically ‘palm wine,’ that is to say, a wine made from the sap of certain palm trees. Such a term may also have a more generic meaning and be applicable to any kind of wine.|There are a number of passages in the NT where one must be particularly careful in the selection of terms to translate wine. For example, in a literal translation of ‘do not get drunk with wine’ could be interpreted to mean that it is permissible for one to get drunk on other types of intoxicating liquors. It may, therefore, be necessary in some languages to render as simply ‘do not get drunk.’|In (κατέδησεν τὰ τραύματα αὐτοῦ ἐπιχέων ἔλαιον καὶ οἶνον ‘he poured on olive oil and wine and bandaged his wounds’) it is important to recognize the medicinal value of oil and wine. In some instances translators have indicated the purpose of such an activity by translating ‘to cleanse and heal his wounds he poured wine and oil on them and bandaged them.’ It may also be possible to add in a marginal note information as to the antiseptic quality of the wine and the value of the oil in the healing process.

meanings.def: a set phrase referring to newly pressed grape juice, unfermented or in the initial stages of fermentation
a set phrase referring to wine drugged with myrrh and used as a stupefying potion
meanings.note: In general, ἐσμυρνισμένος οἶνος must be rendered by means of a phrase or a clause, for example, ‘wine which has been mixed with a drug called myrrh’ or ‘wine mixed with a drug to reduce pain.’ It is, of course, also possible to use an abbreviated phrase such as ‘myrrhed wine’ and then to place the explanation of its function in a marginal note.

meanings.def: drunkenness, implying the consumption of a large quantity of wine
to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being similar to something else in some respect
interrogative references to class or kind

meanings.def: to extend a period of time, with the implication of lack of activity
pertaining to shrinking from or hesitating to engage in something worthwhile, possibly implying lack of ambition
pertaining to being bothersome

meanings.def: pertaining to taking place on the eighth in a series of days
meanings.note: Since in NT times the counting of days involved numbering both the first and the last day in a series, ὀκταήμερος may be rendered as ‘a week later’ or ‘seven days later.’ Compare ἡμέραι ‘eight days’ () as being equivalent to one week; see discussion at.

meanings.def: cardinal number, where there are eight instances of a countable entity
meanings.note: To designate a week, the normal practice in NT times was to speak of ‘eight days,’ since in a series both the first and the last days were counted. The equivalent in many languages would be simply ‘after seven days had passed’ ().

meanings.def: a state of utter ruin or destruction
to cause the complete destruction or ruin of someone or something
the state of having little or inadequate faith
pertaining to having relatively little faith
a relatively small quantity on any dimension
a relatively low point on a scale of extent

meanings.def: a relatively small quantity
pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time

meanings.def: pertaining to having limited or diminished motivation for the attainment of some goal

meanings.def: to regard something or someone as of little value
a degree which almost equals some point on a scale of extent, but not quite

meanings.def: pertaining to being whole, complete, or entire, with focus on unity

g: to be in the company of
