meanings.def: the wife of Ἀνανίας 1
sapphire, usually blue in color (see )
a large container made of woven material, usually grass or reeds; used for carrying a variety of things, including food and produce, and for moving soil from one place to another
meanings.note: In the one context in which σαργάνη occurs (), the basket was evidently rather large, since it was used to let Paul down from an opening in the wall of Damascus. It may very well have been made of braided ropes. In the basket is called σαργάνη, while in the same basket is referred to as ({D:6.149).

meanings.def: a city in western Asia Minor
carnelian or cornelian, usually red in color (see )
onyx, sardonyx, of varying colors (see )
a city on the coast of Phoenicia between Tyre and Sidon
pertaining to what is human or characteristic of human nature
pertaining to being material or physical, with the possible implication of inferior
meanings.note: It is possible that σαρκικός in refers to blessings for the body, but the context would seem to imply blessings of greater significance than those designed only for a person’s body.

meanings.def: pertaining to the natural, physical characteristics of persons and often including their characteristic behavior
(derivative of [f] ‘human nature,’ ) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, but with special focus upon more base physical desires
meanings.note: In some languages the expression τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν in may be rendered as ‘the desires which one’s body has’ or ‘what the body wants.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [c] ‘people,’ ) pertaining to physical human beings
meanings.note: In the phrase ‘human regulations’ can be rendered as ‘regulations made by people.’ For another interpretation of σάρκινος in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to what is human or characteristic of human nature
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to the natural, physical characteristics of persons and often including their characteristic behavior
meanings.note: For another interpretation of σάρκινος in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of [f] ‘human nature,’ ) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, but with special focus upon more base physical desires
meanings.note: For another interpretation of σάρκινος in, see.

meanings.def: the flesh of both animals and human beings
meanings.note: Some languages make an important distinction between the flesh of a living person and the flesh of someone who has been killed or who has died. It would be this latter sense which should be reflected in. In the reference to ‘circumcision in the flesh’ (ἐν σαρκὶ περιτομή) would, however, require the first sense, namely, the flesh of a living person.

meanings.def: a living body
meanings.note: Though the reference of σάρξ in is to the physical body, it may be necessary in some instances to translate this as ‘a human being’ or ‘a person,’ that is to say, ‘Christ appeared as a human being’ or ‘Christ became a person.’ Otherwise, the reader might assume that Christ took on the body of someone else or merely indwelt some miraculous human form rather than actually became a human being

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘flesh,’ ) humans as physical beings
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘flesh,’ ) human nature, with emphasis upon the physical aspects
meanings.note: In a number of languages it would seem strange, if not totally redundant, to speak of ‘physical fathers’ or ‘human fathers’ (), since the term ‘fathers’ would suffice, and any addition would be misleading. In some instances, however, one might use an expression such as ‘our own fathers,’ so as to provide an implied contrast with the heavenly Father. Where it is necessary to qualify the term ‘fathers,’ one may use an expression such as ‘fathers which caused us to be conceived.’

meanings.def: a relatively large group of persons regarded as being biologically related
meanings.note: It may be difficult in some languages to clearly distinguish between culture and race as in. Sometimes this difference can be indicated by saying ‘the woman lived like a Greek, but she was a Syrophoenician’ or ‘… her parents were from Syrophoenicia.’ In translating ‘people of my own race’ in, it may be necessary to say ‘all my fellow Jews’ or ‘all those people of whom I am a part’ or ‘those people who are my roots’ or ‘… my trunk,’ based on the analogy of a tree trunk and branches.

meanings.def: the psychological aspect of human nature which contrasts with the spiritual nature; in other words, that aspect of human nature which is characterized by or reflects typical human reasoning and desires in contrast with those aspects of human thought and behavior which relate to God and the spiritual life
meanings.note: Some scholars understand the meaning of σάρξ[f] as being a person’s lower nature rather than simply human nature, but the distinction between lower nature and higher nature seems to be primarily one arising out of typical Greek thought rather than out of the Semitic background which seems to be so pervasive in the use of the term σάρξ in NT contexts such as. There are, of course, contexts in which σάρξ does refer to that psychological factor in man which serves as a willing instrument of sin and is subject to sin.

meanings.def: human nature, particularly in reference to the physical aspect of human life
meanings.note: In some languages one may more appropriately translate this phrase in as ‘was born like any person is’ or ‘was born like people are normally born.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘flesh,’ ) physical life
(an idiom, literally: desire of the flesh) desire for sexual gratification
(an idiom, literally: flesh and blood) a human being in contrast with a divine being
(an idiom, literally: thorn in the flesh) something which causes serious trouble and difficulty
meanings.note: There are a number of different interpretations of σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί in (see discussion at ).

meanings.def: to sweep by using a broom
the wife of Abraham
the plain along the coast of Palestine
(a borrowing from Hebrew and Aramaic: a title for the Devil, literally: adversary) the principal supernatural evil being
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is a well known proper name for the Devil as the chief of all demons. In other instances, however, he is given a descriptive name, for example, ‘the ruler of the evil spirits,’ ‘the chief of the demons,’ ‘the truly bad one,’ ‘the left-handed one’ (as the one who is opposed to all which is right or correct), ‘the no-good one,’ ‘the avaricious one.’ In some instances a term for the Devil may be highly idiomatic as, for example, ‘the barking one,’ a reference to the Devil’s presumed activity in animal guise.|Some translators have employed for ‘Devil’ the proper name Satan, but this is often not a satisfactory solution. In one language in West Africa, for example, the term Satan had already been borrowed but was understood in the sense of the culture hero of the people and not as a designation for the chief of demons.|See also.

meanings.def: (a borrowing from Hebrew and Aramaic meaning literally: adversary) the usual proper name of the Devil; see also
the Hebrew measure for grain, about a peck and a half or somewhat less than one-half bushel (a bushel consists of four pecks) or approximately twelve liters in the metric system
meanings.note: In the precise amount of flour is not important. What is important is to provide some type of measurement which will indicate a considerable quantity.

meanings.def: an alternative form of,, the Hebrew name of the apostle Paul
to cause a fire to be extinguished
meanings.note: ‘To put out fierce fires’ may be expressed as ‘to cause fierce fires no longer to burn’ or ‘to make large fires stop burning.’ In order to speak of ‘fierce fires’ it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘large, hot fires.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to extinguish a fire,’ ) to cause a fervent activity to cease
meanings.note: Though the particular activity of the Spirit is not overtly indicated in the context of, the book as a whole contains sufficient reference to the activity of the Spirit so as to indicate what is involved.

meanings.def: to cease burning, either because of lack of material to be burned or because the fire has been forcibly extinguished
meanings.note: The expression ‘our lamps are going out’ may be rendered as ‘our lamps will soon not be burning’ or ‘our lamps will burn only a little bit more.’ It may, however, be misleading to speak of ‘lamps burning’ (see discussion in ), and accordingly, it may be much better to translate ‘our lamps will show light only a little bit more’ or ‘the oil in our lamps will burn only a little bit more.’

meanings.def: a reflexive reference to a receptor noted in the immediate context
meanings.note: For the plural, see.

meanings.def: to express in attitude and ritual one’s allegiance to and regard for deity
meanings.note: In a number of languages worship is expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bow down before,’ ‘to lower one’s head before,’ ‘to raise one’s arms to,’ ‘to sing to,’ ‘to honor.’ It is important in selecting an expression for worship to employ a term or phrase which will include various aspects of worship.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to worship,’ ) a place of worship
meanings.note: For another interpretation of σέβασμα in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to worship,’ ) an object which is worshiped
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of ὁ ‘the Emperor,’ ) pertaining to the Emperor
meanings.note: The phrase ‘the imperial regiment’ may be rendered as ‘the group of soldiers who protected the Emperor’ or ‘… who were under the direct command of the Emperor.’

meanings.def: (derivative of σεβαστός ‘revered, worthy of reverence,’ not occurring in the NT) a title for the Roman Emperor and denoting his semidivine status
to express in attitude and ritual one’s allegiance to and regard for deity
meanings.note: In a number of languages worship is expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bow down before,’ ‘to lower one’s head before,’ ‘to raise one’s arms to,’ ‘to sing to,’ ‘to honor.’ It is important in selecting an expression for worship to employ a term or phrase which will include various aspects of worship.

meanings.def: an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
a pliable instrument of binding
meanings.note: In a number of languages a term for chain is simply metal rope. In other languages it may be described as linked rope in contrast with twisted rope, that is, a rope made out of some kind of fiber.|The phrase σειραῖς ζόφου () is admittedly a strange expression, and in some manuscripts this gave rise to a slight change in orthography (σιροῖς; see ) with the resulting meaning being ‘in pits of darkness.’ If, however, one adopts the text ἀλλὰ σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας, it may be possible to interpret the entire expression as ‘but he chained them in the darkness of hell.’
g: chain (made of metal) or rope (made of fiber)

meanings.def: a sudden and severe movement of the earth
meanings.note: Since earthquakes are universal in occurrence, there is normally no difficulty involved in finding some way of speaking about them. However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are used, for example, ‘the devil rolled over’ or ‘mother earth belched.’|In the earthquake is regarded as the cause of the prison foundations shaking, and it may be better to restructure the relationships expressed in as ‘the prison shook because of the earthquake.’

meanings.def: a violent action of the surface of a body of water as the result of high waves caused by a strong wind
meanings.note: Though the term σεισμός[b] obviously implies the strong action of the wind, the focus is upon the violent motion caused by the waves. It might, therefore, be more appropriate to translate as ‘there were huge waves on the sea’ or ‘… on the lake.’ Such a translation would then be appropriate for the following clause.

meanings.def: to cause something to move back and forth rapidly, often violently
meanings.note: In some languages there are quite distinct terms for shaking, depending upon the vigor of the motion and/or the objects which are shaken. Accordingly, one must exercise care in selecting terms which will accurately and adequately represent the nature of the shaking in the various contexts. For example, in the shaking would presumably involve some kind of reverberation, but in the action of the wind suggests whipping something back and forth.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to shake,’ ) to cause extreme anxiety and apprehension, implying accompanying movement
to shake or tremble, often with the implication of fear and/or consternation
meanings.note: In a number of languages there are two distinct terms for trembling, one relating to illness (as in the case of epileptic seizures or the chills and fever associated with malaria) and the other associated with fear.

meanings.def: a Christian of Thessalonica who was a companion of Paul
the port city of Antioch in Syria

a celestial body smaller than the sun that gives light to earth in the nighttime; the moon’s appearance changes over the course of each month as the angle we can see the moon’s half-illuminated surface changes
meanings.note: As in the case of the sun (), there are relatively few difficulties involved in obtaining a satisfactory word for σελήνη ‘the moon,’ though there may also be a tendency to add some kind of honorific or title, for example, ‘mother moon.’ At the same time, certain difficulties may occur in some passages. For example, in it may be misleading to speak of signs occurring ‘in the moon,’ for this might mean ‘inside the moon.’ TEV has resolved the problem somewhat by translating “there will be strange things happening to the sun, the moon, and the stars.” One may also translate ‘the sun, the moon, and the stars will cause signs in the heavens’ or ‘… portents in the sky.’

meanings.def: to suffer epileptic seizures (associated in ancient times with the supernatural power of the moon)
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a fine grade of wheat flour
pertaining to appropriate, befitting behavior and implying dignity and respect
behavior which is befitting, implying a measure of dignity leading to respect
meanings.note: In some languages ‘propriety’ is best expressed as ‘to act in the right way’ or ‘to act as one ought.’

meanings.def: Sergius Paulus, the governor of Cyprus
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause something to be both specific and clear
an event which is regarded as having some special meaning
meanings.note: In translating σημεῖον in, it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘tell us what will happen that will show that you are coming’ or ‘tell us what we will see that will make us know that you are coming.’|σημεῖον as an event with special meaning was inevitably an unusual or even miraculous type of occurrence, and in a number of contexts σημεῖον may be rendered as ‘miracle.’ Certainly that is the referent of the term σημεῖον in (πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦθεωροῦντες αὐτοῦ τὰ σημεῖα ἅ ἐποίει ‘many believed in him as they saw the signs he did’). For the Gospel of John, however, a σημεῖον is not simply a miraculous event but something which points to a reality with even greater significance. A strictly literal translation of σημεῖον as ‘sign’ might mean nothing more than a road sign or a sign on a building, and therefore in some languages σημεῖον in a context such as may be rendered as ‘a miracle with great meaning.’

meanings.def: to pay special attention to something for the sake of a future recall and response
the same day as the day of a discourse
to rot or decay, in reference to organic matter
meanings.note: There may be problems involved in a literal rendering of because it may seem strange to speak of ‘riches rotting,’ since a term for ‘riches’ is likely to refer primarily to money. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘the things that make you rich’ or ‘all the things you have as a rich person.’

meanings.def: smallish brown or gray moth that lays eggs in clothing or other cloth; eggs hatch into very small caterpillars, which feed on the fibers; Tineidae family, probably Tineola biselliella; symbols of decay, ruin, and slow destruction
meanings.note: In the NT the Greek term σής is used only in reference to the larvae of moths, and therefore it is frequently necessary to employ a term in the receptor language for the larvae rather than for the flying insect. This means that frequently an appropriate equivalent is ‘the worms of moths,’ but often one can employ an expression which means simply ‘cloth worms’ or ‘cloth eaters.’|In the effect of the larvae of moths is combined with rust as agents for the destruction of valuable objects. It is rare, however, that one can speak of the destruction caused by moths in the same way as one can describe the effects of rust or tarnish. It may therefore be necessary to talk about ‘moths eating cloth,’ while ‘tarnish ruins precious metal.’

meanings.def: pertaining to that which has been damaged by the larvae of moths
meanings.note: This expression in may often be rendered as ‘your garments have been eaten by worms’ or ‘your garments are full of holes.’

meanings.def: to cause someone to be or to become more able or capable, with the implication of a contrast with weakness
meanings.note: The terms (see ) and σθενόω in are very similar in meaning and serve primarily to intensify the meaning of making persons more able to engage in or to undergo certain experiences.

meanings.def: the fleshy part on either side of the face
meanings.note: Though in many languages there is a specific term for ‘cheek,’ in some instances it may be necessary to use a phrase meaning ‘the side of the head’ or ‘the side of the face.’

meanings.def: to keep quiet, with the implication of preserving something which is secret
the absence of noise
meanings.note: It is possible that σιγή in does not refer to verbal silence.

meanings.def: iron
meanings.note: Since at the present time iron in some form is almost universal throughout the world, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for it. In some instances, in fact, it is such a dominant metal that it is known simply as ‘the metal.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘iron,’ ) pertaining to being made or consisting of iron
a city on the coast of Phoenicia
(derivative of ‘Sidon,’ ) pertaining to Sidon
(derivative of ‘Sidon,’ ) a person who lives in or is a native of Sidon
one who kills someone with intent and as a part of a plot
an intoxicating drink made from grain
meanings.note: Though σίκερα may have a generic meaning and thus refer to any type of intoxicating drink, in the NT it occurs only in, where it contrasts with wine and refers to intoxicating beverages made from grain. Distilled alcoholic beverages, such as whiskey, gin, and vodka, were not known in the ancient world.

meanings.def: a Christian in the Jerusalem church and an associate of Paul
generally regarded as the same person as ()
the name for a system of water supply in Jerusalem; the pool of Siloam was probably the basin into which the water flowed
a cloth or piece of leather wrapped by a workman around his waist or chest to protect his clothes
meanings.note: A σιμικίνθιον may be called in some languages ‘a workman’s cloth’ or ‘a workman’s cloth to protect clothing.’

meanings.def: Simon Peter, one of the twelve apostles
Simon the Zealot, one of the twelve apostles
a brother of Jesus
Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross of Jesus
the father of Judas Iscariot
a tanner in Joppa
a magician of Samaria
a leper
a Pharisee
a rocky mountain on the peninsula of Sinai
mustard plant, a large herb noted for its very small seeds and in some instances growing to a height of three meters (about ten feet)
meanings.note: Note that in (and in the parallel passage ) σίναπι is actually spoken of as a δένδρον tree, evidently a type of rhetorical hyperbole.|Though the mustard plant may not be known in certain areas of the world, the use of mustard as a condiment is widely known, and therefore it is often possible to speak of ‘a plant that produces mustard’ or ‘the plant used in making mustard.’ In order, however, to make the parable meaningful, it may be necessary to have some explanation of this plant in a footnote or glossary.

meanings.def: linen cloth of good quality
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no term for ‘linen,’ and though a word for ‘linen’ may be borrowed, what is important in the NT contexts in which σινδών occurs is primarily the quality of the cloth, not the material of which it was made. Accordingly, many translators have used an expression such as ‘fine cloth’ or ‘good cloth.’

meanings.def: to sift by shaking in a sieve
meanings.note: The expression ὑμᾶς τοῦ σινιάσαι ὡς τὸν σῖτον in is clearly a type of figurative usage and in many languages must be translated as ‘to test you’ or ‘to test you so as to separate the good from the bad.’ In some languages, however, it may be more satisfactory to shift the figure from sifting to winnowing and hence translate ‘to winnow you like a farmer who separates the wheat from the chaff.’

meanings.def: fabric made of threads from the lustrous tough elastic fiber produced by silkworms for their cocoons; highly valued

meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only: ἀλλὰ σιροῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας παρέδωκεν εἰς κρίσιν τηρουμένους ‘but cast them into hell and committed them to the pits of intense gloom to be kept until the judgment’ (apparatus; the text of reads ‘chain,’ ). In this one occurrence of σιρός in the NT, the pit in question is a place of imprisonment until the time of judgment. The expression ‘the pits of intense gloom’ may be translated as ‘pits where it is extremely dark.’|Though most scholars have interpreted σιρός as being equivalent to (), others see a distinction. But there is a danger in attempting to make too many fine distinctions between the meanings of such biblical terms. There is little evidence that biblical writers used such expressions with the same degree of differentiation which some persons would like to find.

meanings.def: pertaining to being well fed on grain and hence fattened
meanings.note: In σιτευτός may, however, mean ‘valuable’ or ‘prize.’ This would simply be an extended meaning of σιτευτός in view of the resulting condition or value of a grain-fed animal. For this interpretation of σιτευτός in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to being valuable or prized on the basis of its being well fed and fat (occurring in reference to a calf)
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: (a diminutive form of ‘grain,’, but not diminutive in meaning) any grain, but with the evident implication of its relevance as food
meanings.note: (See also.) On the basis of this one NT occurrence it is impossible to know whether the meaning of σιτία is ‘grain’ or ‘food,’ since in the phrase σιτία καὶ ποτά ‘food and drink’ (an expression occurring in a number of extrabiblical contexts), the term σιτίον contrasts solid with liquid nourishment.

meanings.def: (diminutive of [a] ‘wheat, grain,’, but without diminutive meaning and occurring primarily in the plural) food consisting principally of grain products
meanings.note: It is, of course, possible in to understand the plural form as ‘grain’ (see ), but the reference is probably to food made from grain, a common meaning of this term in Classical Greek.

meanings.def: pertaining to being well fed on grain and hence fattened
an appropriate portion or ration of food (a type of food allowance)
meanings.note: It is possible to interpret σιτομέτριον in as ‘the proper amount of food’ or ‘the food that was due them’ or ‘the food that should be given (to the servants).’ Since σιτομέτριον is a semantically complex term consisting of two quite distinct components, it is usually necessary to employ a phrase as a proper equivalent.
g: a due amount of food rations

meanings.def: any kind of edible grain, though generally referring to wheat
the plant of wheat
meanings.note: Elsewhere in the NT σῖτος, when used alone, refers to wheat as grain, but even in τοῦ σίτου may be interpreted as a so-called ‘appositional genitive,’ that is, ‘seed which is wheat’ or ‘wheat seed.’|While in some parts of the world wheat as a grain or as a plant is not known, in almost all instances people are acquainted with wheat flour, and therefore it is often possible to translate ‘wheat’ as ‘flour plant’ or ‘plant the grain of which is used to make flour.’ In some languages, however, the only possible equivalent is ‘rice-like plant’ in which ‘rice-like’ means essentially ‘grass-like,’ while at the same time indicating edible grain.

meanings.def: Mount Zion, a hill within the city of Jerusalem
the city of Jerusalem together with its people, particularly in poetic discourse; see also
to refrain from speaking or talking
to lose or not have the ability to speak
meanings.note: It is possible that in means only ‘to say nothing’ or ‘to remain silent’ (), in which case it would probably be better to reverse somewhat the order and translate ‘and you will not be able to speak but will remain silent until the day these things happen.’
g: to not be able to speak

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to be silent,’ ) the process of becoming calm after a storm
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is not possible to translate σιωπάω[c] literally as ‘be still’ since this might imply continue to remain still. Since there is a change in state, it may be necessary to say become still or cease to be stormy.

meanings.def: to cause someone to no longer believe
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand σκανδαλίζω in as meaning ‘to cause offense’ (see ).
g: to cause to give up believing
to make someone no longer believe

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκανδαλίζω ‘to cause to stumble,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause to sin, with the probable implication of providing some special circumstances which contribute to such behavior
to cause someone to experience anger and/or shock because of what has been said or done
meanings.note: See discussion at.
g: to cause someone to be offended

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκανδαλίζομαι ‘to fall into a trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to give up believing what is right and let oneself believe what is false
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand σκανδαλίζομαι in as meaning ‘to let oneself be led into sin’ or ‘to fall into sin as the result of unbelief.’

meanings.def: to fall into sin, with the implication of certain contributing circumstances
to be offended because of some action
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to be offended’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to be bitter against’ or ‘to be stung in the heart.’ In some languages, however, the closest equivalent for some contexts is simply ‘to be angered.’

meanings.def: a trap, probably of the type which has a stick which when touched by an animal causes the trap to shut
meanings.note: In (), (), and σκάνδαλον would all seem to be completely parallel in structure and meaning. As a result, in a number of languages the three terms are reduced often to two, for example, ‘snare’ and ‘trap.’ If there are three different kinds of traps, then, of course, three terms can be used. In some cases, however, it may be preferable to use verbs to express the catching and trapping, and thus one may translate γενηθήτω ἡ τράπεζα αὐτῶν εἰς παγίδα καὶ εἰς θήραν καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον as in TEV, “may they be caught and trapped at their feasts; may they fall.”

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκάνδαλον[a] ‘trap,’ ) that which or one who causes someone to sin
g: that which causes someone to sin
one who causes someone to sin

meanings.def: that which causes offense and thus arouses opposition
to make a hole in the ground and to remove earth with some sharp-edged intrument (for example, a pick or spade)
meanings.note: For another interpretation of σκάπτω in, see.

meanings.def: to dig into the ground, specifically in connection with turning over the earth for agricultural or gardening purposes
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: alternative forms of and, (, apparatus;, apparatus;, apparatus)
a small boat which was normally kept aboard a larger ship and used by sailors in placing anchors, repairing the ship, or saving lives in the case of storms
meanings.note: In some languages σκάφη is equivalent to ‘rowboat’ or ‘lifeboat.’

meanings.def: limb of a human or animal that supports the body and is used for movement; the two human legs extend from the top of the thigh to the foot
clothing as a covering
a Jewish high priest
a collective for any kind of artifact which may be referred to by [a] ‘object, thing’ ()
meanings.note: Wherever possible, it is useful to employ a rather specific term if this is well known in a receptor language. For example, instead of ‘things of a ship’ one may use ‘ship’s gear’ or ‘ship’s rigging.’

meanings.def: any kind of instrument, tool, weapon, equipment, container, or property
meanings.note: The manner in which σκεῦος[a] is translated depends in many instances upon the specific context. It may, of course, be rendered by a highly generic expression such as English ‘thing,’ but wherever the context refers to some particular type of object, it is preferable to employ a specific referent. In, for example, the reference of σκεῦος is generally understood to be the mainsail.

meanings.def: a highly generic term for any kind of jar, bowl, basket, or vase
meanings.note: In and σκεῦος[b] refers to a sheet (as a container) which was let down from heaven in Peter’s vision.|In a number of languages there is no relatively high generic term which may be used to refer to any type of vessel or container, and therefore one must employ more specific terms depending upon the context, even as in the case of most English translations in,, and.

meanings.def: objects which are possessed
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘instrument, thing,’ ) a person in relation to a particular function or role
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘object, thing, instrument,’, or of [b] ‘vessel,’ ) the human body
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret σκεῦος in as meaning ‘wife,’ and for a discussion of this meaning and some of the problems involved in translation, see. A further alternative meaning, and one closely related to the meaning of ‘body’ is ‘sexual life,’ so that this expression in might be rendered as ‘each of you must gain mastery over his sexual life’ or, in the form τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ, ‘your sexual life should be holy and honorable’ (see ).

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [b] ‘vessel,’ ) a woman married to a man, with focus upon the sexual relation
meanings.note: The interpretation of σκεῦος in has given rise to serious divisions of opinion as noted in, where σκεῦος is interpreted as designating a person’s own body. The interpretation of σκεῦος as ‘wife’ is based upon a number of considerations. In the first place, the verb κτᾶσθαι ‘to get, to acquire’ () does not normally go with ‘body,’ while it fits well with the meaning of ‘wife.’ On the other hand, σκεῦος meaning ‘wife’ is nowhere else attested in Greek but is assumed in to refer to a wife primarily on the strength of the particular interpretation of the context, in which ‘immorality’ () in verse 3 and and ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας ‘with a lustful desire’ () in verse 5 are assumed to point to the meaning of σκεῦος as ‘wife.’ In ancient Jewish literature a wife was euphemistically called a ‘vessel’ in contexts relating to sexual relations, and ‘vessel’ is a very common meaning of σκεῦος in Greek. If, therefore, one assumes a Semitic background for this Greek text, the statement in would refer to the need for sexual life to be both holy and honorable (see ).

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to possess a vessel) a euphemistic manner of referring to sexual relations
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand σκεῦος in as one’s wife (see ). σκεῦος in may also be understood as one’s body, and therefore the phrase τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι may be rendered as ‘to control his own body’ (see ).

meanings.def: a portable dwelling of cloth and/or skins, held up by poles and fastened by cords to stakes
meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘tent’ is simply ‘a house made of cloth.’ One should avoid terms which would imply a military tent or a temporary shelter used only on vacations or holidays. In OT times such tents were permanent dwellings of nomadic groups and were moved from place to place as livestock were transferred from one pasture area to another.

meanings.def: the relatively large tent used as a central place of worship by the Jews prior to the building of the Temple
meanings.note: In a number of languages σκηνή[b] may be rendered as ‘the largest tent in which God lived’ or ‘the large tent for worshiping God’ or ‘the holy tent.’ In selecting a proper designation for σκηνή[b], it is important to indicate that the function of σκηνή[b] was essentially the same as that of the Temple; it was only a different type of construction and not a difference of use or of religious relevance.|Since σκηνή[b] refers to one unique object, it is essentially equivalent to a title.

meanings.def: a Jewish festival commemorating God’s provision during the wanderings in the wilderness
meanings.note: In some languages it may be useful to speak of the Festival of Tents as ‘the festival when people lived in tents.’

meanings.def: one who makes tents as an occupation
(figurative extension of meaning of σκῆνος ‘tent,’ not occurring in the NT) temporary habitation in the human body
meanings.note: Only rarely can one preserve in translation the figurative meanings suggested by the terms σκῆνος and σκήνωμα. What is significant in such contexts is the temporary nature of the dwelling, and therefore the relatively brief time which the body is to serve the person who dwells in it. In some cases it may be relevant, therefore, to have a footnote to point out the temporal aspects of this figurative usage of σκῆνος and σκήνωμα[c].

meanings.def: to come to dwell in a place defined psychologically or spiritually (with the possible implication in some contexts of a temporary arrangement)
meanings.note: In all of these contexts, σκηνόω and ἐπισκηνόω are essentially figurative in meaning, for they deal with spiritual existence and residence rather than human residence or dwelling. In translating one should, in so far as possible, try to preserve this important figurative relationship, since it expresses one of the most significant ways in which spiritual and human existence can be combined. In some languages, however, it may be necessary to employ an expression which means simply ‘to be in’ or ‘to continue with,’ since expressions for ‘living’ or ‘dwelling’ may be based upon terms which are too specific in meaning, for example, ‘to eat from the same pot’ or ‘to enter by the same door.’

meanings.def: a dwelling, with the implication of temporary duration
meanings.note: In there is a complex textual problem in which the critical text has τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰακώβ ‘the house of Jacob’ (but in the figurative sense of ‘people’), but the Byzantine text reads τῷ θεῷ Ἰακώβ ‘the God of Jacob.’ It is only with this latter form of the text that σκήνωμα would mean an actual construction or dwelling. If one adopts the form of the critical text, then σκήνωμα would point to ‘a place to dwell,’ in other words, an area or region (see ).

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to take up residence,’ ) a place where one may dwell, with the possible implication in certain contexts of something which is of temporary duration
meanings.note: An alternative reading of the expression σκήνωμα τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰακώβ ‘dwelling place for the people of Jacob’ in has θεῷ for οἴκῳ (see ) and the consequent translation ‘a house for the God of Jacob.’|For another interpretation of σκήνωμα in, see.

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘temporary dwelling,’ ) temporary habitation in the human body
meanings.note: Only rarely can one preserve in translation the figurative meanings suggested by the terms and σκήνωμα. What is significant in such contexts is the temporary nature of the dwelling, and therefore the relatively brief time which the body is to serve the person who dwells in it. In some cases it may be relevant, therefore, to have a footnote to point out the temporal aspects of this figurative usage of and σκήνωμα[c].|It is also possible to interpret σκήνωμα in as meaning a temporary habitation, though referring, of course, to the human body (see ).

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to be in a dwelling, see ) to be alive, with special emphasis upon physical existence on earth
meanings.note: Most languages have rather generic expressions for ‘life’ or ‘to live,’ but sometimes there are idiomatic expressions which may readily fit the types of contexts illustrated by and, for example, ‘to have strength,’ ‘to have one’s eyes,’ and ‘to walk about on the earth.’

meanings.def: shade, as a shelter from light and the heat associated with light
meanings.note: A term for ‘shade’ as an area sheltered from the direct rays of the sun usually differs from a term for ‘shadow,’ which is cast by a particular object blocking rays of light (see ).

meanings.def: the shape or shade cast by an object which blocks rays of light
meanings.note: In (τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις ‘those living in the darkness and shadow of death’), σκιά may be interpreted as being used figuratively of a shadow cast by impending death, that is to say, death is personified in such a way as to suggest that it casts a shadow because of its nearness. One may, therefore, translate τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις as ‘those who live in the darkness of impending death,’ in which case σκιά becomes essentially equivalent to an expression of time.|In a number of languages a term for ‘shadow’ has a number of very important meanings. In some instances it is regarded as a part of personality which goes on to the next world, since a dead person no longer ‘casts a shadow.’ The shadow may also be regarded as a kind of counterpart of the personality, a type of alter ego. In cases of severe illness one may say ‘his shadow has walked away,’ and in many parts of the world the shadow of a person is an important element in the practice of black magic, for to damage a shadow may be regarded as a means of causing harm to a person.

meanings.def: a faint archetype which foreshadows a later reality
to leap or jump, as a possible expression of joy and happiness
meanings.note: For a difference of semantic focus see ).|In σκιρτάω may be regarded as an instance of figurative usage: ἐσκίρτησεν τὸ βρέφος ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτῆς ‘the baby leaped for joy in her womb.’|Though it may seem quite natural to speak of ‘leaping for joy,’ in some cultures this would not be a meaningful combination of words, for leaping might suggest anger, ritual exorcism (driving out demons), or preparation for war. It may, therefore, be necessary in some languages to translate ‘jump for joy’ merely as ‘be exceedingly glad.’ It may be particularly awkward to speak of a fetus jumping in the womb, for obviously it would simply be a rapid movement of the limbs and not actual change of location. Therefore, it may be better to translate in some instances ‘moved quickly to show joy’ or ‘… as a sign of happiness.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to jump for joy,’ ) to be extremely happy, possibly implying in some contexts actually leaping or dancing for joy
meanings.note: χάρητε ἐν ἐκείνω τῇ ἡμέρᾳ καὶ σκιρτήσατε ‘be glad when that happens and dance for joy’, but see also for a different semantic focus. The phrase ‘for joy’ clearly expresses ‘reason,’ and therefore it may be useful to translate ‘dance for joy’ as ‘dance because I am so joyful’ or ‘… so happy.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate
meanings.note: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

meanings.def: pertaining to being harsh and violent
meanings.note: For another interpretation of σκληρός in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to being powerful or strong
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to being harsh or possibly cruel in one’s behavior
meanings.note: In a number of languages σκληρός in may be translated as ‘words that cause pain’ or idiomatically as ‘words that are like daggers.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being hard and demanding in one’s behavior
a stubborn attitude with regard to any change in behavior
meanings.note: In a number of languages stubbornness may be described as ‘refusing to change’ or ‘refusing to think differently.’ In some instances stubbornness may be expressed idiomatically as ‘one’s heart only sees one thing’ or ‘one’s heart is blind’ or ‘one who always says No.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate
meanings.note: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

meanings.def: to cause to be stubborn and obstinate, especially with regard to the truth
meanings.note: In the expression σκληρύνω τὰς καρδίας ‘to cause the hearts to be obstinate’ in, must be understood as ‘the inner self’ (see ) and as such the addition of merely reinforces the meaning of the verb σκληρύνω.

meanings.def: to be stubborn, in the sense of refusing to believe
pertaining to being crooked or winding
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘crooked,’ ) pertaining to being unscrupulous and dishonest
a sharp projection of a woody plant (though possibly a splinter of wood) with the implication of its causing injury and discomfort
meanings.note: In the NT σκόλοψ occurs only in the figurative expression σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί ‘thorn in the flesh,’ and this expression has been subject to a number of different interpretations (see ).

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: thorn in the flesh) something which causes serious trouble and difficulty
meanings.note: There are a number of different interpretations of σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί in (see discussion at ).

meanings.def: to continue to regard closely
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand σκοπέω in as being predominantly a mental process of paying close attention in order to be prepared to respond appropriately (see ).

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to notice carefully,’ ) to be ready to learn about future dangers or needs, with the implication of preparedness to respond appropriately
to exert effort in continually acquiring information regarding some matter, with the implication of concern as to how to respond appropriately
to keep on giving serious consideration to something
g: to let one’s mind dwell on

meanings.def: that toward which movement or activity is directed
meanings.note: The context of σκοπός in is highly figurative, and in some languages it may be better rendered as ‘what I seek to achieve’ or ‘what I wish to accomplish.’ For σκοπός in the idiom κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω, see.

meanings.def: to cause a group or a gathering to disperse or scatter
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to scatter,’ ) to give or distribute generously or in abundance
meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘to give generously’ may simply be rendered as ‘to give much often,’ but one may sometimes employ such figurative expressions as ‘to give from a full heart’ or ‘to give without holding back anything.‘

meanings.def: terrestrial arachnid (eight-legged) with pincers and a poisonous sting at the end of its jointed tail, which it can hold curved over the back; grows to about 13 cm long; known for the pain and danger of its sting, and associated with harsh, inhospitable living conditions
meanings.note: In the two NT occurrences of σκορπίος (), the emphasis is upon the stinging capacity of the scorpion, and if in a particular area of the world scorpions are not known, it is possible to use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a fierce, stinging, little creature.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being in a state of darkness
meanings.note: In some languages ‘dark’ may be most satisfactorily expressed as ‘without light.’

meanings.def: a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see )
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning [a] ‘darkness,’ ) the realm of sin and evil
pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
(derivative of [a] ‘darkness,’ ) to change from a condition of being light to one of being dark
meanings.note: In it may not be difficult to speak of ‘the air becoming dark,’ since this would mean the space above the earth, but it may be difficult to speak of ‘the sun becoming dark.’ In the latter instance, for both and, one may say ‘the sun will no longer shine’ or ‘the sun will not give its light.’|In place of ‘the air became dark,’ it is also possible to speak of ‘the sky will become dark.’

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to become dark,’ ) to become unable to perceive and thus unable to understand
meanings.note: It is rare that one can combine the concept of ‘becoming dark’ with incapacity to understand or comprehend. Sometimes a parallel figure of speech may be employed by using an expression such as ‘to not be able to see.’ For example, in it is sometimes possible to translate ‘their foolish minds became unable to see the truth,’ and in it is sometimes possible to translate ‘they were not able to see with their minds.’
g: to not be able to understand

meanings.def: a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see )
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘darkness,’ ) the realm of sin and evil
meanings.note: It is possible that in σκότος[b] is a figurative reference to the Devil or Satan, since ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους is in a parallel relationship with τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: the gloom of darkness) the dark, gloomy nature of hell as a place of punishment
(an idiom, literally: the outer darkness) a place or region which is both dark and removed (presumably from the abode of the righteous) and serving as the abode of evil spirits and devils
meanings.note: In a number of languages this expression in must be rendered as ‘they will be thrown outside where it is dark.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘darkness,’ ) to change from a condition of being light to one of being dark
meanings.note: In it may not be difficult to speak of ‘the air becoming dark,’ since this would mean the space above the earth, but it may be difficult to speak of ‘the sun becoming dark.’ In the latter instance, for both and, one may say ‘the sun will no longer shine’ or ‘the sun will not give its light.’|In place of ‘the air became dark,’ it is also possible to speak of ‘the sky will become dark.’

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to become dark,’ ) to become unable to perceive and thus unable to understand
meanings.note: It is rare that one can combine the concept of ‘becoming dark’ with incapacity to understand or comprehend. Sometimes a parallel figure of speech may be employed by using an expression such as ‘to not be able to see.’ For example, in it is sometimes possible to translate ‘their foolish minds became unable to see the truth,’ and in it is sometimes possible to translate ‘they were not able to see with their minds.’
g: to not be able to understand

meanings.def: worthless or unwanted material that is rejected and normally thrown out
(derivative of Σκυθία ‘Scythia,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Scythia, a region north of the Black Sea, and regarded by the GrecoRoman world as utterly pagan and uncivilized
pertaining to being sad and discouraged
to cause trouble or harassment
to suffer trouble or harassment
meanings.note: In σκύλλου can perhaps be best rendered in some languages by supplying a pronoun, for example, ‘do not bother yourself’ or ‘do not trouble yourself’ or even ‘do not cause yourself difficulty.’

meanings.def: that which is taken away by force, particularly in the case of war
pertaining to being eaten by worms (a reference to the occurrence of worms in ulcerous tissue)
meanings.note: In some languages it is important to make a clear distinction between intestinal parasites and the grubs of flies which feed on ulcerous tissue.

meanings.def: small, soft, legless, tube-shaped creatures that have no bones or shells. They typically feed on overripe fruit, rotting meat, and similar things; most are larvae that hatch from the eggs laid by flies or some beetles; symbols of uncleanness, decay, and death
meanings.note: In the reference is clearly to the type of maggots which feed on refuse.|In a number of languages a very important distinction is made between three different types of worms: (1) maggots, (2) worms that live in the ground, so-called ‘earthworms,’ and (3) intestinal worms. It is essential that an appropriate term be employed in order to avoid meaninglessness or misunderstanding.

meanings.def: (derivative of emerald, ) consisting of emerald, emerald-like, (see )
emerald, green in color (see ).
an aromatic resin of a lily-like plant, often used for embalming a corpse
meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only: φέρων σμῆγμα σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης ‘bringing perfumed ointment of myrrh and aloes’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: the aromatic resin of certain bushes
meanings.note: Myrrh was used as one of the ingredients involved in the process of embalming a corpse. Most translators borrow a term for myrrh and then use some kind of marginal note to explain that myrrh was a valuable aromatic substance often used in preserving a corpse. See.

meanings.def: a city on the west coast of Asia Minor
wine drugged with myrrh and used as a stupefying potion
meanings.note: In general, ἐσμυρνισμένος οἶνος must be rendered by means of a phrase or a clause, for example, ‘wine which has been mixed with a drug called myrrh’ or ‘wine mixed with a drug to reduce pain.’ It is, of course, also possible to use an abbreviated phrase such as ‘myrrhed wine’ and then to place the explanation of its function in a marginal note.

meanings.def: a city located near the Dead Sea and destroyed because of its evil; possible identification with Tel Hammam, northeast of the Dead Sea
the son and successor of David
a stretcher or plank used for carrying a corpse to a place of burial
pertaining to a receptor
a small piece of cloth used as a towel, napkin, or face cloth
a follower of Jesus
the capacity to understand and, as a result, to act wisely
the content of what is known by those regarded as wise
knowledge which makes possible skillful activity or performance
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret σοφία in as wisdom which makes possible correct understanding (see ).

meanings.def: a document or book containing wise sayings (as in the phrase ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the Wisdom of God,’, a possible reference to the OT or to apocryphal wisdom literature, possibly even a book which has been lost)
meanings.note: If one understands ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ as being a reference to a book, one could translate the statement in as ‘for this reason, the book entitled The Wisdom of God has the words: …’ On the other hand, the phrase ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ in may mean merely ‘God’s wisdom’ (), and therefore this expression in could be rendered as ‘God in his wisdom said’ or ‘God, who is wise, said.’

meanings.def: to cause a person to have wisdom and understanding
(derivative of [c] ‘specialized knowledge, skill,’ ) to have specialized knowledge involving the capacity to produce what is cleverly or skillfully made
g: to know how to create skillfully
to know how to contrive cleverly

meanings.def: pertaining to specialized knowledge resulting in the skill for accomplishing some purpose
meanings.note: In some languages one may render the phrase ‘expert builder’ () as ‘one who knew just how to build best.’

meanings.def: pertaining to understanding resulting in wisdom
a person of professional or semi-professional status who is regarded as particularly capable in understanding the philosophical aspects of knowledge and experience
a country at the western end of the Mediterranean Sea
to cause a person to shake violently in convulsions
to wrap a child in swaddling clothes (long strips of cloth)
g: to clothe in strips of cloth
to wrap up in strips of cloth

meanings.def: to indulge oneself excessively in satisfying one’s own appetites and desires
to pull or drag, requiring force because of the inertia of the object being dragged
a Roman military unit of about six hundred soldiers, though only a part of such a cohort was often referred to as a cohort
to scatter seed over tilled ground
meanings.note: In many languages there is a problem of translating σπείρω literally as ‘to scatter seed,’ since this is interpreted as an exceedingly wasteful manner of sowing, but unless one translates more or less literally and then provides some explanatory footnote, the parable loses much of its significance for many cultures.

meanings.def: a soldier who acts as a courier to carry confidential information
meanings.note: In σπεκουλάτωρ may also have the meaning of ‘executioner’ (see ).

meanings.def: one who carries out official executions on the basis of orders from military or government officials
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret (a borrowing from Latin) as meaning ‘courier,’ possibly a soldier who had special duties to carry messages of a confidential nature (see ).

meanings.def: to pour out an offering as an act of worship or ritual observance
meanings.note: In some languages it may be almost meaningless to speak of ‘a person being poured out,’ and therefore it may be more appropriate to translate this expression in as ‘but if my blood is to be poured out upon the sacrifice.’ In and in (the other occurrence of σπένδω in the NT), the contexts are highly figurative.

meanings.def: the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
meanings.note: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (, σπέρμα, ), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘seed,’ ) posterity, with emphasis upon the ancestors role in founding the lineage
meanings.note: See discussion at.

meanings.def: a derivative and imparted nature
meanings.note: If in some languages it is not possible to speak literally of ‘God’s nature,’ it may still be possible to render the second clause in as ‘because something of what God is like is in him’ or ‘because he has in himself something of what God is like.’

meanings.def: (idioms, literally: to raise up seed) the male role in begetting children
meanings.note: In contexts such as,, and it may be important to add a note concerning levirate responsibilities, that is to say, the requirement for a younger brother to beget children by a deceased older brother’s wife and the reckoning of such an offspring as being the descendant of the older deceased brother.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of a term based on the practice of birds in picking up seeds) one who acquires bits and pieces of relatively extraneous information and proceeds to pass them on with pretense and show
meanings.note: The term σπερμολόγος is semantically complex in that it combines two quite distinct phases of activity: (1) the acquiring of information and (2) the passing on of such information. Because of the complex semantic structure of σπερμολόγος, it may be best in some languages to render it as ‘one who learns lots of trivial things and wants to tell everyone about his knowledge,’ but in most languages there is a perfectly appropriate idiom for ‘a pseudo-intellectual who insists on spouting off.’ For a different focus on the meaning of σπερμολόγος in, see.

meanings.def: (a figurative expression, literally: one who picks up seed; originally a reference to birds picking up seed, but figuratively applied to a person who is an information scavenger) one who is not able to say anything worthwhile in view of his miscellaneous collection of tidbits of information
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy
meanings.note: For another interpretation of σπεύδω in, see.

meanings.def: to cause something to happen soon
meanings.note: It is also possible to render this meaning of σπεύδω in as ‘doing your best to cause …’

meanings.def: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: a cave or den generally large enough for at least temporary occupation by persons (since such places were often used for habitation or refuge by those who were refugees or thieves, σπήλαιον has in certain contexts the connotation of a ‘hideout’)
meanings.note: In the reference of σπήλαιον is literal, since people actually hid themselves in such caves. In, however, the reference is to the Temple, which has been made a kind of ‘cave’ or ‘den,’ and since the connotation of the term suggests a ‘hideout,’ this is obviously a reflection upon the activities and motivations of those who had commercialized the Temple in Jerusalem.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σπιλάς ‘a rock or reef washed by the sea,’ not occurring in the NT) an unrecognized source of danger or peril
meanings.note: σπιλάς in may also be understood as meaning ‘spot’ or ‘stain’ (see ).

meanings.def: that which constitutes an unwanted spot or stain upon something
meanings.note: It is also possible that in σπιλάς means an ‘unseen danger,’ in that it may refer to a rock which is mostly or completely covered by the sea (see ).

meanings.def: that which constitutes an unwanted spot or stain upon something
to cause a spot or stain upon something
to experience great affection and compassion for someone
the inner parts of the body, especially the intestines
(figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘intestines,’ ) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling
meanings.note: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον[b], κοιλία[c], and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

meanings.def: experiencing great affection and compassion for someone
meanings.note: In the phrase ἐν σπλάγχνοις Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ is ambiguous. It may mean ‘because of the compassion which Christ Jesus himself has for you’ or ‘… for me.’ On the other hand, it may also be interpreted as characterizing the kind of love which Paul has for the believers, for example, ‘how I long for all of you, even with the kind of love Christ Jesus himself has for you.’

meanings.def: one for whom there is deep affection or compassion
(an idiom, literally: to be restricted in the bowels) to restrict one’s affection for someone
meanings.note: In it is also possible to understand στενοχωρέομαι as meaning ‘to live with severe restrictions’ (see ), and σπλάγχνα may be interpreted as a psychological faculty of intent and feeling (see ).
g: to not respond with affection to someone

meanings.def: a porous material used to absorb liquid
meanings.note: In the only type of NT context in which σπόγγος occurs (;; ), it serves as a container for cheap wine offered to Jesus on the cross.

meanings.def: the residue from a burned substance
meanings.note: It may be important in rendering σποδὸς δαμάλεως to indicate that the ashes are the result of the animal having been burned as a sacrifice, for example, ‘the ashes of a heifer burned as a sacrifice.’ Otherwise, the relationship between ‘ashes’ and ‘heifer’ may be difficult, if not impossible, for readers to understand.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σπορά ‘sowing of seed,’ not occurring in the NT) the instrumental means of birth
(derivative of ‘to sow,’ ) grain growing in a field
meanings.note: In a number of languages there are distinct terms for various stages of growth of grain, and in view of the context of the account in and parallel passages, it is important to indicate that the grain was essentially ripe.

meanings.def: the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
meanings.note: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (,, σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’|See also for ‘seed’ used figuratively of descendants.

meanings.def: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy
to do something with intense effort and motivation

Accordingly, ‘all the runners in the stadium’ may very well be rendered as ‘all the runners who are racing.’ The focus here is upon the competition rather than upon the type of place in which the competition took place.

a pole stuck into the ground in an upright position with a crosspiece attached to its upper part; used as a means of execution
meanings.note: In (τοῦτον ἠγγάρευσαν ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ ‘they forced him to carry Jesus’ cross’) the reference is probably to the crosspiece of the cross, which normally would have been carried by a man condemned to die.|Because of the symbolism associated with the cross, translations of the NT in all languages preserve some expression which will identify the cross, not only as a means of capital punishment, but as having a particular form, namely, an upright pole with a crossbeam. In some receptor languages the term for a cross means simply ‘crossbeam.’ In other instances it is composed of a phrase meaning ‘crossed poles.’ It is important, however, to avoid an expression which will suggest crossed sticks in the form of X rather than a cross consisting of an upright with a horizontal beam. If at all possible one should employ a term or phrase which may be used in an extended sense, since in so many contexts the term ‘cross’ refers not only to the instrument of Christ’s death, but to the event of execution. It also becomes a symbol of the message of forgiveness and of reconciliation. Because of these extended meanings, it is important to choose a form which can, if at all possible, support these additional meanings.

meanings.def: to execute someone by nailing that person to a cross
meanings.note: It is rare that one can find in receptor languages a technical term or phrase meaning specifically ‘to crucify.’ In general, a phrase must be employed, since this type of execution is no longer practiced. One can, for example, use such expressions as ‘to nail to a cross bar’ or ‘to nail up on wood’ or even ‘to nail up high.’

meanings.def: the dense spiky cluster in which the seeds of grain such as wheat and barley grow (restricted in NT contexts to references to wheat)

meanings.note: In general, the types of roofs referred to in the NT are flat-top, made of pounded dirt, sometimes mixed with lime or stone, and supported by heavy beams. In view of the various types of activities described as taking place on the housetop, it may be important in some languages to indicate either in the text or in a marginal note the fact that such housetops were flat and that there was usually easy access to such roofs.
