meanings.def: to press in hard from all sides
(an idiom, literally: to hold the ears closed) to refuse to listen to what is being said
meanings.note: In some languages the refusal to hear may be expressed idiomatically as ‘they put their hands over their ears’ or ‘they closed their ears’ or ‘the words never entered their heads.’

meanings.def: to experience a state or condition, generally involving duration
to experience great psychological pressure and anxiety
to continue with close attention and devotion
g: to continue to give oneself to
to continue to apply oneself to

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to be held together from) to be in a mental state between two alternatives
meanings.note: In a number of languages the rendering of this statement in must be expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘my mind is pulling me in two directions’ or ‘my thoughts are going in two different directions’ or ‘my heart is speaking two different words to me.’
g: to be pulled in two directions

meanings.def: to be happy as the result of the pleasure derived from some experience or state
meanings.note: In a number of languages one may speak of ‘one’s inner being’ as ‘one’s liver’ or ‘one’s heart’ or ‘one’s abdomen’ (employing a reference to one of the organs of the body as a focal element of the personality). But in some languages a more figurative and idiomatic expression may be employed, for example, ‘one’s inner counterpart’ or ‘the little one who stands inside of a person.’ It is often this central or crucial aspect of the personality which must be referred to in contexts speaking of the type of pleasure or delight which one might have in the law of God.

meanings.def: a pattern of behavior more or less fixed by tradition and generally sanctioned by the society
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘custom’ or ‘habit,’ but the same meaning is communicated by verbal aspects or adverbial phrases indicating habitual action. For example, in the case of one may translate in some languages ‘as is the way in which Jews always bury people,’ and for one may translate ‘this is not what we constantly do.’

meanings.def: a person who is of one’s own age
to bury someone along with someone else
meanings.note: In συνθάπτω is used figuratively, since it evidently had not yet acquired a conventional figurative meaning. In a number of languages it is necessary to mark this figurative usage by means of a simile, for example, ‘we were, so to speak, buried with him.’

meanings.def: to break or shatter a solid object into pieces, with the implication of destruction
to press in hard from all sides
(an idiom, literally: to break the heart) to cause great sorrow and grief
meanings.note: It is rare that one can reproduce in a literal form the idiom συνθρύπτω τὴν καρδίαν. A frequent equivalent of ‘to break one’s heart’ is ‘to cause one to cry.’ In some languages one may even have ‘to cause one’s heart to cry.’

meanings.def: to employ one’s capacity for understanding and thus to arrive at insight
to be able to understand and evaluate
to indicate approval of a person or event, with the implication that others adopt the same attitude
to cause something to be known by action
meanings.note: In a number of languages the expression ‘to show oneself to be’ may best be rendered as ‘to cause people to know that one is,’ and therefore this expression in may be rendered as ‘in everything causing people to know by what we do that we are servants of God.’

meanings.def: to bring together or hold together something in its proper or appropriate place or relationship
meanings.note: In it may not be easy to indicate clearly the relationship of the phrase ‘in him’ to the rest of the expression, namely, ‘all things hold together.’ Some translations have expanded the expression ‘in him’ to ‘in union with him’ or ‘in view of the fact that we are joined together with him.’|It is also possible to understand ἐν αὐτῷ as indicating agent, so that this expression in may mean ‘by means of him all things hold together.’

meanings.def: to stand together with someone
meanings.note: It is, of course, essential to avoid the idiomatic meaning of ‘to stand with’ in a sense of ‘to support.’ In this context the emphasis is simply upon being present with.

meanings.def: to come into existence, with the implication of acquiring form and substance
to travel together with
meanings.note: In a number of languages it may be necessary in speaking of ‘travelling’ to indicate whether a single journey is involved or whether one is going from place to place. In it is evidently a single journey.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to travel with,’ ) a group of persons travelling together
g: a group of those travelling with

meanings.def: to be aware of information about something
to share information or knowledge with
meanings.note: The sharing of information may be expressed in as ‘his wife also knew about it.’
g: to know something together with someone else

meanings.def: to conduct oneself in relation to a person with whom one lives
to be built together with some other object or objects
meanings.note: The context of is, of course, figurative.

meanings.def: to converse with someone, including a clear implication as to reciprocal response
to be at a place which is next to something else
meanings.note: In a number of languages the concept of ‘being next to’ may be best expressed as ‘there was no space between.’

meanings.def: to acquire information, with focus upon the event of perception
to come to understand clearly on the basis of perceived information
a state of mental distress, involving acute anxiety
to give detailed instructions as to what must be done
a point of time marking the end of a duration
meanings.note: As in the case of a number of expressions involving ‘end,’ it may be important to use a verb meaning ‘to finish,’ for example, ‘so it will be like that when the age finishes’ or ‘… when there isn’t any more of the age.’

meanings.def: to bring an activity to a successful finish
meanings.note: It is also possible to render this phrase in as ‘for he will settle the account,’ the implication being that he will accomplish what he has said he would do.

meanings.def: to cause to exist by virtue of its having been finally accomplished
(derivative of ‘end,’ ) to occur or happen at the end of a duration
to cause a duration to come to an abrupt end, with the implication of sooner than expected
meanings.note: There are a number of different opinions with regard to the meaning of συντέμνω in. Translators are accordingly encouraged to consult commentaries and to provide for significantly different interpretations in translations.

meanings.def: to cause something to continue along with something else
to exert mental effort in storing information so as to have continual access and use of it
meanings.note: An equivalent of ‘to keep in mind’ may be ‘to keep thinking about’ or ‘to continue to think about’ or even ‘not to stop thinking about.’
g: to cause oneself to be fully aware of

meanings.def: to work out a joint arrangement
pertaining to a relatively brief period of time, implying some measure of reduction or shortening
to come together quickly to form a crowd
(a figurative extension of meaning of συντρέχω ‘to run with,’ not occurring in the NT) to be closely associated with others in a particular type of behavior or conduct
to break or shatter a solid object into pieces, with the implication of destruction
to cause damage to an object by crushing
meanings.note: It is difficult to know precisely what the reference is in the use of συντρίβω in. The obvious result is severe pain, but it is not possible to tell precisely what symptoms are involved in what is described as being crushed by the demon.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [b] ‘to crush,’ ) to overcome, with the resulting crushing of the power of the opposition
a state of destruction and ruin
meanings.note: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘leaving ruin’ except in the sense of going off from ruin. Accordingly, it may be necessary to render this expression in as ‘they cause ruin and misery wherever they go.’

meanings.def: a person offered parental care and/or adoption along with the reference person, though not related by blood
meanings.note: It is possible, however, that σύντροφος in has the meaning of ‘a close friend from childhood’ (see ).|In some languages ‘a foster brother’ may be referred to as ‘a person who becomes a brother by being adopted’ or ‘a person who grows up just as though he were a brother.’

meanings.def: a close friend on the basis of having been brought up together
meanings.note: Some scholars, however, understand σύντροφος in as being an instance of [a] 'foster brother' (see ).

meanings.def: to come near to or to reach, with the implication of some type of association
a Christian woman in the church of Philippi
to act hypocritically along with others
to help by joining in an activity or effort
meanings.note: In a number of instances it is not necessary to specify the joint effort or activity, since this is supplied by the context itself as, for example, in in which ‘coming to help’ indicates clearly the joint efforts. But in some languages it may be important to use a specific expression rather than a generic one. Accordingly, ‘to come and help them’ in may be rendered as ‘to come and work with them.’

meanings.def: to suffer great anguish or pain together, with the implication of an important and creative event
a plan for taking secret action against someone or some institution, with the implication of an oath binding the conspirators
a city on the east coast of Sicily
a region to the north and east of Palestine and known as Aram in OT times
(derivative of ‘Syria,’ ) a person who is a native of Syria
(derivative of Συροφοινικία ‘Syro-Phoenicia,’ not occurring in the NT) a woman who is a native of Syro-Phoenicia
meanings.note: See also discussion at.

meanings.def: two shallow and treacherous Mediterranean gulfs along the north African coastline
to pull or drag, requiring force because of the inertia of the object being dragged
to drag or pull by physical force, often implying resistance
to cause a person to shake violently in convulsions
a sign which has been previously agreed upon as having a particular meaning or significance
meanings.note: If a language has no specific term for ‘signal’ or ‘sign,’ one may indicate the implications of σύσσημον by translating the first part of as follows: ‘the one who betrayed him told them how he would indicate who Jesus was; he said, The one whom I kiss is the man.’

meanings.def: a person who is a member of a group, with emphasis upon his coordinate relation to other members of the group
meanings.note: The concept of ‘being a co-member’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘a person who is counted along with others,’ so that in one may translate ‘the Gentiles are counted along with the Jews in sharing in the promise’ or even ‘the Gentiles along with the Jews share in the promise.’

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘to recommend,’ ) pertaining to being commended or recommended
meanings.note: It may be necessary to restructure considerably the components in an expression such as ‘we need letters of recommendation to you,’ for example, ‘we need letters written to you which recommend us’ or ‘… which say, These men are good.’

meanings.def: to crucify someone at the same time that another person is being crucified
to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
to remove from a place by taking away or carrying away
meanings.note: In συστέλλω may also be interpreted as meaning ‘to wrap up’ (see ).

meanings.def: to wrap up an object, with the implication of getting it ready to remove
meanings.note: For another interpretation of συστέλλω in, see.

meanings.def: to groan or to sigh together with someone else
meanings.note: In συστενάζω is used figuratively. It may be difficult to speak of ‘all of creation groans together,’ since the phrase ‘all of creation’ would seem to be a total unit. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘all of creation groans together’ as ‘all parts of the creation groan together’ or ‘everything that has been created is groaning at the same time.’

meanings.def: to correspond to something else in certain significant features
meanings.note: In a number of languages συστοιχέω in a context such as may be best rendered as ‘points to’ or ‘is really talking about,’ so that one may render this expression in as ‘Mount Sinai … really points to the present Jerusalem’ or ‘Hagar … really points to the present Jerusalem.’ The full form of may be rendered as ‘Hagar, who stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia, represents the present Jerusalem.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of συστρατιώτης ‘fellow soldier,’ not occurring in the NT) one who serves in arduous tasks or undergoes severe experiences together with someone else
meanings.note: A strictly literal translation of συστρατιώτης in might imply that Paul himself was a soldier and therefore, in a sense, a secret agent of some military force. Accordingly, it may be necessary to employ a simile, for example, ‘who works like a fellow soldier’ or ‘one who experiences great hardships along with us.’
g: one who works arduously along with

meanings.def: to cause to come together, whether of animate or inanimate objects
the movement of two or more objects to the same location
meanings.note: In a number of languages important distinctions are made in terms referring to gathering or assembling of animate beings. The distinctions are usually based upon the number of individuals, the distance which they have come, and whether or not the individuals in question constitute a membership group or whether they are merely a loose aggregation. In view of these types of distinctions, it is likely that quite different terms will be required for the various contexts listed for this set of related meanings.

meanings.def: disorderly mob revolt, with special implications of uproar and disturbance
meanings.note: In a number of languages the meaning of ‘riot’ may be best expressed as ‘people shouting strongly against’ or ‘people shouting and fighting against’ or ‘a mob shouting against the government.’

meanings.def: a plan devised by a number of persons who agree to act against someone or some institution
meanings.note: See and its footnote.

meanings.def: to form or mold one’s behavior in accordance with a particular pattern or set of standards
meanings.note: In order to express the concept of ‘conforming one’s life’ it may be necessary in some languages to indicate the factor of change, for example, ‘to change one’s life so that it will be like.’

meanings.def: a city in Samaria
the son of Hamor (τοῦ Συχέμ, apparatus)
a city in Samaria
slaughtering, either of animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
(an idiom, literally: day of slaughter) a time of destructive judgment
meanings.note: The reference of the phrase ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς in is the destructive judgment of God, but it is possible that σφαγῆς should be interpreted in a more literal sense of ‘destruction’ rather than mere condemnation.

meanings.def: that which is offered as a sacrifice
meanings.note: The terms σφάγια and θυσίας semantically reinforce one another and are here combined essentially for emphasis.

meanings.def: to slaughter, either animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
a very high point on a scale of extent and in many contexts implying vehemence or violence
a very high point on a scale of extent and in many contexts implying vehemence or violence
to use a seal to close or to make something secure
meanings.note: For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved with ‘seal,’ see.

meanings.def: (derivative of [c] ‘mark, seal,’ ) to put a mark on something, primarily to indicate ownership but possibly also to mark group identity
to arrange to give something to someone in a secure manner
meanings.note: For a somewhat different interpretation of σφραγίζω in, see.
g: to turn over to in a secure way
to give in a secure manner

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to seal,’ ) to deliver something safely to a destination
meanings.note: It is also possible that σφραγισάμενος in serves to confirm the significance of the collection which has been raised. For a somewhat different interpretation of σφραγίζω in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of [e] ‘validation,’ ) to demonstrate by authentic proof the truth or validity of something
an engraved object used to make a mark denoting ownership, approval, or closure of something (normally done by pressing into heated wax and usually attached to a document or letter)
meanings.note: In some languages the closest equivalent to ‘seal’ or ‘signet’ is the mark made by the seal, for example, ‘the symbol of his name’ or ‘the mark of his ownership.’ In certain contexts one may employ a phrase such as ‘the instrument by which a mark is made.’

meanings.def: the substance which bears the imprint of a seal or signet (see [a], ), used for sealing a document or for showing ownership or endorsement
meanings.note: In one may speak of ‘the wax that keeps the scroll closed,’ but in some languages it may be better to use a more general statement, for example, ‘the substance with which the scroll is sealed’ or ‘the substance that kept the scroll closed.’

meanings.def: the impression of a signet ring or seal, primarily indicating ownership
meanings.note: One may also translate this clause in as ‘who do not have the mark on their foreheads which shows that they belong to God.’

meanings.def: the mark or impression made by a seal or stamp
that which confirms or attests to the genuineness of something
the joint connecting the foot to the leg
a degree which falls just short of some point on a scale of extent
meanings.note: The equivalent of this expression in in some languages is ‘all the people in the town came, but some did not’ or ‘only a few of the people in town didn’t come.’

meanings.def: the form or nature of something, with special reference to its outer form or structure
meanings.note: In σχῆμα does not refer to the physical form of the earth but to the way of life in the world. The reference is primarily to culture rather than to physical form. It is possible, therefore, to render this expression in as ‘the way of life in this world is passing away.’

meanings.def: appearance as an element of outward form
to split or to tear an object into at least two parts
meanings.note: In some languages the meaning of σχίζω in may be best expressed as ‘the sky tore’ or ‘there was a slit in the sky’ or possibly ‘there was suddenly an opening in the sky.’ The adverb ‘suddenly’ may provide some of the implications of the splitting involved in the verb σχίζω.

meanings.def: to split or divide into two parts
(derivative of [a] ‘to split, to tear,’ ) the condition resulting from the splitting or tearing
meanings.note: The separation indicated by σχίσμα[a] may be quite different in some languages, depending upon the substance involved, for example, cloth, leather, paper, and clouds.

meanings.def: a division into opposing groups, generally two
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of ‘causing division’ is literally ‘to cause two groups in place of one group,’ but more frequently the equivalent is expressed in terms of attitudes, for example, ‘to cause people to be angry at one another’ or ‘to cause people not to like one another’ or ‘to cause people to think of one another as enemies.’

meanings.def: thick cord formed by twisting or braiding several strands together; made of a variety of materials, including palm fibers, linen, or reeds
meanings.note: The ropes mentioned in would obviously have been rather thick, while in the whip which Jesus made in driving the animals and merchants out of the Temple would probably have consisted of strong cords.

meanings.def: to engage actively and earnestly in some activity over a period of time
to be empty, with special reference to a dwelling
a building where teachers and students met for study and discussion
meanings.note: In it is better to use a translation such as ‘lecture hall’ rather than ‘school,’ since one does not wish to give the impression of the typical classroom situation characteristic of present-day schools. One may translate the relevant context of as ‘every day Paul discussed with people in the lecture hall which belonged to Tyrannus’ or ‘… in a hall where Tyrannus often taught’ or ‘… lectured.’

meanings.def: to rescue from danger and to restore to a former state of safety and well being
to cause someone to experience divine salvation
to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
meanings.note: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

meanings.def: the physical body of persons, animals, or plants, either dead or alive
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction must be made between the body of a living person and a dead body (or corpse). Other languages distinguish between the bodies of persons and the bodies of animals, and frequently the term for a body of a plant is distinct from those referring to persons or animals. Often a term for body consists of a phrase, for example, ‘flesh and bones,’ and in a number of languages a reference to the body is made primarily by referring to the person himself. For example, in (‘has poured this ointment on my body’) the appropriate equivalent may be ‘has poured this ointment on me.’ In certain instances ‘body’ may be rendered as something which is experienced. For example, in ‘glorify God through your body’ may be rendered as ‘glorify God through what you do’ or ‘… do in your body.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σῶμα[a] ‘body,’ ) a person as a physical being, including natural desires
(a figurative extension of meaning of σῶμα[a] ‘body,’ ) believers in Christ who are joined together as a group, with the implication of each having a distinctive function within the group
meanings.note: Though in some languages it may seem relatively strange to speak of an organization of persons as a ‘body,’ it is important to try to preserve in one way or another this figurative meaning of σῶμα, since it plays such an important role in various phases of Paul’s teaching. It is frequently necessary, however, to change the metaphor into a simile, as has already been suggested in the translation of.

meanings.def: a slave as property to be sold, with the probable implicaton of commerce
an entity which corresponds to an archetype or foreshadowing
(an idiom, literally: heavenly body, occurring in the NT only in the plural) the luminous objects in the sky: sun, moon, and other planets and stars
meanings.note: See also.|The phrase σῶμα ἐπουράνιον is a highly generic expression which in the plural is sometimes translatable as ‘lights in the sky,’ but more often than not it may be necessary to identify the various heavenly bodies as ‘sun, moon, and stars.’ In certain contexts one may also wish to identify the planets, often spoken of as ‘wandering stars’ or ‘moving stars’ (reflecting the etymology of the English word planet, which is derived from a Greek word meaning ‘wanderer’). These are, of course, not to be confused with shooting stars and comets in the sky.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to leave home from the body) euphemistic expressions for dying
(derivative of [a] ‘body,’ ) pertaining to a physical body
(derivative of [a] ‘body,’ ) pertaining to a physical body
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret σωματικῶς in as meaning ‘in reality,’ that is to say, ‘not symbolically’ (see ).

meanings.def: pertaining to being real (in the sense of material) in contrast with being symbolic
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: a Christian in Beroea

(an idiom, literally: to heap coals of fire on the head, but the historical background of this idiom is not known, and hence to some extent the meaning is uncertain) to treat someone in such a positive manner as to cause that person to be ashamed or embarrassed
(a figurative extension of meaning of ‘to heap up’; see ) to be engaged intensively and extensively in some activity
meanings.note: It is possible to interpret the usage of σωρεύομαι in as referring to a state of being ‘burdened by sins’ or ‘burdened by the guilt of sin.’
g: to be given over to doing

meanings.def: a leader of a synagogue in Corinth
meanings.note: Many scholars consider Σωσθένης[a] and Σωσθένης[b] to be the same person.

meanings.def: a Christian of Corinth
meanings.note: Many scholars consider Σωσθένης[a] and Σωσθένης[b] to be the same person.

meanings.def: a person who sends greetings in
(derivative of [a] ‘to rescue, to save,’ ) one who rescues or saves
(derivative of [b] ‘to save,’ ) one who saves
to rescue from danger and to restore to a former state of safety and well being
a state of having been saved
the process of being saved
meanings.note: Although it is difficult and sometimes impossible to determine whether σωτηρία refers to the state of being saved () or the process of being saved, in some languages it is obligatory to choose one or the other meaning.

meanings.def: pertaining to divine salvation
the means by which people experience divine salvation
the message about God saving people
to be able to reason and think properly and in a sane manner
meanings.note: The meaning of σωφρονέω[a] is often expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to have right thoughts,’ ‘to have one’s head,’ ‘to have straight thoughts,’ or ‘to have thoughts that do not wander.’
g: to be in one’s right mind

meanings.def: to have understanding about practical matters and thus be able to act sensibly
to instruct someone to behave in a wise and becoming manner
to have understanding about practical matters and thus be able to act sensibly
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand σωφρονισμός in as moderation and sensible behavior (see ).

meanings.def: to behave in a sensible manner, with the implication of thoughtful awareness of what is best
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of the stem σωφρο ‘to behave in a sensible manner,’ ) pertaining to being sensible and moderate in one’s behavior
meanings.note: In a number of languages terms such as [b] (), [b] (),, and σωφρόνως may be rendered as ‘to have right thoughts about what one should do’ or ‘to let one’s mind guide one’s body.’

meanings.def: to have understanding about practical matters and thus be able to act sensibly
to behave in a sensible manner, with the implication of thoughtful awareness of what is best
(derivative of the stem σωφρο ‘to behave in a sensible manner,’ ) pertaining to being sensible and moderate in one’s behavior
meanings.note: In a number of languages terms such as [b] (), [b] (), σώφρων, and may be rendered as ‘to have right thoughts about what one should do’ or ‘to let one’s mind guide one’s body.’

meanings.def: a place for the lodging of travellers
meanings.note: ταβέρνη occurs in the NT only as a part of a place name, Τριῶν Ταβερνῶν ‘Three Taverns’ ().

meanings.def: the Aramaic name of a Christian woman in Joppa whose name was interpreted as ()
a proper and correct order
an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
pertaining to that which has been decided upon in advance
to be sorrowful and complain, presumably on the basis of wretched circumstances
hardship resulting in wretchedness
meanings.note: ‘Wretchedness’ may be expressed idiomatically in some languages as ‘to have nothing’ or ‘to have even one’s shirt in rags.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being in a wretched state, either mentally or physically
pertaining to weighing a talent or 125 Roman pounds of twelve ounces each or approximately ninety pounds (English weight) or forty kilograms
meanings.note: It may, however, be better to use in an expression with a more general sense, for example, ‘great stones of hail weighing almost a hundred pounds’ or ‘… forty kilos.’

meanings.def: a Greek monetary unit (also a unit of weight) with a value which fluctuated, depending upon the particular monetary system which prevailed at a particular period of time (a silver talent was worth approximately six thousand denarii with gold talents worth at least thirty times that much)
meanings.note: In what is important is the relative number of talents or sums of money. In a number of translations the respective amounts are stated in terms of local currency. For example, in English one may speak of five thousand dollars as equivalent to five talents, though in terms of buying power, five talents would be worth much more than five thousand dollars. What is important, however, in this story is not the precise sums of money but the relative amount which was given to the different servants.|The ‘ten thousand talents’ referred to in would be equivalent to millions of denarii. The sum in this parable is perhaps greatly exaggerated, precisely in order to emphasize the vast differences between the two debts. It is also true, of course, that in ancient times persons with extensive mercantile businesses sometimes became slaves as a result of defeat in war, and they were purchased by business syndicates together with their business enterprises, which they would continue to manage.

meanings.def: (an Aramaic word in an emphatic form) the designation for a little girl, probably implying affectionate concern
a room in the interior of a house, normally without windows opening to the outside
meanings.note: In the emphasis is upon the strictly private location of the inner room. In such a context one may translate ‘a strictly private room’ or ‘a small room in the center of the house.’

meanings.def: a room for the storage of valuables
meanings.note: ταμεῖον[b] and θησαυρός[a] may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In θησαυρός[a] is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

meanings.def: an ordered or arranged sequence
a proper and correct order
meanings.note: In τάξις may refer to the orderly manner in which the church at Colossae conducted its affairs or carried on its worship.

meanings.def: kind or type of entity, implying a contrast-comparison to other similar entities
meanings.note: It is possible that τάξις in refers to a kind of priest on the basis of being in a particular grouping or order of priests, but there seems to be no reference to any higher rank or position.

meanings.def: (compare ταπεινός[c] ‘of low status,’ ) pertaining to being discouraged and lacking in hope, with the possible implication of some association with low social status
pertaining to being unpretentious in one’s behavior
meanings.note: In some languages the expression ‘humble in spirit’ or ‘humble in heart’ may be expressed as ‘speaking only soft words’ or ‘without shouting at others.’

meanings.def: pertaining to having low and humble status
pertaining to being meek, with the implication of low status
the quality of humility
meanings.note: The rendering of ταπεινοφροσύνη in as ‘false humility’ is justified in terms of the context, but there is nothing in the word ταπεινοφροσύνη itself which means ‘false.’ It would be possible to render ταπεινοφροσύνη in as ‘subjection to,’ and one might render the entire expression as ‘in abject worship of angels.’ In other languages ‘false humility’ may be rendered as ‘just pretending to be humble’ or ‘appearing to be humble but really being proud.’

meanings.def: pertaining to having the attitude of humility
to cause something to become low in height
meanings.note: For another (probably preferred) interpretation of, see.

meanings.def: to cause something to become level
meanings.note: One might argue that in is to be understood as ‘to be brought low,’ but in contrast with πληρωθήσεται, which refers to filling up valleys, ταπεινωθήσεται should perhaps be understood as referring to ‘leveling off’ mountains and hills. For this other interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: to cause someone to be in a low status
(derivative of [b] ‘humble,’ ) to cause someone to be or to become humble
meanings.note: A strictly literal rendering of ‘he who humbles himself’ could be misunderstood as ‘one who despises himself’ or ‘one who has no regard for himself.’ In the context of it is often important to use an idiomatic expression which will adequately convey the meaning, for example, ‘one who causes his heart to bow down’ or even ‘one who makes his heart small.’

meanings.def: to cause someone to become disgraced and humiliated, with the implication of embarrassment and shame
to live in circumstances regarded as characteristic of low status
meanings.note: In a number of languages ταπεινόομαι in may be rendered as ‘to live like poor people.’
g: to live like those of low status

meanings.def: the quality of unpretentious behavior, suggesting a total lack of arrogance or pride
meanings.note: In some languages humility is expressed indirectly by an idiomatic phrase, for example, ‘to live without strutting’ or ‘to walk without wanting to be noticed.’

meanings.def: the state of low status, with the probable implication of humility
to cause movement, usually as the result of shaking or stirring
meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only: ἄγγελος γὰρ κυρίου κατὰ καιρὸν κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ καὶ ἐταράσσετο τὸ ὕδωρ ‘from time to time an angel of the Lord would come down in the pool and cause the water to move’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to stir up,’ ) to cause acute emotional distress or turbulence
to cause people to riot against
the motion resulting from a mass being stirred up or shaken
meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only: ὁ οὖν πρῶτος ἐμβὰς μετὰ τὴν ταραχὴν τοῦ ὕδατος ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο ‘the first person to go into (the pool) after the water had been moved was healed’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: disorderly behavior of people in violent opposition to authority
meanings.note: This word is found as a variant reading only: λιμοὶ καὶ ταραχαί ‘famines and riots’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: a serious disturbance
a state of acute distress and great anxiety, with the additional possible implications of dismay and confusion
meanings.note: Since τάραχος refers to the type of extreme anxiety which borders on fear, it may be possible in some languages to use a double expression, ‘were greatly distressed and afraid.’

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘Tarsus,’ ) a person who lives in or is a native of Tarsus
the capital of Cilicia in southeast Asia Minor
(derivative of τάρταρος ‘Tartarus,’ ‘hell,’ as a place of torture or torment, not occurring in the NT) to cast into or to cause to remain in Tartarus
meanings.note: In many cases it is confusing to add still another term for a designation of hell by transliterating the Greek τάρταρος, and so most translators have preferred to render ταρταρόω as either ‘to cast into hell’ or ‘to keep in hell,’ thus using for ‘hell’ the same term as is employed for a rendering of the Greek term ().

meanings.def: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
meanings.note: Though τάσσω in has sometimes been interpreted as meaning ‘to choose,’ there seems to be far more involved than merely a matter of selection, since a relationship is specifically assigned.

meanings.def: to cause someone to be in a state involving an order or arrangement
to give detailed instructions as to what must be done
to propose something to someone
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand τάσσω in as meaning ‘to arrange,’ but in it would seem that τάσσω implies not only proposing a date but obtaining an agreement.

meanings.def: to do something with devotion, with the possible implication of systematic, regular activity
male bovine; large ruminant animal with horns and cloven hoofs; used for sacrifice and for meat, as a beast of burden, or for pulling a cart or a plow
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘bull’ is simply a generic term for cattle to which is added a specific designation such as ‘male.’

meanings.def: a place for burying
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand ταφή in the context of as a reference to the process of burial, and one may therefore translate as ‘they used the money to buy the Potter’s Field to bury foreigners.’

meanings.def: a construction for the burial of the dead; often a natural cave or hewn out of bedrock
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between a grave (a hole in the ground in which a corpse is placed) and a tomb (a construction built above the surface of the ground for housing a corpse). In some contexts, however, it may be better to use a more generic expression, for example, ‘places where people are buried’ or ‘places where corpses are placed.’ In it is important to avoid a term which would designate merely graves, for the demoniac who met Jesus was not living down in graves in the ground, but had found some habitation either in burial caves or in tombs constructed above ground.

meanings.def: pertaining to a low probability of occurrence
pertaining to a very short extent of time
meanings.note: In ταχέως refers clearly to the relatively brief period of time before the Galatians abandoned their earlier convictions.

meanings.def: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time
pertaining to a very short extent of time
meanings.note: In ταχινός may refer to the swift nature of the destruction or to the fact that destruction comes after a relatively brief period of time.

meanings.def: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time
a very brief period of time
meanings.note: In τάχος evidently refers to a brief period of time before fulfilling the admonition to leave Jerusalem.
g: quickly (in combination with the preposition ἐν)

meanings.def: pertaining to a very short extent of time
meanings.note: In ταχύ probably refers to the short period of time between Mary‘s hearing about Jesus and her getting up to go out to meet him. It is, of course, also possible to interpret ταχύ in as referring to the rapidity of Mary‘s movement in getting up and going out to meet Jesus.|Again, in the emphasis is upon the brief period of time before Judas is to do what he had set out to do.

meanings.def: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time
a marker of a close relationship between coordinate, nonsequential items
a marker of a close relationship between sequential events or states
a marker of a totality of two closely related elements
a marker of a totality of two closely related elements
a marker of a closely related coordinate set
a particularly strong permanent wall, primarily the wall built around a city for its protection
meanings.note: In a number of languages a translator must make a clear distinction between a wall of a house and a city wall. The wall of a house may be called ‘a side of a house’ and an inner wall ‘a partition in a house,’ while a city wall is often related to terms such as ‘barricade’ or ‘fence.’ Hence, a city wall may be called ‘a fortified fence around a city.’

meanings.def: that which causes something to be known as verified or confirmed
meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘convincing proof’ is rendered as ‘that which causes one to know for sure’ or ‘… with certainty.’

meanings.def: (extension of meaning of [a] ‘child, offspring,’ ) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
meanings.note: It may be impossible to translate τεκνία literally as ‘my children’ in since this might suggest a kinship relationship between the author of 1 John and the people to whom he is addressing his letter. A more satisfactory equivalent in some languages is often ‘my dear friends’ or ‘my dear ones.’

meanings.def: to give birth to a child
meanings.note: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

meanings.def: to give birth to a child
meanings.note: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

meanings.def: one’s immediate offspring, but without specific reference to sex or age
meanings.note: In languages in which there is no generic term for ‘child’ or ‘offspring,’ one may use ‘son’ or ‘daughter’ or ‘son and daughter,’ singular or plural, depending upon the context.

meanings.def: successive following generations of those who are biologically related to a reference person
meanings.note: In the case of [c], τέκνον[b], and [b] (), the reference is not to one’s immediate descendants or offspring (that is to say, to one’s sons or daughters) but to a successive series of such persons, one’s descendants. In some languages such descendants may be called merely ‘the children of one’s children,’ and in other languages one may refer to descendants as ‘those who follow one’ or ‘those who come later.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of τέκνον[a] ‘child,’ ) inhabitants of a particular place
meanings.note: Only rarely can one preserve the figurative significance of τέκνον[c] as a designation of the inhabitants of an area. Readers are too likely to understand such a reference as applicable only to children who live in a particular place. Even the use of a simile does not assist appreciably, since it would be interpreted as likening the inhabitants of an area to children, probably in the sense of their being immature or incapable. For example, the expression the people of Jerusalem like children would probably lead to serious misunderstanding.

meanings.def: (extension of meaning of τέκνον[a] ‘child, offspring,’ ) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate τέκνον in as ‘child,’ since this might immediately suggest that Jesus was declaring himself to be the father of this man. Furthermore, the paralytic was evidently an adult male. A more satisfactory equivalent would be ‘my dear man’ or ‘my dear fellow.’

meanings.def: a person who looks to another as being, so to speak, a father in the faith and thus becomes a disciple of that person
meanings.note: It is also possible that τέκνον in is to be understood simply as an affectionate way of talking about persons who in one way or another are in a dependent relationship to someone (see ).

meanings.def: a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
g: one who has the characteristics of

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: children of light) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also and
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’

meanings.def: to raise a child to maturity by providing for physical and psychological needs
meanings.note: To raise or bring up children may be expressed in a number of different ways, for example, ‘to give food to children,’ ‘to take care of children,’ ‘to be a parent to children,’ ‘to cause a child to become an adult,’ or ‘to make a child become like oneself.’

meanings.def: one who uses various materials (wood, stone, and metal) in building
meanings.note: There is every reason to believe that in biblical times one who was regarded as a τέκτων would be skilled in the use of wood and stone and possibly even metal.

meanings.def: pertaining to being perfect in the sense of not lacking any moral quality
meanings.note: Compare the meaning of τέλειος[e] mature in.

meanings.def: pertaining to being truly and completely genuine
pertaining to having no defect whatsoever
pertaining to that which is fully accomplished or finished
pertaining to being mature in one’s behavior
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret τέλειος in as meaning ‘perfect’ (see ).|In it is possible that τέλειος also means maturity of behavior, but it is usually interpreted as ‘being perfect,’ since the comparison is made with God (see ).

meanings.def: pertaining to an adult human being
meanings.note: Though in τέλειος is to be understood in a literal sense, the context as a whole is figurative.

meanings.def: one who is initiated into a religious community of faith (a meaning which reflects the occurrence of τέλειος as a technical term for persons initiated into the mystery religions)
meanings.note: In a number of languages ‘initiated’ () may be best expressed as ‘to become a member of’ or ‘to become a believer in.’ It is possible, however, to interpret τέλειος in and as mature spirituality or a state of being spiritually mature (see ).

meanings.def: maturity in thought and behavior
a state of perfection, implying some process of maturity
to make perfect in the moral sense
meanings.note: For another interpretation of τελειόω in, see.

meanings.def: to cause to be truly and completely genuine
meanings.note: For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: to bring an activity to a successful finish
to be completely successful in accomplishing some goal or attaining some state
meanings.note: For another interpretation of τελειόω in, see.

meanings.def: to admit into or initiate into faith (possibly based on technical usage in the mystery religions)
meanings.note: It is important that in τελειόω is to be understood in the sense of a functional stage of religious attainment: ‘I have already become an initiate.’ For another interpretation of τελειόω in, see.

meanings.def: to cause to happen for some end result
to attain a state as a goal
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result
to make perfect in the moral sense
to cause to happen for some end result
one who makes possible the successful completion of something
to produce completely mature fruit
(figurative extension of meaning of τελευτάω ‘to end,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death
(figurative extension of meaning of τελευτή ‘end,’ not occurring in the NT) the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death
to bring an activity to a successful finish
(derivative of [a] ‘end,’ ) to occur or happen at the end of a duration
to cause to happen for some end result
to obey as a means of fulfilling the purpose of a rule or standard
meanings.note: The phrase ‘to obey the Law’ in may be rendered simply as ‘to do what the Law says one must do.’

meanings.def: to pay tax or tribute (used absolutely or with a noun complement meaning ‘tax’ or ‘tribute’)
a point of time marking the end of a duration
meanings.note: There are serious problems involved in rendering τέλος[a] in and in similar contexts. In a number of languages one simply cannot say ‘the end will come’; rather, it may be necessary to say ‘that is the finish’ or ‘everything is finished.’ In the context of, however, it may be best to translate ‘God will finish everything.’ The phrase εἰς τέλος in may also be understood as an idiomatic expression involving a degree of completeness (see ).

meanings.def: the result of an event or process, with special focus upon the final state or condition
meanings.note: In some languages τέλος in may be rendered simply as ‘what would happen’ or ‘what would finally happen.’

meanings.def: the purpose of an event or state, viewed in terms of its result
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result
meanings.note: It is also possible to understand the phrase ἕως τέλους in the temporal sense of ‘to the end’ (see ).|It is also possible to understand τέλος in the expression εἰς τέλος in as a temporal expression, with εἰς () as a marker of an extent of time, so that this passage may be rendered as ‘and in the end wrath has come down on them’ or ‘and wrath has at last come down on them’ (see ). In this context ὀργή may very well be translated as ‘punishment’ (), and in many languages it is necessary to indicate the agent of such punishment. The same ambiguity with εἰς τέλος occurs in in the clause εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς, meaning ‘he loved them completely’ or ‘he loved them to the end’ (see ).

meanings.def: payments customarily due a governmental authority
meanings.note: The term τέλος[e] differs from () in being somewhat more generic in meaning. In certain contexts τέλος[e] may refer to various kinds of direct taxes, customs duties, and tribute money, but in contexts such as in which also occurs, τέλος probably refers primarily to customs duties, while refers to a direct poll tax upon all adult males.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: the end) a marker of a conclusion to what has preceded, but not necessarily the conclusion of a text
(derivative of [e] ‘to pay taxes,’ ) one who collects taxes for the government
meanings.note: Since Jews who farmed the taxes for the Romans (that is to say, who paid Roman authorities for the privilege of collecting taxes) were considered traitors to their own people, the term τελώνης has strongly negative connotations in the NT. In any translation of the Gospels it may be especially important to have an adequate marginal note designed to explain the basis for the hostility which many people had toward tax collectors.

meanings.def: (derivative of [e] ‘to pay taxes,’ ) a place where taxes or revenue was collected from those entering a town to sell produce
meanings.note: In the ancient world taxes were primarily of two types: (1) a head tax on each individual (which was relatively small) and (2) revenue or tribute paid for goods and produce brought into an area for sale. The latter was essentially a kind of ‘sales tax,’ but paid by the seller who obviously increased the prices of goods accordingly.

meanings.def: an unusual sign, especially one in the heavens, serving to foretell impending events
meanings.note: In ancient times a portent might consist of a particular arrangement of the planets, an unusual display of northern lights, a conspicuous comet, or a cluster of falling stars. For a discussion of ‘sign,’ see.

meanings.def: a person who sends greetings in
an attorney who accused Paul before Felix
cardinal number, where there are four instances of a countable entity
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘from the four winds’ or ‘from the four directions’ is simply ‘from every direction.’ The Greek expression does not mean from only four specific directions, but rather from every direction.

meanings.def: fourteenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
cardinal number, where there are forty instances of a countable entity
possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a very long period of time
meanings.note: Though most translations render ἔτη τεσσεράκοντα as ‘forty years,’ the expression probably is to be understood as meaning an unusually long period of time. See also discussion at.

meanings.def: (literally: forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
meanings.note: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

meanings.def: (shortened form of [c] literally, forty days) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
meanings.note: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

meanings.def: pertaining to a period of forty years
pertaining to the fourth in a series of days
fourth in a series involving either time, space, or set
a fourth part of an object, series, or mass
meanings.note: For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved, see.

meanings.def: to function as a tetrarch (see )
g: to be the governor of a region

meanings.def: a ruler with rank and authority lower than that of a king and one who ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities
pertaining to having four equal sides and four right angles
a detachment of four soldiers
cardinal number, where there are four thousand instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are four hundred instances of a countable entity
a period of four months
four times as much in quantity
any four-footed animal, either wild or domesticated
meanings.note: A high percentage of languages appear to have no generic term to identify all kinds of quadrupeds whether wild or domesticated. Rather, they tend to make quite clear distinctions between wild and domesticated animals, and therefore it may be necessary to indicate both types in those contexts where the reference is to both wild as well as domesticated animals. For example, one may sometimes speak of ‘animals of the grass and animals of the forest’ or ‘animals of the barn and animals of the mountains.’|In the reference is primarily to wild animals, since for the most part wild animals would be those designated as unclean. However, swine were also regarded as unclean, and they were domesticated.

meanings.def: (derivative of τέφρα ‘ashes,’ not occurring in the NT) to destroy by reducing something to ashes
meanings.note: It is possible to render ‘to reduce to ashes’ as ‘to burn up completely’ or ‘to destroy by fire and leave only ashes.’

meanings.def: an activity involving specialized training and skill
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no special term for ‘craft,’ but an equivalent of this clause in may be rendered as ‘for their work was making tents’ or ‘they earned money making tents’ or ‘they customarily made tents.’

meanings.def: one who customarily engages in a particular craft or occupation
to become liquid, either by melting or condensation
pertaining to a particularly clear or plain visual image
meanings.note: In both διέβλεψεν () and ἐνέβλεπεν () occur. Some scholars assume that the two expressions are essentially equivalent in meaning, but others believe that διέβλεψεν is to be understood as ‘to look intently’ or ‘to focus one’s eyes upon.’

meanings.def: a reference to the size of something (occurring rarely in an absolute sense)
a degree which is comparable to some other expression of degree
meanings.note: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of this expression in may be ‘that earthquake was indeed very great.’

meanings.def: to cause a state to continue
meanings.note: In the reference to ‘girl’ may be either a man’s daughter or a man’s fiancée. Because of the ambiguity of this statement in and in view of the cultural complications involved, especially because of differences of customs in different parts of the world, it is important that translators add a note at this point explaining the difference of interpretation and some of the cultural implications.

meanings.def: to continue to hold in custody
meanings.note: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

meanings.def: to continue to obey orders or commandments
to continue to hold in custody
meanings.note: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

meanings.def: a place of detention
meanings.note: Practically all languages have terms for a jail or a prison, though in some instances a descriptive phrase is employed, ‘a place where people are tied up’ or ‘a place to be chained.’ In some instances, highly idiomatic expressions are used, ‘a place for eating iron’ or ‘a room with rats.’

meanings.def: to continue to obey orders or commandments
a city on the west shore of the Lake of Galilee
the Lake of Tiberias, also known as the Lake of Galilee
the Roman emperor Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus, who ruled from 14 A.D. to 37 A.D.; compare
to put or place in a particular location
to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
to remove or take off clothing
to explain something, presumably by putting forward additional or different information
to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
to cause a state to be
to cause someone to experience, with the implication of subjecting a person to something
(an idiom, literally: to put a plan) to suggest a plan of action
(an idiom, literally: to put into the ears) to listen carefully to, with the implication of not forgetting
meanings.note: For another interpretation of this idiom in, see.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to place in the ears) to continue to bear something in mind
meanings.note: For another interpretation of the idiom τίθεμαι εἰς τὰ ὦτα in, see.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to place in the heart) to store information in the mind, with the implication of its being valuable
g: to treasure up in the heart
to store in the mind as valuable

meanings.def: (idioms, literally: to place in the heart, and: to place in the mind) to engage in the process of deciding
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret the phrase ἐν τῷ πνεύματι in as being a reference to the Holy Spirit and accordingly, the passage may be translated as ‘Paul, led by the Spirit, decided to travel through Macedonia.’

meanings.def: (idioms, literally: to put at someone’s feet) to present something to someone who is reckoned as having superior status or position
(an idiom, literally: to place the knees, a Latinism) to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
meanings.note: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
meanings.note: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’

meanings.def: to give birth to a child
meanings.note: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

meanings.def: to cause the growth and production of plants
to pluck or pick by pulling off or out of
the father of Bartimaeus
to attribute high status to someone by honoring
to determine an amount to be used in paying for something
meanings.note: It would also be possible to translate ‘the price set on him by the people of Israel’ as ‘the amount the people of Israel had agreed to pay for him.’

meanings.def: to provide aid or financial assistance, with the implication that this is an appropriate means of showing respect
g: to provide for the needs of as a sign of respect

meanings.def: honor as an element in the assignment of status to a person
the worth or merit of some object, event, or state
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of ‘value’ is almost always in terms of ‘importance.’ This is particularly true if one is speaking of objects which are normally not bought and sold. Accordingly, one may render this particular expression in as ‘those parts of the body which we think of as not being so important, to these we grant particular importance’ or ‘… we consider as being very important.’|It is also possible to interpret τιμή in as a degree of honor or appreciation (see [a], ).

meanings.def: the amount of money or property regarded as representing the value or price of something
meanings.note: It would be wrong to assume that τιμή in necessarily means ‘a high price.’ The notion ‘high’ comes from the contextual reference to the death of Christ. In, however, the implication is that a price was set and that the payment has been made. If the passive expression in must be made active, one may translate as ‘Christ bought you with a price’ or ‘Christ paid for you.’

meanings.def: compensation given for special service, with the implication that this is a way by which honor or respect may be shown
meanings.note: τιμή[d] in the sense of compensation is related in meaning to [c] to support, to provide for () and τιμή[c] cost (), but in it is also possible to understand τιμή in the sense of τιμή[a] honor, respect (), and therefore one may speak of the elders as receiving double honor.

meanings.def: pertaining to being of considerable value or worth
meanings.note: It is possible to interpret λίθους τιμίους in as a unit which means ‘precious stones’ (see ), but in this figurative context of a foundation, the reference may very well be more general.

meanings.def: pertaining to high status, involving both honor and respect
(derivative of [a] ‘valuable, precious,’ ) a large quantity of costly, valuable possessions
meanings.note: ‘Wealth’ may usually be rendered by ‘the many valuable possessions.’

meanings.def: a friend and coworker of Paul
one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem
to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve
to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve
to experience something bad, often in retribution for some wrongdoing
an interrogative reference to someone or something
an interrogative reference to reason
meanings.note: The expression τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί (literally ‘what for me and you?’) in is an adage meaning ‘for what reason are you saying or doing this to me?’ In some languages it may be preferable to translate as ‘why do you ask me this?’ In one may translate ‘what do you want with us?’

meanings.def: a reference to someone or something indefinite, spoken or written about
(occurring only in a predicate position) a reference to someone or something of prominence or distinction
meanings.note: For a treatment of τις[b] as part of an idiom in, see.

a brief notice used primarily for identification
a friend and companion of Paul
an alternative form of, (, apparatus)
an emphatic marker of result, often associated with exhortation
an emphatic marker of result, often associated with exhortation
pertaining to being of such a kind, often with the implication of a degree of uniqueness or distinctiveness
pertaining to being like some identified entity or event
a reference to that which is of such a kind as is identified in the context
g: of a kind such as this

meanings.note: A literal translation of the phrase ‘whitewashed wall’ is rarely meaningful. meanings.note: In rendering τόπος[b], περιοχή, or γραφή[a], it is often possible to use a rather general term such as the place or the part. meanings.note: In some languages the latter part of this expression in may be rendered as ‘helping in this way and being an apostle’ or ‘helping in this way as an apostle.’ For another interpretation of τόπος in, see.

meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of this expression in may be simply ‘to undertake the work of an apostle’ or ‘to be an apostle in serving.’ For another interpretation of τόπος in, involving a shift in focus, see.

the inhabitants of a place
