In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

meanings.def: small green plants (and in NT contexts referring primarily to green grass in a field or meadow)
meanings.note: In referring to small green plants, a number of languages employ two quite different terms, one indicating specifically grass (with leaves having parallel veins) and the other designating all other types of annual plants (those having branching veins in the leaves). In it is important to employ a term which would include grass and other plants with parallel veins, since the weeds in this passage imitate the appearance of wheat, which does have parallel veins in the leaves.

meanings.def: the young growth of a plant arising from a germinating seed
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between different kinds of ‘sprouts.’ Certain sprouts have only a single blade (for example, grass), while others are double (as in the case of beans). In the reference is to a grass-like plant with a single blade

meanings.def: the husband of Joanna, a follower of Jesus
dust, soil (see also )
meanings.note: ‘Shake the dust from your feet’ may be expressed as ‘kick the dust from your feet.’ In some instances, however, the more appropriate equivalent would be ‘get rid of the dust from your feet’ or even ‘remove the dust from your feet and leave it there.’

meanings.def: to conduct oneself in a particular manner with regard to some person
to behave or to conduct oneself with respect to certain means
to engage in the activity of making use of something
to make use of instruments
meanings.note: In βοηθεία is best regarded as a technical nautical term for supports (ropes or cables) used in aiding a ship in danger (see ).

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to lack,’ ) that which is lacking and particularly needed
that which should be or happen, with the implication of need or lack to be made up
an activity which is needed
a person who is in debt
that which should be or happen, with the implication of propriety
to lack something which is necessary and particularly needed
economic resources, usually implying an abundance of such assets
a generic term for currency, occurring mostly in the plural
meanings.note: It would also be possible to translate ἤνεγκεν τὸ χρῆμα in as ‘he brought the proceeds from the sale.’|In (προσήνεγκεν αὐτοῖς χρήματα ‘he offered them money’) the reference of χρήματα would appear to be cash.
g: money (normally a reference to actual coins)

meanings.def: to make known a divine revelation
g: to reveal a message from God

meanings.def: to give a name or title to
(derivative of [a] ‘to make known a divine revelation,’ ) the content of a divine revelation or utterance
pertaining to having a valid use or function
meanings.note: In some languages, χρήσιμος in may be expressed as ‘helpful.’ For example, ‘it is of no use’ may then be rendered as ‘it isn’t helpful’ or ‘it does not help.’

meanings.def: the sexual function or use of the same or opposite sex
meanings.note: It is often possible to refer to ‘natural sexual function’ as ‘sexual relations with the opposite sex’ or ‘men having sexual relations with women.’ ‘That which is contrary to nature’ may be expressed often as ‘men having sexual relations with men’ and ‘women having sexual relations with women.’ In many societies homosexuality is almost unknown, but there are always ways of speaking about such relations in a euphemistic manner.

meanings.def: to provide something beneficial for someone as an act of kindness
eloquent and attractive speech involving pleasing rhetorical devices
pertaining to being superior for a particular purpose or use
meanings.note: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate as ‘the old wine tastes better’ or ‘the old wine is fine to the taste’ or, in an idiomatic expression, ‘the old wine makes the tongue dance.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being useful and benevolent
(derivative of ‘to act kindly,’ ) pertaining to being kind
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘God is kind’ is ‘God is good to’ or ‘God does what is good for.’

meanings.def: pertaining to that which is pleasant or easy, with the implication of suitability
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is necessary to translate χρηστός by a negativized equivalent, for example, ‘it is not difficult to bear.’

meanings.def: an event or activity which is useful or benevolent
meanings.note: In the case of [b] () and χρηστότης[a], an equivalent often contains an expression meaning ‘to help.’ For example, the expression ‘what is useful’ is often rendered as ‘that which helps people’ or ‘that which proves good for people.’

meanings.def: to provide something beneficial for someone as an act of kindness
(figurative extension of meaning of χρῖσμα ‘to anoint,’ not occurring in the NT) to assign a person to a task, with the implication of supernatural sanctions, blessing, and endowment
meanings.note: It is rare that one can employ a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα in such contexts as and, since ‘to pour oil upon someone’ as a means of conveying a supernatural blessing and endowment for a task is culturally very rare. A strictly literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα as ‘to pour oil upon’ is likely to be interpreted either as an insult or as an event preparatory to setting a person on fire and thus to destroy or to torture. Accordingly, in place of a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα, it is often necessary to employ some such expression as ‘to be appointed by God’ or ‘to be given a special task by God.’

meanings.def: one who is identified as a believer in and follower of Christ
(literally: one who has been anointed) in the NT, titles for Jesus as the Messiah, but in many contexts, and especially without an article, Χριστός becomes a part of the name of Jesus; see )
meanings.note: In a number of languages Χριστός (or Μεσσίας) as a reference to the Messiah occurs in a transliterated form based either on Χριστός in Greek or on Messiah in Hebrew. However, in some languages an attempt is made to represent the significance of the terms Χριστός and Μεσσίας by translating ‘God’s appointed one’ or ‘God’s specially chosen one’ or ‘the expected one,’ in the sense of one to whom everyone was looking for help and deliverance.

meanings.def: (the Greek translation of the Hebrew and Aramaic word ‘Messiah’) a proper name for Jesus; see also
(figurative extension of meaning of χρίω ‘to anoint,’ not occurring in the NT) to assign a person to a task, with the implication of supernatural sanctions, blessing, and endowment
meanings.note: It is rare that one can employ a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα in such contexts as and, since ‘to pour oil upon someone’ as a means of conveying a supernatural blessing and endowment for a task is culturally very rare. A strictly literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα as ‘to pour oil upon’ is likely to be interpreted either as an insult or as an event preparatory to setting a person on fire and thus to destroy or to torture. Accordingly, in place of a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα, it is often necessary to employ some such expression as ‘to be appointed by God’ or ‘to be given a special task by God.’

meanings.def: to extend a state or an event beyond an expected time
to spend a considerable period of time in a state or activity
g: to spend a long time in

meanings.def: an indefinite unit of time (the actual extent of time being determined by the context)
points of time consisting of occasions for particular events
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no general term for ‘time’ or ‘occasion.’ In some contexts it is simply not necessary to have such a term. For example, in rendering one may translate ‘when the harvest comes, I will say to the reapers’ or ‘when people begin to harvest, I will say to the reapers.’ In other contexts, a term which normally refers to some unit is employed in a generic sense, as in the case of Greek ὥρα which means literally ‘hour’ but is frequently used as a generic expression for a point of time, as in. In χρόνος may often be rendered by a generic expression such as ‘day,’ for example, ‘when it was almost the day for God to keep his promise.’ In the case of, the nearness of the time may be indicated as ‘very soon the Son of Man will be handed over.’|Though it seems quite ordinary in English for one to speak of ‘time coming’ or ‘… drawing near,’ this type of figurative usage is impossible in many languages. The equivalent may be simply ‘will soon be’ or ‘is about to happen.’ The expression οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου (literally ‘my time has not yet come’) in denotes that it is not yet the occasion for a particular event (see καιρός in and compare ) but that it will soon be. In these contexts the expression may be rendered as ‘there is still time’ or ‘I will soon do it.’ In and (οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ ‘his time has not yet come’) the reference is to the occasion of his eventual arrest, implying that it will indeed happen.

meanings.def: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present
to experience a duration of time
meanings.note: In a number of languages χρονοτριβέω may be best rendered as ‘to remain for a time’ or idiomatically as ‘to sit for a time.’

meanings.def: gold (the most highly valued metal in the ancient world)
meanings.note: Terms for gold are widespread throughout the world even as the presence of gold or knowledge about gold is likewise almost universal. Therefore, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘gold.’

meanings.def: object or objects made of gold
meanings.note: Gold jewelry may be referred to as ‘pretty things made out of gold,’ but rather than say that the woman was ‘covered with gold ornaments’ (), it may be far more appropriate to say ‘she wore many gold ornaments’ or ‘many gold ornaments were fastened to her clothes.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: silver and gold) a generic expression for currency
pertaining to the wearing of a gold ring
chrysolite (yellow quartz or yellow topaz), golden yellow in color (see )
chrysoprase, a greenish type of quartz (see )
gold (the most highly valued metal in the ancient world)
meanings.note: Terms for gold are widespread throughout the world even as the presence of gold or knowledge about gold is likewise almost universal. Therefore, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘gold.’

meanings.def: gold money, gold coin
(derivative of [a] ‘gold,’ ) pertaining to being made or consisting of gold
to be adorned with gold objects
meanings.note: In the phrase κεχρυσωμένη χρυσίῳ involves semantic redundany or what one may also speak of as semantic reinforcement.
g: to be covered with gold adornments

meanings.def: skin or surface of the human body
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction must be made between the skin of an animal and the skin of a human being. A further distinction is often made between skin as a part of a living animal or human and skin which has been removed from the body and presumably made into leather (see, ).

meanings.def: pertaining to a disability that involves the imperfect function of the lower limbs
dry land, in contrast with the sea
meanings.note: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

meanings.def: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration
meanings.note: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.
g: district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)

meanings.def: a rural area in contrast with a population center
meanings.note: A rural area is often identified by a term or phrase meaning ‘extension of fields’ or ‘place of field after field’ or ‘area of farms.’

meanings.def: land under cultivation or used for pasture
the inhabitants of a region
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of ‘a region going out’ (), since the term for ‘region’ cannot substitute for ‘the people of the region.’ Therefore, all such references must be made personal.

meanings.def: to move on from one place to another
meanings.note: In translating it may be necessary to add an element which suggests swallowing, since something which enters a person’s mouth does not automatically go into the stomach. Accordingly, it may be necessary to translate ‘anything that goes into a person’s mouth and is swallowed goes on then into his stomach.’ It would also be possible to say ‘anything that goes into one’s throat goes on then into a person’s stomach.’|In χωρέω[a] appears to be used figuratively in the statement ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐμὸς οὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν ‘my word makes no progress in you,’ but it is also possible to interpret χωρέω in this context as referring to an adequate place, for example, ‘my word finds no room in you’ (see ).

meanings.def: to be a quantity of space
to be able to accept a message and respond accordingly
meanings.note: It is possible to understand χωρέω in as meaning ‘to be able to understand.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [b] ‘to have room for,’ ) to be friendly disposed toward someone
to separate objects by introducing considerable space or isolation
to dissolve the marriage bond
meanings.note: Expressions for divorce are often based on terms meaning literally ‘to send away,’ ‘to separate from,’ or ‘to leave one another.’ However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are employed, for example ‘to send him off with his clothes,’ ‘to untie the knot between them,’ or ‘to throw away her hearthstones.’|Some persons have attempted to make an important distinction between ἀφίημι in and χωρίζω in on the assumption that ἀφίημι implies legal divorce, while χωρίζω only relates to separation. Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

meanings.def: to separate from, as the result of motion away from
to cause to be at a distance
land under cultivation or used for pasture
a marker of negatively linked elements
meanings.note: It would be wrong to restructure to read ‘he made everything in all creation,’ for in the Scriptures God is spoken of as the Creator, but the creation was done ‘through the Word.’ If one must restructure, it may be possible to say ‘he was involved in everything that was created’ or ‘he took part in creating everything.’|In χωρίς does not specify the particular relationship but only indicates the lack of relationship or involvement. This, of course, is negated by οὔτε, so that one may translate this portion of as ‘nor is woman without some relationship to man, nor is man without relationship to woman.’ In view of the overall context, one may then render the passage simply as ‘woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.’ In some languages, however, it may be necessary of ‘wife’ and ‘husband,’ since terms for ‘man’ or ‘woman’ may be wrongly interpreted in a strictly erotic sense.|Because of the double negation of, in some languages it may be necessary to employ a positive equivalent, for example, ‘for woman is dependent on man and man is dependent on woman’ or ‘a wife is dependent on her husband and a husband is dependent on his wife.’|The expression ‘apart from any works’ in may be rendered in some languages as ‘and what a person does, does not count’ or ‘and this is not because of what one does.’

meanings.def: to something which occurs separately or by itself
the direction between north and west
meanings.note: The difference in expression is due to designating the directions of the wind either as the direction from which the wind comes or the direction toward which the wind blows. See commentaries.|In rendering directions which are not cardinal points, one may often use a variety of expressions, for example, ‘between north and west’ or ‘from the north a little west’ or ‘to the north of west.’ A high percentage of languages designate directions by reference to the rising and setting of the sun. Accordingly, may be rendered as ‘a harbor that is open to the sea to the left of the setting sun and to the right of the setting sun.’

meanings.def: to sing songs of praise, with the possible implication of instrumental accompaniment (in the NT often related to the singing of OT psalms)
g: to sing a song of praise

meanings.def: a song of praise (in the NT probably a reference to an OT psalm)
an individual who pretends to be a close member of a socio-religious group but is not (see,, and )
meanings.note: It is frequently necessary to make explicit the full implications of ‘false brother’ by translating ‘one who pretends to be a fellow believer in Christ but is not.’
g: one who only pretends to be a fellow believer in Christ

meanings.def: one who claims to be an apostle but is not
(derivative of ‘to lie,’ ) one who utters falsehoods and lies
meanings.note: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’

meanings.def: one who teaches falsehoods
meanings.note: In rendering ψευδοδιδάσκαλος, it is important to avoid an expression which will simply mean that a person pretends to be a teacher and is not. What is important here is that the individual teaches what is not true.
g: teacher of what is a lie

meanings.def: one who utters falsehoods and lies
meanings.note: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’

meanings.def: to communicate what is false, with the evident purpose of misleading
meanings.note: The Greek term ψεύδομαι and the English equivalent ‘to lie’ involve more than simply telling what is not true, for this could occur without an intent to deceive or mislead. ψεύδομαι, therefore, involves not only the communication of a falsehood but also the intent to deceive.

meanings.def: to provide a false or untrue witness
meanings.note: A person who gives false witness may deceive in two aspects, (1) in pretending to have been an eyewitness to an event and (2) in saying what is not true, but the focal element in ψευδομαρτυρέω is the fact that what is said is not true.

meanings.def: (derivative of ‘to testify falsely,’ ) the content of what is testified falsely
(derivative of ‘to testify falsely,’ ) one who testifies falsely
meanings.note: The focal element in the evidence provided by a ‘false witness’ is the fact that what is said is not true.|It is also possible that such a person has pretended to have been present and thus an eyewitness of an event, but that is not the focus of the meaning. In fact, a false witness may have been present but at the same time may later provide false evidence as to what took place. It is possible to render ψευδόμαρτυς in some languages as ‘one who pretends to know about something but is really lying in what he says’ or ‘one who lies about what he pretends to have seen.’

meanings.def: one who claims to be a prophet and is not and thus proclaims what is false
(derivative of ‘to lie,’ ) the content of a false utterance
one who claims to be the Christ or the Messiah but is not
pertaining to being falsely or wrongly called by a name
(derivative of ‘to lie,’ ) the content of a false utterance
meanings.note: It may be important in some instances to restructure the semantic relationships in this clause in, for example, ‘if my lie makes God’s truth appear more glorious.’

meanings.def: one who utters falsehoods and lies
meanings.note: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’

meanings.def: to touch by feeling and handling, implying movement over a surface
meanings.note: There are a number of problems involved in the rendering of, for there are several radical shifts in figurative meaning. The specific reference is to ‘the Word of life’ which seems like a purposely ambiguous reference to Jesus Christ. The statement about ‘hearing the Word’ would seem to refer to a message, but the reference to ‘seeing’ implies some type of object. To emphasize the concrete nature of such an object (namely, the person of Christ), this statement about ‘touching’ is included, but in some languages a reference to ‘feeling and handling’ might imply quite a wrong connotation or even improper activity, particularly if the object involved is specifically a person.

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to touch, to feel,’ ) to make an effort, despite difficulties, to come to know something, when the chances of success in such an enterprise are not particularly great
to count up or calculate a total
meanings.note: This process of ‘adding up the number of the beast’ involved calculating the total based upon the numerical values of each of the letters of the name. For another interpretation of ψηφίζω in, see.

meanings.def: to come to understand the meaning of something by figuring it out
meanings.note: The third person imperative form ψηφισάτω in is extremely difficult to render in some languages, and even in English the expression ‘let him understand’ is quite misleading, since it might imply permission rather than polite command. In some languages the equivalent of this third person imperative is an expression such as ‘should understand’ or ‘ought to be able to understand.’ For another interpretation of in, see.

meanings.def: a small stone, possibly used for casting a vote or as a magical amulet
meanings.note: A number of different suggestions have been made as to the reference of ψῆφος in. Some scholars believe that the white ψῆφος indicates a vote of acquittal in court. Others contend that it is simply a magical amulet; still others, a token of Roman hospitality; and finally, some have suggested that it may represent a ticket to the gladiatorial games, that is to say, to martyrdom. The context, however, suggests clearly that this is something to be prized and a type of reward for those who have ‘won the victory.’

meanings.def: providing harmful information about a person, often spoken in whispers or in low voice, with the implication that such information is not widely known and therefore should presumably be kept secret
one who habitually engages in gossip
a small piece of food (normally bread)
meanings.note: In,, and (apparatus) the reference is to small crumbs or pieces of food that might fall from the table. In some languages an equivalent is ‘a small bit of food’ or ‘a tiny bite of food.’|This word is found as a variant reading only: ἐπιθυμῶν χορτασθῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων τῶν πιπτόντων ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης ‘being glad to eat the scraps that fall from the table’ (apparatus).

meanings.def: a small piece of food (normally bread)
meanings.note: In,, and (apparatus) the reference is to small crumbs or pieces of food that might fall from the table. In some languages an equivalent is ‘a small bit of food’ or ‘a tiny bite of food.’

meanings.def: the essence of life in terms of thinking, willing, and feeling
meanings.note: It is also possible to render ψυχή in as ‘purpose’ or ‘desire,’ for ψυχή focuses upon the total psychological being involved in struggling for the faith.|ψυχή[a] is often glossed as ‘heart’ or ‘desire.’ Compare the following: περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου ‘my heart is sorrowful even to the point of death’; ἵνα μὴ κάμητε ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ἐκλυόμενοι ‘so do not let your hearts become discouraged and give up’ (for ψυχή in the idiom κάμνω τῇ ψυχῇ, see ); ἀλλ ὡς δοῦλοι Χριστοῦ ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς ‘but with all your heart, do what God wants, as slaves of Christ’. In these passages, however, ψυχή refers really to the entire being of a person, so that may very well be rendered as ‘my sorrow is so great it almost kills me.’ may also be rendered as ‘so do not let yourselves be discouraged and give up,’ and may be appropriately rendered as ‘but with your whole being, do what God wants, as slaves of Christ.’|The meaning of ψυχή in the sense of the person as an individual is treated under [c] () as, for example, in (εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ‘you will find rest for yourselves’).|Even in those contexts in which ψυχή refers to existence beyond death, it may be referring figuratively to the person. For example, in (οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην one may translate ‘you will not abandon my soul to Hades’ or ‘you will not abandon me to the grave.’|It is important to distinguish ψυχή[a], signifying a psychological faculty, from [b], meaning ‘physical life, life principle’ (). Note, for example, the occurrence of [b] in (διϊκνούμενος ἄχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος ‘it cuts all the way through to where physical life and spirit meet’). Note also the occurrence of [b] in αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς, καὶ ὁλόκληρον ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἀμέμπτως ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τηρηθείη ‘may the God who gives us peace make you holy in every way and keep your whole being - spirit, life, and body - free from all fault at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ’).|In certain contexts ψυχή would appear to be in contrast with () and () as, for example, in ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐν ὅλω τῇ καρδίᾳ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλω τῇ ψυχῇ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλω τῇ διανοίᾳ σου ‘you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and soul and mind’). Because of the three terms, some have insisted that there must be at least three quite different parts of human personality. Others, however, have concluded that instead of being three parts of personality, these are only three different perspectives which one may employ in thinking about or describing human personality. Still others would contend that the use of the three terms,, ψυχή and, only emphasizes the totality of human personality, and no clear-cut distinctions can possibly be made. Certainly the referents involve considerable overlapping. One could translate with complete justification as ‘you shall love the Lord with all your heart and life and mind.’ In fact, in many languages it is impossible to distinguish between, ψυχή, and, and therefore it may be necessary to translate as ‘you shall love the Lord your God with all that you desire and with all that you think’ or ‘you must love the Lord your God with all your being.’

meanings.def: the existence of a human being, or other living creature, sustained by the presence of air to breathe and food to eat
meanings.note: In rendering ψυχή in it may be necessary to indicate more precisely the relationship between ‘to seek’ and ‘life,’ for example, ‘they seek to destroy my life’ or ‘they seek to cause me no longer to live.’|In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘life.’ It may therefore be necessary to change all passages which speak of ‘life’ into a corresponding expression using a verb-like form meaning ‘to live.’

meanings.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘inner self, mind,’ ) a person as a living being
(an idiom, literally: living soul) any living creature, whether animal or human
meanings.note: Though the phrase ψυχὴ ζωῆς is highly generic in meaning, its specific reference in is to creatures of the sea, and therefore in most languages one must translate simply ‘fish’ or ‘that which lives in the sea.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to be tormented in soul) to experience mental torment involving sorrow mixed with anger
g: to be tormented in one’s heart

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to cause a person’s attitude to be bad against) to cause someone to have hostile feelings of dislike toward someone
(an idiom, literally: to become tired in spirit) to gradually lose one’s motivation to accomplish some goal
(an idiom, literally: to acquire one’s soul or to acquire one’s life) to save oneself from grave danger or death
(an idiom, literally: to hand over life) to expose oneself willingly to a danger or risk
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘risking one’s life’ is ‘exposing oneself to death’ or ‘showing that one is willing to die’ or ‘walking into the danger of dying.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: to do something with regard to one’s life) to save or preserve one’s own life
(an idiom, literally: a sword goes through one’s soul) to feel the intense pain of sorrow
(an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
meanings.note: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’

meanings.def: pertaining to being material or physical, especially in relation to life processes
meanings.note: In some languages, however, it is impossible to translate σπείρεται in as ‘sown,’ and one must therefore translate this expression as ‘when buried, it is a physical body.’

meanings.def: pertaining to human nature (possibly contrasting with [c] and [c] ‘natural, human,’, in focusing somewhat more on so-called higher endowments of personality)
meanings.note: For another interpretation of ψυχικός in, see.

meanings.def: (derivative of [a] ‘inner self,’ ) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, in contrast with that which is under the control of God’s Spirit
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘unspiritual’ is simply ‘one who is not guided by God’s Spirit’ or ‘one who does not live in accordance with God’s Spirit.’ For another interpretation of ψυχικός in, see.

meanings.def: pertaining to being cold, as of weather conditions
pertaining to being cold, as of objects and masses
(a figurative extension of meaning of ψύχομαι ‘to become cold,’ not occurring in the NT) to diminish significantly in intensity
to cause someone to eat
(a figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to feed, to give to eat,’ ) to give away or dole out, with the probable implication of bit by bit
a small piece or bit of bread
meanings.note: In it may be necessary to use a phrase such as ‘a broken-off piece of bread’; otherwise the inference might be that the ψωμίον was simply a scrap or crumb of bread. In some languages the appropriate equivalent of ψωμίον in this type of context is ‘a bite of bread.’

meanings.def: to rub something under pressure to make it smaller
meanings.note: By rubbing the heads of wheat, the disciples were able to remove the chaff and the so-called ‘beards,’ the stiff projections arising from each kernel. This process would be equivalent to threshing and would thus be condemned by the Pharisees as work on the Sabbath.

meanings.def: a marker of direct address (functionally equivalent to the traditional vocative)
meanings.note: Often left untranslated.

meanings.def: the last in an inclusive series beginning with (), implying an all-inclusive sphere of authority and high status
meanings.note: For a discussion of the relationship of ω to and its different translations, see.

meanings.def: a position relatively near the speaker, writer, or viewpoint person
meanings.note: Though ὧδε[a] and ἐνθάδε may seem to be rendered in some contexts as to here or hither, the semantic component of movement is not found in ὧδε[a] or ἐνθάδε, but in other words in the context indicating movement.

meanings.def: a reference to a present object, event, or state in terms of its relevance to the discourse
a particular melodic pattern with verbal content
meanings.note: In a number of languages it is impossible to use a combination such as ‘to sing a new song.’ One can, however, often use an expression such as ‘to sing with new words’ or ‘to utter a new song.’|In employing terms for ‘to sing’ or ‘song,’ it is important to avoid an expression which will apply only to some restricted type of music, for example, translated hymns using melodies from Western Europe.

meanings.def: to experience pains associated with giving birth
g: to suffer pain in connection with giving birth

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to suffer birth pain,’ ) to suffer intensely (similar to birth pain)
meanings.note: πάντα δὲ ταῦτα ἀρχή ὠδίνων ‘all these things are simply the beginning of great suffering’, a reference to the so-called Messianic woes (see ).

meanings.def: to experience pains associated with giving birth
g: to suffer pain in connection with giving birth

meanings.def: (figurative extension of meaning of [a] ‘to suffer birth pain,’ ) to suffer intensely (similar to birth pain)
shoulder
meanings.note: In rendering the reference to the shoulder is often incorporated into the verb expression itself, that is to say, in a number of languages there are different verbs indicating the manner of carrying, for example, in the hands, on the shoulders, on the head, on the back, etc.

meanings.def: to acquire possessions or services in exchange for money
any kind of egg, but primarily a chicken egg
meanings.note: In some languages a distinction is made between eggs produced by birds and those produced by such other animals as reptiles and amphibians. In this one NT context the reference is, of course, to the egg of a hen.

meanings.def: points of time consisting of occasions for particular events
meanings.note: In a number of languages there is no general term for ‘time’ or ‘occasion.’ In some contexts it is simply not necessary to have such a term. For example, in rendering one may translate ‘when the harvest comes, I will say to the reapers’ or ‘when people begin to harvest, I will say to the reapers.’ In other contexts, a term which normally refers to some unit is employed in a generic sense, as in the case of Greek ὥρα which means literally ‘hour’ but is frequently used as a generic expression for a point of time, as in. In χρόνος may often be rendered by a generic expression such as ‘day,’ for example, ‘when it was almost the day for God to keep his promise.’ In the case of, the nearness of the time may be indicated as ‘very soon the Son of Man will be handed over.’`|Though it seems quite ordinary in English for one to speak of ‘time coming’ or ‘… drawing near,’ this type of figurative usage is impossible in many languages. The equivalent may be simply ‘will soon be’ or ‘is about to happen.’ The expression οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου (literally ‘my time has not yet come’) in denotes that it is not yet the occasion for a particular event (see καιρός in and compare ) but that it will soon be. In these contexts the expression may be rendered as ‘there is still time’ or ‘I will soon do it.’ In and (οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ ‘his time has not yet come’) the reference is to the occasion of his eventual arrest, implying that it will indeed happen.

meanings.def: an indefinite unit of time which is relatively short
meanings.note: For languages which have no term for an indefinite unit of time which is relatively short, it may be necessary to approximate the time span in the context, for example, ‘for several months’ or possibly ‘for a year or so.’

meanings.def: one-twelfth of a day, measured from sunrise to sunset (in any one day the hours would be of equal length, but would vary somewhat depending on the time of the year)
meanings.note: Since the hours were counted beginning at sunrise, the seventh hour would be approximately one o’clock in the afternoon. For other references to numbered hours, see,,, and.

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: much hour) a point of time relatively late in view of the circumstances (late in the afternoon or in the evening)
(an idiom, literally: the present hour) an emphatic reference to a point of time which is simultaneous with another point of time
pertaining to being beautiful, often with the implication of appropriateness
pertaining to a point of time which is particularly appropriate
meanings.note: It is also possible to interpret in as implying something which is fine (see ).

meanings.def: to produce a howling or roaring sound, typically of wolves, but also applicable to lions
meanings.note: For languages spoken by people who are acquainted with the behavior of lions in the wild, there should be no difficulty in obtaining a specific term applicable to lions. In the case of other languages, one can often use a more generic expression such as ‘to make a great noise.’

meanings.def: a relatively weak marker of a relationship between events or states
a marker of discourse content, whether direct or indirect
meanings.note: The marking of direct and indirect discourse varies greatly from language to language. In some instances there is no marker at all; in other cases one marker precedes and another follows. In still other instances a repetition of an expression of speaking occurs at the end of a quotation, whether direct or indirect. In a number of languages written usage differs appreciably from spoken usage, because intonation so often marks introduced discourse in the spoken form of a language.

meanings.def: a marker of an event indicating how something took place
a point of time which is prior to another point of time, with the possible implication in some contexts of reason or cause
an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
a marker of cause or reason, implying the special nature of the circumstances
a marker of purpose, with the implication that what has preceded serves as a means
a marker of result, often in contexts implying an intended or indirect purpose
a degree which approximates a point on a scale of extent, either above or below
a relatively high point on a scale involving exclamation
meanings.note: In a number of languages an expression of high degree in an exclamation can only be reproduced as an expression of intensive degree in a non-exclamatory form. For example, the statement in ‘how great must the darkness be!’ must be rendered in a number of languages as ‘the darkness is very, very intense’ or ‘it is very, very dark there.’

meanings.def: (an idiom, literally: as to speak a word) an expression used to introduce an alternative form of expression as an interpretation of what has been said
a point of time subsequent to another point of time, with an interval as brief as possible
meanings.note: In some languages the equivalent of ‘as soon as possible’ would involve a verb meaning ‘to hurry’ or ‘to do something quickly.’ Accordingly, may be rendered as ‘with instructions from him that Silas and Timothy hurry to join him.’

meanings.def: (an Aramaic expression meaning ‘help, I pray’ or ‘save, I pray,’ but which had become a strictly liturgical formula of praise) a shout of praise or adoration
meanings.note: In ὡσαννὰ τῷ υἱῷ Δαυίδ may also be rendered as ‘praise to you, Son of David’ or ‘we praise you who are the Son of David’ or ‘… a descendant of David.’|Though for many early Christians, and especially those of Jewish background, ὡσαννά would be known from its Aramaic background as meaning ‘help’ or ‘save,’ nevertheless, its association with liturgical expressions involving praise and exaltation resulted in the expression acquiring quite a different significance; hence, a phrase such as ‘hosanna in the highest’ became equivalent to ‘praise be to God.’ For growing numbers of Christians without Jewish background, ὡσαννά probably acquired much the same meaning as it now has in English.

meanings.def: a marker of similarity which approximates identity
a relatively weak marker of a relationship between events or states
a degree which approximates a point on a scale of extent, either above or below
a prophet of Israel
a somewhat more emphatic marker of similarity between events and states
a somewhat more emphatic marker of similarity between events and states
a marker of result, often in contexts implying an intended or indirect purpose
a marker of purpose, with the implication that what has preceded serves as a means
the state of having acquired an advantage or benefit
to provide assistance, with emphasis upon the resulting benefit
to be successful in accomplishing some goal, with the implication that such might be useful
pertaining to a benefit to be derived from some ob ject, event, or state
meanings.note: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘benefit’ or ‘beneficial’ is often ‘that which helps.’ Accordingly, in one may render ἡ γὰρ σωματικὴ γυμνασία πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστὶν ὠφέλιμος as ‘physical exercise helps to a small extent’ or ‘if one exercises one’s body, that helps a little.’
